Chapter 1 — The Last Climb

[Quiet, precise narration; restrained institutional pressure and careful new beginnings]

Brom knelt in the pine needles with his right hand open, like a man about to push a stuck door.

"Ready."

Cael was not ready, but he set his left forearm across his chest anyway, braced it, and nodded.

It was the third morning out of Ardenmere, and the fire was down to a red eye in the ashes. Lira was still rolled in her blanket at the edge of the clearing, awake and pretending not to be, because watching the two of them fail before breakfast had become one of her small pleasures on the road. Cold air came down off the hills above the camp and smelled of wet stone.

Brom's palm met his forearm.

The push always started slow. Brom let a little Iron Skin harden through his hand first, so that the contact arrived like a flat stone rather than a palm, and then he leaned. The force came in steady and even, a fraction of a real strike, the kind of weight a man could count.

Cael waited for it to arrive in full. That was the first thing the road had taught him: the fragment did nothing with force that was still on its way. It woke only when the force was already his, already inside the bone, and by now the waking had a feel he could recognize, a tightening low in the chest, a sense of something gathering.

He reached for it.

The force gathered and began to turn, and for a quarter of a heartbeat he held a piece of Brom's push the way a person holds water in cupped hands. Then he had to decide where it went.

It wanted to go down.

He felt it slide toward his left knee along the same lazy path it had taken two days ago, toward the joint that still remembered being used as a drain. The memory was so exact that his whole body flinched from it before his mind had finished recognizing what it was.

He let go.

The gathered piece spilled out of him harmlessly, and his forearm bore what was left of the push like any arm. Brom eased off.

"You dropped it."

"It was going to my knee again."

"You're sure."

"Same road as last time." Cael flexed the knee and found only the faint ache that had been there since the first day, fading, with nothing new on top of it. "It wants the nearest joint. If I don't give it somewhere better before it moves, it picks for itself."

Brom considered that the way a smith considers a bar of iron, turning it slowly before deciding what it was good for.

"Then give it somewhere better first."

"That's the whole problem."

"No. That's the whole answer. The problem is you're deciding late." He set his hand again. "Again."

They went on until they had made twelve tries between them, and most of the twelve were failures of one kind or another. On the next two nothing caught at all; the fragment sat in him like a word on the tip of the tongue, present and unreachable, and Brom's push simply arrived and left. On the fourth he caught something and sent it the wrong way, not into the knee this time but into his own right shoulder, the one the Reydan bout had already used hard. It flared so sharply that he hissed through his teeth and Brom stopped at once.

"Shoulder."

"Shoulder." He rolled it. Under the new hot line he could feel the old complaint, the one that announced itself on certain angles. "Better than the knee."

"Better how?"

"The shoulder's already paying. It's an account that's open."

Lira's voice came from the blanket. "That is the worst thing I have ever heard a person say about his own body."

"You're awake."

"I'm always awake. Keep going. I want to see you do it right once before I have to walk all day next to someone sulking."

He did it right on the seventh try.

The force arrived, and he waited until it was in the bone, and before it could pick a road of its own he chose one for it — out, back along the line it had come in, into Brom's own braced arm — and held that choice steady while the fragment gathered.

A quarter of the push went home.

It went back into Brom's wrist with a small, solid knock, like a door shutting in another room. Brom's eyebrows lifted. Under the Iron Skin his forearm had felt it, and Cael knew he had felt it, because nobody read where weight had gone better than Brom did.

Then the bill came.

It always came the same way, running up through the shoulder and across the breastbone in a band of heat and pressure, as if someone had laid a hot iron bar along his collarbones and leaned on it. For two breaths he could not fill his lungs, and he waited them out on his knees in the pine needles.

"There," Brom said quietly. "Quarter."

"Quarter," Cael managed.

He caught a quarter twice more before they broke camp, on the tenth try and the twelfth, and each of those cost what the seventh had cost, no more and no less. That was oddly comforting. A price that stayed the same was a price he could plan around. The tries in between went nowhere, because he had reached a breath too early while the push was still coming and the fragment had simply not answered. He was almost grateful for those; a failure that did nothing was the cheapest lesson the fragment had to offer.

Lira was sitting up by then, blanket around her shoulders, eating the last heel of yesterday's bread.

"Three in twelve."

"Three in twelve."

"On a push Brom could do while asleep."

"He'd have to be asleep for me to catch more than a quarter of it."

She grinned. "That's honest, at least."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He wrote it up while Brom kicked dirt over the fire.

The Power Log lay open on his knees, a binder now, its rings stiff with cold. Once it had been a single slim notebook, and he had added pages so many times since then that the original cover was mostly a memory; he had long ago given up pretending the binder was tidy. It was not tidy. It was honest, and those had turned out to be different things.

Every fragment had its own section, and every section used the same four headings, because the same four questions had turned out to matter every time: Function, which was what it did; Benefit, which was what it was good for; Cost, which was what it took from him; and Integration, which was how much of it answered when he called. He had not so much invented the format as surrendered to it, because every other way of writing about the fragments had eventually collapsed into bragging or panic, and the four headings allowed neither.

He turned to the newest section and wrote.

Compression-adjacent. Road session, third morning. Function: catches force already inside the body and sends it back out. Must wait for the force to arrive. Reaching early gets nothing. Benefit: none in a real fight yet. Cost: shoulder and breastbone, two breaths of not being able to breathe. Same price on every success. Integration: partial. Three of twelve. A quarter of a slow push each time.

Then he added the line that mattered most.

If I don't choose the road before the force moves, it chooses the nearest joint. Knee on day one. Shoulder today. Choose first. Always choose first.

When he had read it back, he turned to the front of the binder, where the oldest notices were copied out, and went through the four confirmed fragments as a carpenter runs a thumb along his chisels before starting work, not to learn anything, only to know they were all still there.

Wind-adjacent was first, and Lira's. It was an evasion framework he had once needed a full second to assemble and now did without thinking, reading a strike off an opponent's body a half-beat before it landed and moving him into the space beside it. Its range was the length of a fight. Its price was fatigue, and a choice of direction he had to make before he moved, and against faster opponents it read less. He had shown it on the circuit a hundred times.

Pressure-adjacent was second, a redirect borrowed from a Bronze-tier fighter named Feryn who had beaten him fairly. It had three clean uses mapped, each paid for in the right shoulder, and it worked at contact and nowhere else. Nobody outside the three of them had ever been told it existed.

Iron-adjacent was third, and Brom's: a pressure-read along the skin that told him where a person's weight was about to go. It worked at contact and out to a few paces, thinner with distance and thinner still with speed, and it was quiet enough that people who watched him fight saw only that he was rarely surprised.

Compression-adjacent was fourth. Days old. Bad at everything.

Its notice was copied out on the page in front of him exactly as it had arrived, the night after his last circuit bout.

FRAGMENT ACQUIRED
unnamed — Compression-adjacent. Duration: sustained. Integration: partial.
Tier equivalent: unknown.
Note: force absorption component. Damage redirect, contact range.

Nothing in it had changed overnight. Contact range. Partial. Unknown.

Behind the four sections sat a fifth page, set apart from the rest, with a date, a short account of an afternoon in Brom's sparring circle, and a single line underneath.

Session nine. Could not reproduce. Still don't know what that was.

He did not add anything. He never did. That page was for reading, not for writing; he shut the binder and got to his feet. His knee did not hurt and his shoulder did, which by the log's arithmetic was an improvement, and he decided to count it as one.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The road climbed all morning, through scrub at first and then low oak, and then out into open hill country where the grass had been cropped short by sheep and drystone walls stitched the slopes into uneven squares. The sky was high and pale. Early autumn had put a cool edge on the wind without yet taking the green out of anything.

They walked three abreast where the road allowed it and single file where it didn't, and they had been doing it for so long that none of them noticed the switching anymore.

"How many of them will be Copper?" Lira asked.

She asked Brom, not Cael, because Brom was the one who had grown up close to an academy's way of thinking; Velmere had been a family that kept tutors. He thought about it for fifty paces.

"Most. Same as everywhere. Six in ten of anyone who fights for a living is Copper, and most people who Kindle into Copper stay there."

"Most adults."

"Most adults. They get to Rank Four or Five, the gains slow down, they stop pushing. They get a trade. They have a family. Copper's enough to work a dock or run a stall. Nobody needs Iron to bake bread."

"I'd like to see Iron bread."

"You'd break a tooth."

Cael knew the numbers, as everybody in Valdris knew them. But he had never heard them said by someone who had been raised to think of them as a ladder his family expected him to climb. Ten ranks in each tier, with Rank Ten as the threshold. And to cross from one tier into the next you needed two things, the rank you earned through use and a formal evaluation at a registered Arbiter station that confirmed it. Copper, Iron, Bronze, Silver, Gold, and after Gold the tiers became history and then rumor. Most people stopped on the first rung. A quarter made Iron, the journeyman's tier of professional fighters and serious tradespeople, the ones who kept pushing. One in ten made Bronze. Silver was the kind of tier that got your name said in other cities.

"Greyvane's a minor-tier academy," Brom went on. "They take Copper and Iron and turn out Bronze, if they're lucky. A Silver graduate would be a good year for them."

"Quenna is Silver."

"Quenna is faculty. They buy faculty." Brom shrugged. "They can't buy students. Students go where the prestige is."

Lira kicked a stone off the road, and it bounced down the slope through the sheep, who ignored it.

"Then what are we?"

She meant herself and Brom, who were both Copper on paper and both carried an honest rating from Vell's circuit ledger that said something else.

"Iron-equivalent," said Brom.

"Which means what, at an academy?"

It was a fair question, and Cael had been chewing on it since Ardenmere. On the circuit, Iron-equivalent had meant what it said: Vell rated you by what you did on her floor against whoever stood across from you, and if you beat enough Iron-tier fighters, consistently, her ledger called you Iron-equivalent, whatever your registry document said. It was a rating of results, and the circuit trusted results.

"It means you can beat Iron fighters," he said slowly. "It doesn't mean an Arbiter has said you're Iron. It doesn't give you an Iron rank. It doesn't move you up the ladder."

"So it means nothing."

"It means something. It just means it to the people who were watching."

Lira walked on without answering.

"I'm Copper," she said. "On paper. I'm going to walk in that gate as Copper, and people who never saw me fight are going to read the word and think they know what it means."

"Yes."

"I hate that."

"I know."

"I'm going to hate it less than I would have a year ago, though. That's the strange part. I can feel myself hating it less."

She was looking straight up the road with her chin a little high. Cael thought of himself beside her: Iron-equivalent by the same honest ledger, because he had beaten an Iron Rank Eight in front of six hundred people, and on paper no tier at all, no rank, not even Copper, only a word on his registry file that was not a tier but a classification the registry had never known what to do with. He had stopped needing to say that out loud months ago. He noticed now that he had also stopped needing to think it every hour, and that was new, and he filed it away to write down later.

At the midday rest Lira tried, for perhaps the fifth time since Ardenmere, to get Brom to show her a declaration.

"Just one. The first one. The one you got at Kindling."

"No."

"I showed you mine."

"You described yours. You never showed me."

"Describing is showing."

"It isn't," said Brom, unbothered, eating cold barley from a tin with every sign of contentment. "You know it isn't."

Cael knew it too. Declarations were the language an Arbiter used, and every practitioner received them from Kindling on: a small glowing sigil only you could see, and then words in a form only you could read, telling you what your Path had just given you at your new rank. They were the private record of a person's growth, written in a hand nobody else ever saw. People did share them, brothers sometimes, or married couples, or a teacher and a student who had trusted each other for years. But you did not ask, any more than you would ask to read someone's letters, and you did not show unless showing meant something. Lira knew all of this perfectly well. She asked because she liked watching Brom refuse.

"Tell me the shape, then. Not the words."

Brom set the tin down.

"There's a header. It names the Path and the tier and the rank. Then a line with the ability's name in brackets. Then a sentence about what it does, sometimes two. How far it reaches. When it works. That's all." He picked the tin up again. "It's very plain. People think it'll be poetry. It's more like a receipt."

"A receipt," Lira repeated, delighted.

"A good receipt. It tells you exactly what you paid for."

Cael found himself listening harder than the conversation deserved. His own notices were nothing like that. A declaration named a Path, a tier, a rank and an ability; his notices began with two words in capitals, Fragment Acquired, and gave every ability the same name, which was no name at all. Where a declaration would name a Path, his gave an adjacency, near something and never the thing itself, and where a declaration gave a tier and rank, his said only Tier equivalent: unknown. A declaration was a receipt. His notices were more like a note left on a table by someone who had been in the room and gone.

"What's yours look like?" Brom asked him suddenly.

"You've read the log."

"I've read your copies. I've never asked what it's like when one arrives."

It was a very Brom question, Cael thought. Brom had been studying him for most of a year and had never once asked something he could find out by watching.

"Quiet," he said. "No sigil. Nobody's there. It's just suddenly in front of me, like a line someone already wrote. The words don't change if I look away."

"Like a ledger."

"Like a ledger."

Brom nodded slowly. "Then you got Vell's version and I got the receipt."

Lira laughed out loud, and a pair of sheep looked up at her in mild disapproval. Cael laughed too, more surprised by it than anything, because for as long as he had carried the notices he had thought of them as a lack, a declaration that had come out wrong. Brom had just set the two side by side as if they were simply two different kinds of record. He would think about that later. Probably in writing.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

The last stretch of the climb came in the early afternoon, and the road grew better as it rose. Somebody had cut the verges back within the month, there was new gravel in the ruts, and the wall beside them had been rebuilt in places with stones paler than the old. Cael noticed all of it, because maintenance meant somebody whose job was maintenance, and a place that kept its road kept other things too.

A hill town showed itself in pieces: slate roofs, smoke from cooking fires, and somewhere below them a mill wheel turning slowly with a deep wooden groan they heard long before they saw it. The wind carried cut grass and wet stone and, under those, bread.

Lira lifted her head like a hound.

"Later," said Brom.

"I didn't say anything."

"You smelled it. I watched you smell it."

Above the town the road forked, one branch bending down toward the roofs and the other climbing on.

"Town or academy?"

"Academy," said Cael and Brom together, and Lira laughed and was ten paces up the hill before either of them moved.

Greyvane came over the brow of the hill a quarter-mile later, and it was small.

That was Cael's first clear thought. In the weeks since Quenna had first said the name he had built the place much larger in his head, and here instead was a wall of old grey stone, plain and weathered, laid in the coursing of something far older than any school. A gate of iron-strapped oak, newer, set into it. And beyond the wall a few roofs, a training yard with a wall of its own, a long building with uneven windows, and further back a clean-cut building three floors high, the only thing in sight that looked as if it had been built on purpose for what it was now.

That was all.

A bell rang somewhere inside, once, slow and unhurried, marking some hour of the day that had nothing to do with them.

Cael stopped walking. He did not mean to; his feet simply stopped, and Lira and Brom went on two paces before they stopped as well and looked back at him.

"What."

"Nothing."

"You're doing the thing."

"I'm not cataloguing." He was, and he knew he was. The wall was old waystation stone; the gate was two generations newer at most. There was a single clerk's booth set into the gatehouse instead of a guardroom, which meant the place logged people far more often than it stopped them. "I'm looking."

"Those are the same thing for you."

"Not always."

She waited, and Brom waited, and below them the mill wheel groaned. He tried to name what he was feeling and could not, and decided that was all right. The afternoon light was coming in low across the wall and turning the old stone almost gold, and there had been a time, not so long ago, when he would not have stopped for that. Ardenmere had taught him to look at a place before deciding what it meant.

"It's small," he said finally.

"It's small," Lira agreed.

"I like that it's small."

Brom kept his eyes on the wall while they climbed another twenty paces. "It's the size it is. It isn't pretending. That's rarer than big."

They walked the last quarter-mile together, and at the gate the clerk had a list.

She was a woman of about forty with ink stains on two fingers of her writing hand and the patient face of someone who copied things all day. She did not get up. She ran a finger down the page in front of her, stopped, and read the names back without looking at them.

"Brom, standard. Lira, re-certification. And Cael, on the observer track." Then she did look up, at each of them in turn, fitting faces to the ink. "The three of you are on my list. Go past the yard. The first door is intake, and they know you're coming."

That was all she said, and it was enough.

Cael lingered at the booth for a breath after there was any reason to. It was a small thing, and he knew it. Every institution in the world kept lists; Denvash had kept one, the certification office had written his name on a schedule before he'd ever asked to be written down. The Compact had him in a registry that ran the length of the continent. But those had all been the same kind of list, a door opening because a rule said it had to, and this was a different kind. Someone in this building had looked at his name weeks ago and decided it belonged on the far side of the gate, and had written it down in ink before he arrived, trusting that he would come.

Most of his life he had been handled as paperwork, walking into rooms where he had to prove he existed before anyone would hand him a chair.

His name was already here.

"Cael," Lira said quietly, from inside the gate.

He realized he had stopped again. "Coming."

He walked through behind them, and the gate's shadow passed over him and was gone. On the far side the yard opened up, swept and empty, with chalk lines faint on the packed earth, and a bell rang again at a different pitch from the first. He did not know what that bell meant. He would learn, and he noticed, with something close to surprise, that he wanted to.

For once he did not reach for the notebook. He only noticed the feeling and let it sit there unwritten.

Lira would have called it a miracle.

Chapter 2 — Three Lines

[Quiet, precise narration; restrained institutional pressure and careful new beginnings]

The intake room had three desks, and that told Cael most of what he needed to know before anyone spoke.

It was a low old room built from the same grey stone as the wall, with ceiling beams close enough that Brom ducked under the first one out of caution and then looked faintly embarrassed when he saw he hadn't needed to. Four other arrivals sat on a bench along the back wall with their bags at their feet, and a window let the afternoon in so that the light lay across the floorboards in a long pale square. Each of the three desks had its own clerk and its own line, and above each line hung a small painted board.

Standard Enrollment.

Re-certification.

The third board was blank.

"That's you," Lira murmured.

"It might be for transfers."

"Transfers go in the standard line. I asked the gate woman while you were having your moment." She nudged him. "Blank board. That's you."

He looked at it, a board somebody had hung up and then not known what to paint on, and thought it was the most accurate sign anyone had ever made about him.

Brom went first, because his line was empty. His clerk was a brisk young woman with her sleeves rolled to the elbow. She took his papers, scanned them, and turned them face up on the desk in one smooth motion: a Copper-tier certification from a registered Arbiter station, Iron Skin Path, and a clean record of two seasons' documented circuit work with Vell's stamp at the bottom of every page.

"Standard. Good."

She wrote and stamped. She asked him two questions, his age and whether he had any injuries the floor instructors should know about, and entered the answers in a neat column, checked something on a list, and stamped again. Cael, waiting on the bench, counted the time without meaning to, because he counted most things without meaning to.

Eleven minutes.

At the end of them the clerk reached into a drawer and set a small metal disc on the desk in front of Brom, coin-sized and stamped with the academy's crest, a tower above a road, very simply cut.

"Your enrollment tag. It opens the training hall, the lecture wing, the residence wing and the library. Keep it on you. Supper's at the seventh bell, and orientation for new students is tomorrow after the first. Upper corridor of the residence wing, third door on the left. Your name's on it."

Brom looked at the tag. "That's it?"

"That's it."

He picked it up and turned it once in his fingers, and his face did something Cael had not seen it do before. On anyone else it would have been a smile. On Brom it was a kind of quiet astonishment, as if he had put his weight on a step expecting it to creak and it had simply held.

He came over to the bench and held the tag up between two fingers.

"Eleven minutes," said Cael.

"You counted."

"I count everything."

Brom sat down beside him and looked at the tag again.

"Two years I've been the complicated one. Every room. Every hall. My family, the circuit, all of it. You can't just be a Copper Iron Skin from a good estate who walked away from the estate; there's always a question after." He shook his head slowly. "She didn't ask the question."

"Maybe she didn't know there was one."

"Maybe there isn't one here."

He put the tag in his pocket, took it out again a moment later as if it might have changed its mind, found it hadn't, and put it away properly.

"I'm going to find my room. I've never had a door with my name on it."

He left, and Cael, watching him go, was smiling.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Lira's line took most of an hour.

Her clerk was an older man with half-moon spectacles and the slow, careful manner of someone who had handled difficult paper before, and he did not hurry. From a box at his elbow he took a thin file, and it took Cael a moment to understand that it was her Fenmark file. It had arrived here before she had, because academies talked to one another about the students they had thrown out. The clerk laid it open beside a printed sheet of rules and compared the two line by line, moving a finger down each in turn, making a small mark now and then.

Lira stood in front of the desk with her arms folded. There was a chair, and she did not sit in it, and she did not look at the file. Cael knew that stance. He had seen her take it across a sparring circle a hundred times while she waited out an opponent she hadn't finished measuring, weight even and shoulders loose and nothing given away.

The bench emptied and filled again. A boy with a Blade Path crest on his collar went through the standard line in nine minutes, and a tall girl was sent away to fetch a missing letter and came back flushed.

At last the clerk set a single sheet on the desk and turned it to face her.

"I'm required to read this aloud, each clause, and you'll confirm you understand it."

"I can read."

"I know you can. It's the procedure."

She nodded once.

From where he stood, Cael could read the heading whether he wanted to or not. Acknowledgment of Prior Standing. The clerk read it in a flat, even voice: that Fenmark Academy had ended her enrollment; that the record of that ending was to stand as written; that her candidacy for re-certification at Greyvane was granted on the understanding that she accepted that record as accurate and did not dispute it as a condition of entry.

"Do you understand the clause?"

"Yes."

"There is a separate process for a formal dispute, should you wish to pursue one later. It is not connected to your enrollment here and would go through channels outside this academy." He tapped a small unmarked box at the bottom of the sheet. "You may note an intention to dispute. It doesn't affect your candidacy."

"I understand."

He turned the sheet toward her a little further and laid a pen beside it, and she read it herself, slowly.

Her jaw did most of the talking. A small muscle worked at the hinge of it, tightening and easing and tightening again, while the rest of her face stayed perfectly still. Cael understood that he was watching two years of a thing being held down by force to a size that would fit an intake desk. She had spent those two years refusing to say expelled without saying wrongly right after it; he had heard her do it in Ardenmere to strangers who had not even asked.

She picked up the pen and signed, and she did not mark the box.

The clerk blotted the signature, put the sheet in the file and the file in the box, and gave her a disc like Brom's, crested like his, with one difference: under the crest, small and neat, someone had stamped a single raised dot. She looked at the dot, then put the tag in her pocket without a word, and when she came over to the bench she sat down beside Cael and stared at the opposite wall.

"Well."

"You didn't mark the box."

"No."

"You could have."

"I know." She breathed out. "I could have marked it and fought about it later. I could have stood there and told that nice man exactly why Fenmark was wrong; I've had the speech ready for two years." She turned her head and looked at him. "I'd rather have a bed in this place than be proved right on paper about what Fenmark did to me at fourteen. That's new, for me. Wanting the one thing more than the other."

"How does it feel?"

She was quiet a long time.

"I was ready for it to be Fenmark all over again. That day, standing in a room while somebody reads you what you are." She looked down at her hands. "It doesn't. It feels like setting a pack down at the end of a road. I didn't know how much it weighed until it was on the ground."

Then she stood up abruptly, the way she did when a feeling threatened to become a conversation.

"Go and see what they make of you. I'll be on the wall outside."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Nobody called him forward, because there was no line for him to stand in. Instead, as the old clerk finished stacking Lira's box, a door at the side of the room opened and Quenna came through it.

She was as he remembered her from the Ironyard: about forty, dark hair cut short and plain, a grey coat with no ornament on it at all, a leather folder under one arm, and the faint air of a woman who had been arguing with someone in another room and had won, but only just.

"Cael. Come and sit."

She did not hand him to a clerk. She led him to the third desk, under the blank board, and sat on the far side of it herself. He registered that it could be read two ways — as a courtesy, because she had brought him here and meant to see him through it, or as a warning, because he was the kind of case that could not be trusted to a clerk. After a moment he decided it was both, and that both were reasonable.

"This will take some time, and I'm going to be honest with you about why. There isn't a form for you."

"I noticed the board."

The corner of her mouth moved. "The carpenter asked what to paint on it. Nobody could tell him."

The afternoon went in pieces. Papers came to the desk in twos and threes: a letter of acceptance; a copy of his circuit record with Vell's stamp; a form that asked for his Path and tier and rank, which Quenna read, frowned at and set aside; another that asked the same questions in different words; and a third, older, with a line reading registry document attached, which led to a long, quiet search through her folder. His registry document was in there. She had obtained a copy from somewhere, and he saw the corner of it as she leafed past, and the word in brackets, before she covered it again.

Twice she excused herself and went through the side door, and through it, faintly, he heard her voice and another voice, low and patient, going back and forth. The words did not carry, but the tone did, and it was the tone of two people trying very hard to fit a large thing through a small opening without breaking either.

A boy from the kitchen brought tea on a tray. Cael thanked him, held the cup in both hands, and forgot to drink it. The patch of sun from the window crept down the back wall, crossed the floorboards toward the desk legs, and went thin. The other clerks finished their days; the man with the half-moon spectacles nodded to Quenna on his way out, and the young woman who had enrolled Brom gave Cael a look he read easily as better you than me. The bench emptied. Somebody, somewhere, lit a lamp.

He did not mind, and that surprised him. He had imagined this afternoon a dozen times on the road, and in every version he had been angry by now, or frightened, or both, and instead, watching Quenna come back from her second argument with a fresh sheet in her hand and her mouth set, he understood that what he was looking at was not a wall and not someone trying to keep him out but a building straining, in good faith, to find words for him. He had been described in bad faith before, in Denvash and in a market square and in a hundred small moments on the circuit before Vell's ledger gave people something better to go on. Good faith was slower. It was worth a whole afternoon.

"Here," Quenna said at last.

She turned a long printed form toward him. It had his name at the top in a clerk's careful hand, a seal pressed into the bottom corner, and a blank signature line with a pen laid neatly beside it. Above the signature line was a box labeled Category of Enrollment.

The box said unclassified observer.

He read it.

Beneath the category, in smaller type, a printed note explained what the category was. It was reserved for any prospective practitioner who has not yet undergone formal Kindling assessment. Such students were usually children whose families had asked for early schooling before their certification appointments. A Path, a tier, a rank, any record from an Arbiter: the category conferred none of those. What it did confer was a seat in lectures, training under supervision, and academic standing.

He read the category line again.

Unclassified observer.

He reached for the tea, found it had gone lukewarm, and set it down without drinking.

He read the category line a third time, and the gloss under it. Has not yet undergone formal Kindling assessment.

The tea was colder when he looked at it again. He did not reach for it this time.

"I underwent it." His voice came out quieter than he meant it to. "I was fourteen. Denvash. There's a record."

"There is."

"Then this is wrong."

"There's a record, and the classification on it is one the Compact's own schedule never defines." She said it evenly, without softening it; she had never softened anything she'd said to him. "This category exists for anyone without a standard classification issued by an Arbiter. A child who hasn't Kindled has no standard classification. Neither do you. Yours isn't standard. The schedule has no line for what yours is."

"So you found a gap."

"I didn't make it. It was already there. I'm only using it."

He looked at the line again. "It says something that isn't true. In ink."

"Every word on that page is used correctly, and it will bear any reading anyone cares to give it. That matters; that's what protects you." She leaned forward slightly. "What holds up less well is the purpose. The people who drafted the provision were thinking of twelve-year-olds whose parents wanted them to sit in on lectures. They were not thinking of you. Someday someone will read this form more carefully than a clerk does, and they will ask about the purpose."

"So someone will come and read it properly."

"Yes."

She did not hesitate over it, and he was grateful.

"And then?"

"Then we need to be established fact before they get here." She laid one finger on the seal. "A student with a monthly assessment record. Public, dated, signed by the people who watched. Each month you spend here, passing, in ink, makes the case against you a little harder to make."

"And if they argue anyway?"

"Then they'll have to argue their way past a stack of dated pages first. I've backed worse odds than these, Cael. I don't back anything I expect to lose."

His eyes stayed on the form. He thought of the four other people the registry had ever written his word against, four cases, all of them gone within weeks, whose names he did not know and whose number he had carried since he was fourteen the way he carried his own heartbeat. This form would not make him a fifth. It would make him something else, not a known problem with a file but an error the registry had never been asked to hold. Progress, of an odd sort. He was not sure it was better. As far as he could see, no other door stood open.

He picked up the pen and signed in the careful hand he used for the Power Log, the slow, square hand he had learned to keep for anything he meant to stand behind.

The ink dried. Neither of them mentioned how far the words sat from the truth. Quenna knew it, he knew it, the empty room seemed to know it, and saying it aloud would not have made the page more honest.

Then Quenna did something he had not expected. She lifted the signed form, and he saw that it was three sheets, not one, pressed together with a thin layer of copying paper between them. She separated them with practiced fingers. The top sheet went into her folder. The second she slid across to him. The third had a line printed across its head that the others did not — Registry Copy, for Notation — and she initialed it in the margin, folded it twice, and put it into a long brown envelope already addressed in a clerk's hand to the regional registry office.

"What's that?"

"Routine." She sealed the envelope. "Any enrollment that attaches a registry document goes up to the regional office to be noted against the file. It leaves with the town post on the third day."

"Does anyone read them?"

"Usually a clerk enters a line and files the sheet." She set the envelope on the corner of the desk, square to the edge. "Usually."

He looked at the brown envelope, with his name inside it and the hollow word on his form, sitting on a desk in a room that was getting dark, and did not like it there at all.

Quenna took a disc from her folder and slid it across to him. It was the same size as Brom's, but it had no crest; where the crest should have been, someone had stamped a hollow circle, a ring with nothing in the middle.

"Provisional access. It opens what Brom's opens. Anyone who checks it will learn that the reason isn't theirs to ask."

He turned it over. The back was blank.

"Welcome to Greyvane." There was something under the flatness of it that was almost gentle. "Supper's at the seventh bell. You've missed the sixth. I'd eat."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Lira and Brom had claimed the low wall beside the intake door, and they had left a space between them that was exactly his width, with the evening's last light lying along the stones. He saw it from twenty paces off and it did something to his chest. They had sat on walls like this in more towns than he could count, and he had never once had to ask where to sit.

He sat.

"Well?"

"I'm an unclassified observer. In writing. With a signature."

Brom considered that. "That isn't you."

"No."

"Do you mind?"

Cael gave it an honest answer, because an honest answer was the only kind he trusted himself to give about something that mattered.

"Less than I expected. The words hold up; Quenna's right about that. I've spent so long being something the paperwork had no name for that one more wrong form hardly shows." He paused. "I'm still going to write about it."

"Two pages," said Lira. "Possibly three."

"The form's not what interests me," said Brom, "for whatever that's worth."

"What is?"

"That they built anything at all." Brom looked across the yard at the old wall going grey in the dusk. "Most places don't build you a door. They let you walk around the outside until you work out there isn't one. This one's the wrong shape. Fine. You've been getting through wrong-shaped things since I met you."

Lira stared at him. "Did you just say something wise before supper?"

"I'm hungry. It loosens me up."

"Show me the tag," she said to Cael, and when he held it out she tilted it toward the last of the sky so that the hollow circle caught the light. "A ring with nothing in it."

"Quenna says it means the reason isn't theirs to ask."

"It means please don't ask." She handed it back, sounding very slightly pleased. "Mine has a dot. Brom's has a tower. You have a hole. We're a set."

Brom took his own tag out and checked that the tower was still there. It was.

A bell rang somewhere beyond the training yard, not the seventh, Cael could tell by the pitch, but some earlier signal in a rhythm he had not learned yet. He got the binder out anyway and wrote it plainly, without decoration.

Enrolled. The word is doing a lot of work.

He looked at the line, and then added a second one beneath it, smaller.

It isn't doing it alone.

Lira read it over his shoulder without asking, as she always had, and said nothing, only bumped his arm with hers once. And then the seventh bell rang, and the three of them got up and went to find out what an academy fed people.

It was barley: barley and onions and a little mutton, ladled out in a long low room that had plainly been a stable once, its old hay door bricked up but still outlined in the wall. Students sat in loose groups at trestle tables, most of them already talking over empty bowls, and a few looked up when the three of them came in, and most didn't.

Brom ate two bowls with an expression of deep contentment.

"It's honest food," he said, when Lira looked at him. "It doesn't pretend to be anything."

"It's porridge with ambitions."

"It's barley. Barley has never once lied to me."

"Neither has a rock, and I don't eat those either."

Cael ate. It was hot and plain and there was enough of it, and he was more tired than he had known. Three days of walking and a whole afternoon of sitting still had left him hollow in a way the barley filled quite well. Afterward the three of them climbed to the residence wing, where the corridors bent wherever the old building had needed them to bend and the doors were of six or seven different ages and woods, each with a small painted board beside it. Brom's was across the corridor from his, and Lira's was two doors down. Passing the stair, Cael noticed a roster pinned to the wall that showed empty rooms in two other halls, which meant that someone had put the three of them together on purpose, someone who had decided before they arrived that they were a unit. Quenna, almost certainly. He did not mention it. He suspected the others had noticed too, and that none of them wanted to say it aloud and make it smaller.

"Good night," said Lira at her door.

Brom stood in front of his own door a moment before opening it, read his name on the board, and went in and shut the door softly behind him.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Bed, desk, shelf: the room held those and very little else, between whitewashed walls, and its one window showed him the blank grey side of the training yard's wall, which asked nothing of anybody. Cael set his pack down, sat on the bed, and listened: feet on a stair, a latch somewhere, voices through the wall too faint for words, a door closing, water moving in a pipe. In a week he would know which latch was which and whose feet those were. He had done it in Ardenmere, and at Hesk's long before that, without ever thinking of it as work. Tonight he knew none of them. Tonight they were only the sounds of a place that had decided to have him.

He lit the lamp and took out a sheet of paper. He had made a promise in a boarding house in Ardenmere with Hesk's letter open beside him — I'll write when I arrive — and he had arrived, and that was all there was to it.

He wrote slowly.

Hesk —

I'm here. Greyvane is small, smaller than I imagined. There's an old wall, older than the school, and a hill town below it with a mill and a baker Lira had already smelled from a quarter-mile away.

The gate clerk had our names on a list, all three of them. I don't know how to explain why that mattered so much. I think you'll understand without my explaining it.

He paused over the next part and thought about leaving out the form. He did not leave it out. Hesk had never once asked him to make anything smaller than it was.

They've enrolled me under a category meant for children who haven't Kindled yet. It's called unclassified observer. It isn't true, and everybody at the table knew it wasn't. The woman who brought me here says the words will hold up, and I think she's right. I signed it. I want you to know I signed it with my eyes open.

Brom got through intake in eleven minutes and didn't know what to do with himself. Lira signed a paper that said Fenmark was right about her, and she says it felt like putting something down. I'm not sure yet what it felt like for me. I'll tell you when I know.

You told me to find more people who have seen me clearly and haven't left. I haven't found new ones yet. But I came through the gate with two, and there's a woman here who argued with someone in a back room all afternoon to find a word for me. That might be the start of a third.

I'm well. The shoulder still complains on certain angles.

I'll write again after the first assessment.

Cael

It was not long, but Hesk's letters were never long either. He folded it, wrote the Denvash direction on the outside, and set it on the desk to go down to the town. It would leave, he realized, on the same third-day post as Quenna's brown envelope. He sat looking at the folded letter with that thought, two pieces of paper with his name on them going down the same hill in the same bag to very different readers.

Then he opened the binder to the back pages, where he kept the things that were not fragments, and thought about the board above the third desk, the blank one, a carpenter asking what to paint and nobody knowing. He thought, for the first time with no fear in it at all, that he would rather be a blank board somebody had bothered to hang than a painted one in a building that wanted him gone.

He wrote that down too. Then he blew out the lamp and lay in the dark, listening to the building he didn't know yet, and fell asleep before he had learned a single sound.

Chapter 3 — The Ledger

[Quiet, precise narration; restrained institutional pressure and careful new beginnings]

He worked on the question all through breakfast, because it was not a hard question to ask but it was a hard one to ask well. He had learned that the first shape a question took was usually the shape that made it easiest to answer badly.

Why did you take me? was the wrong size: too small. It invited a small answer, a kindness or a shrug, the sort of thing that wears off in a hard season. What do you get out of this? sounded too sharp for a first meeting with the man who ran the building he slept in. He tried four more versions in the margin of the binder while Lira stole the crust off his bread and Brom ate his porridge with slow, serious attention, and every one of them leaned too far toward himself.

He found it on the walk across the yard.

Why did this academy take the risk?

Not me, but the risk. A man could tell a kind story about a boy, and it was much harder to tell a kind story about a decision that had to be paid for. If Cael asked about the decision, he might be shown the accounts.

He wanted the accounts.

He had to sit through orientation first. It was held in the main hall after the first bell for the eleven students who had arrived that week. It was run by a senior instructor with a carrying voice and a long wooden pointer that he never once pointed at anything. He used it instead to tap the floor at the end of each rule, as if nailing the rule down. Cael sat at the end of the second bench with Lira on one side and Brom on the other, and wrote.

The bells came first. "First bell is assembly, and any scheduled assessments," the instructor said, and tapped. "Second and third are lectures. Fourth is the midday meal. Fifth and sixth are the training floors. Seventh is supper. Eighth is lamps out in the residence wing." Tap. "Miss the seventh and you'll find out what the eighth tastes like, which is nothing." Then the rule about the residence wing after the eighth bell, which was that there was no residence wing after the eighth bell, only your own room, and anyone found in the corridors would be asked politely where they were going and then, less politely, why.

Then the standings.

"Greyvane keeps a board. You'll find it in the formal yard, and every student with full standing is on it." Tap. "You are ranked by your record this term, within your cohort. Not by your tier, and not by your rank, but by what you do on our floors against our students in bouts we schedule and record. A Copper student with a good term can sit above an Iron student with a poor one. It happens often enough that the Iron students learn to take it seriously."

A boy on the front bench put up his hand. "Who's first?"

"An Iron Rank Two in his third year. Glass Path. He has been first for some time." Nothing changed in the instructor's voice, but something in it suggested that every intake asked the same thing. "You'll meet him. If you want his place, the board is open."

Lira made a small, interested sound under her breath, and when Cael glanced at her she was looking at nothing in particular with the face she wore when she was setting something aside for later.

"Advancement." Tap. "Some of you will reach Rank Ten in a tier while you're with us. When you do, your instructor will certify the rank, and you will walk down the hill to the certification station in the town, which is a registered Arbiter station, and you will be evaluated. If the evaluation confirms it, you cross. If it doesn't, you come back and keep working, and nobody here will hold it against you." Tap. "Rank is earned on our floors. Tier is confirmed down there. We do not confuse the two, and neither should you."

Cael wrote that down carefully — Rank is earned. Tier is confirmed. — and underlined confirmed. He knew there was a station in every town of any size; he had walked into one in Denvash at fourteen with Hesk's hand on his shoulder and walked out with a word in brackets. He had not known until this moment that this hill town had one too, a half-hour's walk below the wall, where children from the observer track would go to be Kindled and students from the standard track would go to be measured, and where he would never, so far as he could see, have any reason to go at all.

He was looking at his own tag. The hollow circle. Nothing to certify and no tier to confirm.

Brom shifted on the bench beside him, very slightly, so that their shoulders touched. He did not look over. He only stayed there, a solid weight, until the instructor had moved on to the rules for the library.

At the end the tracks were read out, standard and re-certification and transfer, and then, after the smallest pause, "Observer," and two names: a girl Cael did not know, and his own. Somebody on the front bench turned around to look, and then a second person did, and Cael looked back at them pleasantly until they turned away again.

"You enjoyed that," Lira murmured.

"A little."

"Good. You'll need to."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The stair to the provost's office climbed the inside of the old building in a tight square, and every step had been worn hollow in the middle by people going up to be told things. Cael counted thirty-one of them. At the top the door was already open. He knocked on the frame anyway, because an open door was not the same thing as an invitation, and he had learned the difference in other buildings.

"Come in. Sit. There's one chair, and it belongs to whoever's standing in the doorway."

The first thing Cael saw was the window. It was tall and narrow and took up most of the wall behind the desk, and it looked down on the training yard, so that a man sitting here kept his back to the door and his face to the students. Cael noted that before he noted the man. A room would tell you where its owner's attention went, if you let it.

The rest was plain. There was a desk with a blotter, a pen and three letters squared against one corner, and a single chair across from it. A man who kept only one visitor's chair did his talking one person at a time. Along the wall to the left ran a shelf of thin brown books, all of a size and all the same tired colour.

Naveth sat with both hands flat on the blotter. He was past sixty, long in the face and lean everywhere else, grey at the temples and grey through the rest, and his skin had the weathering of somebody who had spent years under a bigger sky than this hill's. He did not get up.

"You're my observer."

"Cael, sir."

"I know. My signature's on your acceptance, under Quenna's." He tipped his head at the chair, and Cael sat. "Most new students climb those stairs wanting to be told they're welcome. You've climbed them with a question. I can see it on you. Ask it before it goes stale."

"Why did this academy take the risk?"

Naveth didn't answer. He studied Cael instead, and it was a different kind of study from the one Cael was used to. Arbiters and clerks and Compact men had all looked at him as though he were something to be fitted into a box, and every one of them had learned that he would not fit. This was more like the look a joiner gives a beam he is about to trust with a floor: where will it bend, and how much will it take.

"Most of them ask why I took them," Naveth said at last. "You asked about the academy. So you've already wondered whether you've fallen in with a gambler or a fool, and you were too polite to say so."

"I wasn't going to say either."

"No. But it's the right thing to wonder, and I'd think less of you if you hadn't." He turned in his chair, ran a finger along the brown books without looking at them until it stopped on one, drew it out, and laid it open on the blotter facing Cael. "Before I explain anything, read me an entry. Any entry."

The page was ruled in columns: a name, a year, the tier and rank a student came in with, and the tier and rank they left with. Under each entry someone with small, tidy handwriting had added a line.

"Copper Rank Two at intake," Cael read. "Kindled at sixteen. Left at Bronze Rank Three. Twenty-four."

"Kindled two years after everyone else. The large schools won't look twice at a late Kindler; they assume something went wrong inside. Something went right, as it turned out. It only went right slowly. Another."

Cael's finger moved down the column. "Classification disputed at intake. Re-evaluated in the fourth year. Stone Path changed to Anchor Path."

"Four years to put that right. Somebody in this building was sure the registry had made a mistake, and stayed sure until the registry agreed." Naveth said it quietly, with the satisfaction of a man touching a scar that had healed well. "She teaches on the coast now. Another."

"Re-certification candidate. Expelled from—" There was a school's name in the column, and Cael stopped short of it; it was not his to say aloud. "Copper Rank Nine coming in. Iron Rank Four going out."

"Her old instructors wrote her up as a discipline problem. What she was, was a girl with a temper and a better eye than theirs." Naveth closed the book and kept his hand on its cover. "That shelf holds sixty years of those."

Then he raised one finger.

"Here's what I learned before I ever saw this hill. Before this I kept a mid-tier academy, eleven years of it, and it was a good school. Every few years we turned out a Silver prospect, and our Iron graduates went on to Bronze. And every year the best two or three would leave us for somewhere larger, because we had taught them so well that a larger school noticed and made them a better offer. I got very skilled at growing things for other people to keep."

"So you came here instead."

"Eventually. In between there was a decade I won't bore you with. I told people I was between posts. I was really between ideas." He said it without any shine on it, the way a man reports weather that has already passed. "Once I was here, most of a year went by before I saw what this small place gave me that the big ones never had."

A second finger joined the first.

"A school this size will never get a student the system has priced correctly. Give a girl a clean file, a Silver forecast and a good family, and she goes where the floors are better and the placements are surer. That door is shut to us and always will be. So we hunt the other way, among the ones it has priced wrong. Late Kindlers. Disputed files. Re-certification cases the big schools won't touch because they're a nuisance to process." He tapped the brown cover once. "A clerical error costs almost nothing to take on, and a great deal to have been wrong about. This school has lived for sixty years in the space between those two prices."

He set both hands flat again.

"Every student in this building is someone's clerical error, Cael. You're simply the largest one we've ever had the nerve to sign for."

Cael sat in the plain chair and understood what he had been given, and what he had not. It was not warmth. In the first months after Denvash he had wanted warmth badly, had wanted some grown person to be moved by a boy's bad luck, and it had gone the same way every time. On the day of his Kindling the certification office had been gentle with him. The clerk had lowered her voice. She had apologized for the classification while her other hand stamped it. Then the appointment ended, and the gentleness ended with it, on the step outside, at the exact moment the door shut. Naveth was offering something else. He had opened a book of numbers and shown Cael why he was worth having, and that steadied Cael more than kindness would have. Anybody could call kindness back without warning. An incentive came with its terms written down, and you could read the terms, and you could see from a long way off when they were going to run out.

There was one more thing, and he put it quickly, while his nerve still held.

"And when I stop paying off?"

Naveth nodded slowly, like an examiner when a candidate finds the question under the question.

"Then I was wrong, and the school lives through it. It has before. Plenty of names in those books went nowhere much. A few washed out before the first frost." His palm rested on the cover. "That's the half people forget. We take the students other schools priced wrong, knowing from the start that some of those bets won't come in. The losses don't sink us."

"And the ones that come in?"

"They're what keep the roof on."

Cael turned that over and found another question under it. "Where's Quenna in the ledger?"

Naveth's face did not quite smile. It looked, rather, like the face of a man who has watched an arrow go where he aimed it.

"Quenna priced you."

Cael waited.

"She sat in that chair with your file on her knee and her argument already written out, and she put her own name on this desk as surety." Naveth pressed his palm to the blotter, lightly. "She's done that for hard cases since before this was my office. On the merits of a student, I have never once seen her wrong."

He stopped. Cael watched him weigh whether to say the rest, and watched him decide.

"Where she has been wrong, now and then, is in the bill for being right. You ought to know how that bill gets paid, so I'll tell you. If this goes badly, it lands on you first. Then on her. Then on me. That's the order of the ledger." He looked straight at Cael. "Better you get it from this chair today than sit up some night doing the sum yourself and wondering who kept it from you."

Cael kept very still. Some part of him had known. Quenna had come to the Ironyard and watched him for months without saying a word. She had built her offer like a legal argument, because she knew that one day someone would argue against it. He had seen her stake, and he had never let himself sit down and total it. Now someone had totalled it for him, out loud, in a bare office with its window turned to the yard.

"Thank you," he said.

The words came out smaller than what stood behind them. Two words could not hold it, and he let them go anyway.

"Thank me with your assessments." Naveth was already rising, and that seemed to be the end; there was no handshake and no speech, only a busy man with letters waiting. "Come back when you've got a question worth thirty-one stairs. I suspect you'll know which ones are."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He sat down on a worn step halfway down the stair because he could not wait, and wrote one line in the binder, Showed me the ledger instead of his heart, and then sat with the pen still, adding up the order of who paid, until he realized he had decided something without meaning to. Somewhere between the brown book and the stair, he had decided to pass every assessment this building gave him, not for himself, which he had been doing for years and was good at, but because a woman had put her name on a desk for him and he would not be the bet that cost her it.

The tour began at the second bell. A junior clerk ran it, perhaps twenty, quick and bored, with a slate under one arm and the practiced patter of someone who had given the tour more often than she found interesting, and six new students followed her while Cael walked at the back filling a page in his densest shorthand.

The training hall came first, a single long floor under a high roof, smaller than the Ironyard by a wide margin, divided by chalk lines into six sections that were each big enough for two fighters and an instructor and nothing more. Two were in use. In one, a Blade Path pair ran a drill in total silence; in the other, an instructor called counts and a girl answered each count with a short burst of something that made the air go hazy and warm. It smelled the way every training floor smelled, of chalk dust and old sweat and the singed smell a Path leaves when somebody lets it off too near the boards. What it did not have was noise. At the Ironyard there had always been noise, odds shouted from the rail and the churn of a dozen fights at once, and here there was one voice at a time, an instruction and an answer.

"Six sections," said the clerk. "Supervised blocks only, by the roster. Open sparring runs in the late afternoon for students with full standing. You'll get your blocks from your track instructor."

Full standing, Cael wrote, and underlined it, suspecting already that the phrase did not include him.

The residence wing he knew. The clerk walked them through it anyway and down to the common room, which she called the stable without any sign of thinking it was funny — "It was a stable. Now it's where you eat" — and from there across to the lecture wing, the newest building on the grounds, clean stone and sharp corners and three floors of classrooms, where for the first time she showed a spark of interest.

"Sorted by Path family, not by tier."

A boy beside Cael frowned. "What's the difference?"

"Everywhere else puts the Copper students in one room and the Iron students in another. Here all the movement Paths share a floor, Wind and Current and Storm, and all the hardening Paths share another, Stone and Iron Skin and Shield and Anchor. A Copper Rank One and an Iron Rank Seven of the same family sit through the same lecture. You learn the family first, and then your place in it."

Cael wrote that down twice, in two different places, because it seemed important twice. Every other academy he had ever read about sorted its students by tier. Tier was what institutions ranked people by, the number on a file that decided which doors a person could go through. Sorting by family meant that this place cared more about what a student could come to understand than about where he currently stood on the ladder. He thought it was Naveth's ledger again, written into a building.

Students crossed the paths between the buildings as they walked, in loose, sure lines, never looking up to check the way, and a boy about Cael's age jogged past toward the lecture wing because a bell had just told him to. Cael watched him go with a feeling he had not expected, which was envy, not of the boy but of the bell. He had been his own clock and his own clerk and his own bell for months now, training blocks and circuit dates and recovery days built out of nothing but discipline, with nobody waiting for him to arrive and nobody who would have noticed if he were late, and only now, watching someone else's bell do that work, did he feel how tiring it had been.

The formal yard came last on the ground floor. It sat behind its own wall, open to the sky, the earth packed hard and swept smooth around a single chalk ring, with a low stand of benches along one side for perhaps forty people.

"Scheduled matches. Standings bouts. Some assessments. You don't spar here unless you're told to."

Cael stood at the edge of it longer than the others and tried to picture himself in the ring, alone, in front of a panel. It ought to have frightened him, and it did not, very much. Whatever happened inside that chalk would happen under rules written down where anyone could read them, and hidden rules had hurt him far more often than hard ones.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

"And finally, the archive," said the clerk. "Most of you won't need it."

The archive was the oldest thing on the grounds. It sat at the end of a short passage off the main hall, behind a door darker than any other he had seen here, iron-banded and heavy, set into a frame whose stones had been cut by different hands, in a different century, from the walls on either side of it.

An old woman stood in the doorway. She was in her seventies, small and very straight, with grey hair pinned flat and a pair of reading spectacles hanging on a cord at her neck. The door stood at a careful angle in her hand, wide enough for courtesy and too narrow for anyone to mistake it for a welcome. Cael marked the angle. People made small choices on purpose all day long and never said so, and he had a habit of catching them.

"Prynn," said the clerk. "Archivist."

"Waystation records," Prynn said, before anyone could ask, in the dry, exact voice of someone who had said it many times to students who never came back. "From before this was a school. The academy kept the room when it took the building, and nobody has ever been brave enough to throw anything away."

Through the narrow gap behind her Cael glimpsed shelving that ran back much further than the passage suggested the building could hold, aisles one person wide and every inch of them used. A cooler air leaked out past her, carrying paper, old glue and stone. He knew that smell before he could have said why; it was Vell's archive in Ardenmere.

Prynn looked at him — not at the group, at him — with a frank, weighing look like the one Naveth had given him across the desk. Naveth had been weighing a risk. She seemed to be weighing whether he could read.

"You'll want to come back."

The others were already following the clerk away. Cael hesitated. "Why?"

"Most students say they will," Prynn said. "A few mean it."

She did not shut the door on him. She simply waited, holding it at its exact angle, until he understood that the conversation was over and walked away, and when he glanced back from the end of the passage she was still watching him go.

Anyone coming in by the main hall's entrance walked past the assessment calendar, pinned to an open board with no glass over it. He had walked past it twice that morning without stopping, and on the way back from the archive he stopped. It was ruled into weeks, each with a column of entries in a clerk's small even hand — standings bouts, re-certification reviews, a lecture on declaration theory open to all years, a visiting instructor from somewhere north — and his name was in the second column, at the height of his eye.

Demonstration Assessment, Unclassified Observer Track. Training hall, first bell. Eighth day. And beneath it, in the same hand: Monthly thereafter.

Three lines below, on the same day, Lira's name sat beside Re-certification Review, initial, and further down Brom's name appeared under a standard floor evaluation, all three in the same hand and the same ink and the same size. There was no mark beside his own line to set it apart from the lines above and below, no note in smaller writing explaining what kind of student he was. A name, a category, a date. Every institution that had ever dealt with him had handled him with gloves. The Compact had wanted him invisible, and the certification office had wanted him out of the room. Greyvane had simply put him on the timetable, scheduled like everyone else. He understood, standing there, that being scheduled was its own kind of being seen, and perhaps the safer kind, because it was hard to make a person disappear once his name was on a board in the main hall in ink.

It was also a count. Today was the second day. The eighth was six mornings off, and the brown envelope with his name in it would go down the hill on the third. He had placed the two dates side by side in his head without meaning to, like two weights on a scale, and could not quite take them off again.

A girl of about thirteen stopped beside him, and after a moment he knew her: the other name read out under Observer that morning. She was small and dark-haired, with a slate hugged to her chest, and she read the board with her lips moving until she found something and frowned at it.

"I'm on here," she said, to nobody in particular. "I didn't know I'd be on here."

"So am I."

She looked up, surprised to be answered. "Is it good?"

He thought about it. "I think so. I think it means they're expecting you."

She considered that with great seriousness, then nodded and went off down the hall with her slate held tight, as if she had been handed something she meant to keep.

Cael looked at his own line one more time, and then went to find Brom.

Chapter 4 — One Condition at a Time

[Quiet, precise narration; restrained institutional pressure and careful new beginnings]

Brom was on the defensive-branch floor. Cael could tell how his afternoon had gone before he was near enough to see him.

There was a crowd. It was not a large one, perhaps a dozen students strung along the chalk boundary of the far section, but it had the particular stillness of people who had stumbled onto something worth watching rather than come on purpose. Nobody was talking, and two of them had set their bags down, which meant they had stopped meaning to leave. Cael found a place at the end of the line and looked over a shoulder.

Brom stood in the middle of the section in his usual stance, low and loose, his weight sunk into his heels as if the floor were a slope he had decided to lean against. Across from him stood the broadest student Cael had seen on the grounds, a head taller than Brom and half again as wide, with forearms like fence posts and the calm, patient face of someone who had been asked to stand in front of other people for a very long time and had made his peace with it. His feet were planted shoulder-width apart, and the chalk dust around them had settled into a faint, undisturbed ring. Stone Path, Cael guessed, from the way the boy's weight seemed to go down through his soles and keep going; a fourth-year at least, Iron-tier and probably low in it.

Between them, a little to one side, stood a woman of about fifty. She was not large, and at first glance she was not anything in particular, a lean woman with grey-streaked hair tied back and a plain brown training coat buttoned to the throat. But she stood the way Cael had seen only a handful of people stand, perfectly balanced, every part of her body doing the work it needed to keep her upright and not one ounce more, so that even at rest she seemed to be holding a shield she was not carrying.

Shield Path. It could not have been anything else.

"Wray," the girl beside him whispered to her friend. "Bronze. She's had him out there since the fifth bell."

"Who?"

"The new one. The Iron Skin."

Cael looked at the light through the high windows and did a quick sum. Brom had been on this floor for most of an hour.

Wray raised one finger.

The broad student came forward, and within three exchanges Cael understood that he was watching the most orthodox defensive fighter he had ever seen. Everything the boy did came out of a textbook. He pressed, set his angle, and pressed again, and each strike arrived from exactly the approved line at exactly the approved distance, with his weight committed as far as the form recommended and no further. It was not exciting, and it was not meant to be; it was the kind of pressure that wore people down by never giving them anything to argue with.

Brom met it from underneath, the way Brom met everything.

He let the first strike come to him. Cael watched it land on Brom's forearm and saw the Iron Skin harden there a fraction before contact, the faint dull sheen that came over Brom's skin when his Path took hold, and then he saw the thing he had spent a year studying and still found remarkable: Brom gave. He let the force push him half an inch and then an inch, finding the line of it the way water finds a crack, and at the end of that inch he turned it, so that the broad student's own weight came back around on him from a direction he had not planned for.

The boy staggered half a step.

It was a small thing. In a real fight it would have been an opening. Here Wray simply lowered her finger, and both of them stepped back to their marks. She said something to the broad student, too quietly to carry, and he nodded.

"Again."

This time she had moved Brom's mark. Cael saw it at once, because he had been watching the chalk: Brom's starting line was a full pace closer than before, so that when the broad student came in he came in almost at once, and Brom had far less room to give in. Brom gave anyway. He took the strike on the forearm and sank and found he had nowhere to sink to, his back heel touching the chalk line behind him. He turned the force short and cramped so that it came back around on the broad student with only a little of its weight. The boy did not stagger this time. He shifted his feet, absorbed the small return, and pressed again.

Wray raised her finger. Stop.

She watched Brom without saying anything. Then she spoke to the broad student again, quietly, and moved Brom's mark back to where it had been, and this time she touched the boy's left shoulder.

"From there."

The strikes began to arrive from Brom's left side instead of square on. Cael felt something tighten in his own chest in recognition, because he had fought Brom often enough to know that the left was the side Brom trusted less. It was not a weakness, exactly, but a preference so old that Brom himself might not know he had it; every redirect Brom had ever shown him had turned to the right. Brom took the first angled strike and turned it right, as he always did, and the turn carried the force across his own body and left him a little open on the side he had just been hit from.

The broad student did not use the opening. He had not been told to. Wray's pen moved on the slate she held against her hip.

Somewhere in the fourth change, Cael realized what she was doing. It was what he did with the binder. She was isolating variables — distance, angle, rhythm — changing exactly one condition at a time and holding everything else still, and watching which part of Brom held and which part bent. She was not watching a fight at all. She was taking him apart into the pieces that were structure and the pieces that were habit. Cael felt a strange, sharp pleasure at seeing someone else do it, and do it better than he did, with a living person instead of a page.

Wray raised her finger a fifth time and went to the broad student and spoke to him longer than before. Cael saw the boy frown slightly before he nodded and Wray stepped away.

"Don't finish anything," Cael heard her say as she passed the chalk.

The broad student came in. The strikes looked the same at first, the same textbook line and the same approved distance. But they were short: each one began properly and stopped an inch or two before it would have committed, and pulled back, and began again. Jab, withdraw. Press, withdraw. There was force in all of it, real force, and none of it was ever given away.

Brom took the first one on his forearm and reached for it, and there was nothing to take.

Cael saw the small flicker of surprise cross Brom's face. The give-and-return he had built over two years depended above all on one thing, which was that the person hitting him meant it. A committed strike was a loan; Brom borrowed it, turned it, and paid it back with interest. An uncommitted strike was no loan at all, and there was nothing in it to borrow.

The broad student pressed again, short, and Brom gave half an inch to nothing.

Again.

Again.

The crowd had gone very quiet, so quiet that when somebody behind Cael shifted their weight the sound of it was loud.

Brom's shoulders changed. Cael knew that change. It was the moment, in a long fight, when Brom stopped waiting for a thing to happen and decided to make it happen.

He stepped in.

It was not his style. He came forward off his back heel into the broad student's space and dropped his guard by a hand's width on the right side, an obvious opening, the kind a textbook fighter is trained to punish. He was baiting, offering the boy something worth committing to.

The boy committed.

It was the first full strike in a long while, and it came in hard, the whole weight of a fourth-year Stone Path behind it. It landed on Brom's right ribs before he had finished turning to meet it. The sound was a flat, heavy thud. Brom's breath went out of him in a grunt, and although his Iron Skin had come up in time — Cael saw the sheen of it along his side — Iron Skin did not make a person weightless. Brom slid a full pace back across the chalk and dropped to one knee.

Cael was moving before he knew it, and caught himself at the chalk line with one hand on the shoulder of the student in front of him. The girl beside him made a small sound.

Brom stayed down for two breaths, then three. Wray had not moved. She was watching Brom's face, not his ribs.

He got up. He did it slowly, one hand pressed flat to his side, and Cael could see from the set of his mouth that it hurt. He walked back to his mark without being told, turned, set himself, and looked at Wray.

She studied him. "Full," she said to the broad student. "Commit everything."

The broad student came in with a committed strike, the whole of his weight behind it, a fence post of an arm driving straight at Brom's centre. Brom took it, and gave, and turned it, and this time the turn was clean. The force came around in a short hard arc and went back into the boy along a line he had not braced for, and his planted feet came unplanted for the first time all afternoon. He went sideways a full step and then another, arms flung wide for balance, and ended up on the far side of the chalk with a startled expression on his patient face.

The crowd let its breath out all together, which was not a cheer but was close to one. Wray did not make a sound at all. She wrote on her slate.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]
