When she lowered the slate she walked out onto the floor and stood in front of Brom, who was still holding his ribs.

"Somebody taught you to live through being underestimated. Maybe you taught yourself."

Brom said nothing.

"It isn't nothing. It carried you here. Everything you do waits for someone to give you too much, and most people do, the first time. They see a Copper tag and a stocky boy with no school behind him, they put their whole weight into the first strike, and you take it from them." She tilted her head. "You've built a whole fighter out of other people's mistakes."

"It works."

"It works until someone respects you." Her voice did not rise or harden; it was the voice of someone reading a measurement off a scale. "You've just seen what happens then. A good opponent who takes you seriously won't give you anything to borrow, so you have to go and fetch it. You don't know how to fetch it yet, so you open yourself up and pay with your ribs."

Brom was quiet for a long moment.

"Now I'll teach you the other thing," said Wray. "What to do when the person across from you has stopped making that mistake. You don't have it yet. Learning it will make the last two years look like the easy part."

She turned to the broad student, nodded once in thanks, and dismissed him with two fingers, and he picked up his bag and left without looking at anyone. Then she turned toward the crowd, who scattered at once as if they had all just remembered urgent business elsewhere.

Cael stayed.

Brom was quiet most of the way back to the residence wing. He walked a little stiffly, keeping his right elbow tucked against his side, and Cael matched his pace without comment while the light went long and gold across the yard. Somewhere in the lecture wing a bell rang, the sixth, the last of the floor blocks.

They were nearly at the residence door before Brom spoke.

"I think I have a teacher."

He said it carefully, like a man setting something fragile on a table he was not yet sure would hold it. In all the months Cael had known him, he had never once heard Brom use that word without something sour attached to it, a joke about Velmere's hired instructors or a dry aside about men who taught for money and wanted thanks for it. This time there was nothing attached at all.

"That's good."

"Yes." Brom stopped at the door and looked back across the yard toward the training hall. "She watched me for an hour and found the soft place. You saw it. The waiting. I've been hiding that for two years." He shook his head slowly. "Then, instead of leaning on it, she said she'd mend it."

"Nobody's done that before."

"Plenty of people have found things. My family found things. Every instructor they ever paid for found things, and then they used them to make me fit whatever they'd been paid to make me into." He touched his ribs gingerly. "This is the first one who found a thing and wanted to fix it."

"Are you going to let her?"

"I'd decided before she finished talking." He glanced sideways at Cael, a little wry. "I only noticed afterward. Do you do that?"

"All the time. The binder is mostly me reading what I already chose."

Brom made the low sound in his chest that did him for a laugh, and then winced and pressed his side.

"The big one," said Cael. "Your partner. What's his name?"

An odd look crossed Brom's face. "I don't know. She pointed at him and he came. He never said it, and I don't think he says much of anything." He considered the closed door of the training hall. "He did everything she asked, exactly. Held back when she said hold back. Hit when she said hit. Didn't once try to win."

"That's a talent."

"A rare one. Most people can't stand to lose on purpose for an hour, even when it's their job."

Cael put that away without knowing yet why he wanted it. He only knew that a person who could be furniture for an hour without minding was worth knowing, and that he did not even know the boy's name.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Lira was already at a trestle table in the stable when they came down for supper. She had brought bread — not the kitchen's bread, but a dark round loaf with a crackled crust, wrapped in a cloth and set in the middle of the table like a trophy.

"I found the baker."

"We guessed," said Brom, lowering himself onto the bench with great care.

Lira looked at the way he sat. "What happened to you?"

"I got a teacher."

"And the teacher hit you?"

"A boy the size of a door hit me. The teacher arranged it."

"Good," said Lira with feeling, and tore him off the biggest piece of the loaf.

She had spent the afternoon in the hill town between her own scheduled blocks. She reported on it quickly and without wasted words: it was even smaller up close than it looked from the hill, with one street worth walking and one worth avoiding, a mill, a smithy, a post office in the back of a draper's, and a baker at the bottom of the hill who opened before dawn and was rude to everyone equally, which Lira considered a mark of integrity.

"I'll take your letter down tomorrow. I'm going anyway, and the post goes out on the third day of the week."

He handed it across, and she tucked it inside her coat without looking at the direction, which he appreciated more than he said. Then she grew quieter and turned her cup between her hands.

"There are others on my track."

Both of them looked up.

"Re-certification. I saw the roster for the review room. My name, and three others. Only a handful. But a handful means somebody did this before me and somebody will do it after me, and there's a desk and a procedure and a clerk who knows how to read the clauses aloud." She was looking at the cup. "It's a track."

"Is that good or bad?" asked Brom.

She turned the cup once more before she answered.

"I've been carrying this as if Fenmark invented it just for me. As if they'd looked at me and decided, specially, that I was the problem." She set the cup down. "It turns out there's a desk for it. A queue. Other people standing in it."

"That's not an answer," said Cael.

"Give it a month," said Lira, and from her that counted as hope.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Brom's first full day of coursework was the next day, and he came back from it talking.

Cael heard him before he saw him. He was halfway down the stable stairs at supper, still talking over his shoulder to a second-year who looked faintly alarmed. He went on talking as he set down his tray and as he sat, and it took Cael a moment to understand what was different. Brom usually arrived at a conclusion in silence and reported only its finished shape. This was the process itself, spilling out of him as fast as he could think it, a register Cael had never heard him use.

"Declaration theory. Two blocks of it. A whole lecture hall full of Stone and Shield and Iron Skin and Anchor, all of us sitting there while an old man draws curves on a board."

"Curves of what?" asked Lira.

"Efficiency. How much a declaration gives you, rank by rank, as you refine the form." He ate a spoonful of barley without looking at it. "Half of it's solid. Better than solid. He has names for things I found out by falling over. There's a word for the way I turn a strike. There's a diagram of it."

"And the other half?"

"Wrong."

Lira raised her eyebrows. "The other half of a lecture you've attended once is wrong."

"The half about ceilings." Brom set his spoon down, which in Brom meant he was serious. "The theory says that after a certain point refining your form stops paying. You hit a ceiling. Somewhere in the middle of a tier, past a certain rank, the gains go flat, and after that the only way to get stronger is raw output — more force, bigger declarations. The form's done all it can."

"And you think that's wrong."

"I know it's wrong. I spent two years past where the ceiling's supposed to be, on my own, with nobody telling me there was a ceiling there, and my form went on improving the whole time." He leaned forward. "Every month. Not in great jumps. In small ones. Steadily."

"Then either the lecture's wrong," said Lira, "or you're a freak. Pick one."

"Or there are enough freaks that the rule's no use to anyone." Brom's voice had the intensity he usually saved for a fight. "The curve isn't measuring bodies. It's measuring people who were told where to stop and stopped there. It isn't a limit in the body. It's a limit in the belief."

Cael turned that over. Untrained boys said confident things about doctrine all the time, doctrine built by scholars with shelves of learning behind them, and most of those confident things died at the first hard question. This one might not. Brom wasn't arguing from a book. He was arguing from two years of his own body getting better past the point where the theory said it should have stopped, and nobody had ever told him to stop, so he hadn't.

"You should tell Wray."

"I did."

"And?"

Brom's face did something complicated, as if several expressions were queuing for the same doorway.

"She said, 'Good. Then show me on the floor, not in a lecture hall. If you're right, I'll rewrite the lecture.'"

He said it slowly, word for word.

Lira put down her bread. "She said she'd rewrite the lecture?"

"She teaches the ceiling section to the second-years. She said if I can show her the ceiling isn't there, on the floor, in front of her, she'll stand up and tell them she was wrong." Brom shook his head slowly. "Every teacher I've had before wanted to be right. This one wants to find out."

"Velmere's instructors didn't," said Lira. It was not quite a question.

"Velmere's instructors wanted to be obeyed." Two years of road had taken the edge off that grudge, and he spoke of it now without heat. "Wray wants somebody to test her. That's a different animal entirely."

He went back to his barley, and Cael watched him eat and thought about what two days had done: a tag that had not needed a question, a teacher who had found a weakness and offered to mend it, and a lecture hall full of people who had names for the things Brom had learned by falling over, one of whom was willing to rewrite her own lecture if a Copper-tier boy from nowhere could beat her on a chalk floor. He thought that Brom had been waiting for this place his whole life without knowing it existed. He did not say it, because Brom would have been embarrassed and because it was not his to say, and he did not write it down that night either, though he started to. What he wanted to remember was the look on Brom's face across the barley, and no line in the binder would hold it better than he already did.

Chapter 5 — The Edges of the Room

[Quiet, precise narration; restrained institutional pressure and careful new beginnings]

The Path taxonomy lecture met on the ground floor of the lecture wing, in a room full of thirteen-year-olds.

Cael had chosen it off the schedule on purpose. It was listed as an introductory block, open to observers and first-years. He wanted to hear how Greyvane explained the whole system to someone meeting it fresh, because he had learned it as most children in the Outer District did, in scraps from adults who were busy and later from books he read standing up in other people's shops. He had never once heard it taught from the beginning by someone whose job was to get it right. He had not quite pictured what that would mean. Twenty-two children turned on their benches when he came in, and twenty-two pairs of eyes went to his height and his face and the tag on his coat and back to his face with a new question in them. He was two years older than the oldest of them and a head taller than most. He took the bench at the very back, set the binder on his knees, and tried to look like furniture.

It did not work for about a quarter of an hour.

The girl from the assessment board sat in the second row with her slate. She turned around twice to look at him, the second time with open interest, and when he caught her eye she gave him a small, serious nod. He nodded back, and she seemed satisfied and faced the front.

The instructor was a soft-voiced man in his fifties with ink on his cuffs, and he called the roll from a list. Cael heard the girl answer to "Oona," and she said "Here" as if she were confirming a fact rather than her presence. His own name came last.

"Cael. Observer track." The instructor looked up over the list. "You're welcome to sit in. The material will be familiar."

"Some of it."

"Then you can tell me which parts aren't."

A few of the children laughed. The instructor did not seem to have meant it as a joke, and Cael decided he liked him.

A chart hung on the wall behind the lectern, large and painted on stiff canvas, old enough that its corners had been mended twice. Across the top ran the seven tiers in their colours: Copper in dim orange, Iron in silver-grey, Bronze in warm gold, Silver bright as a coin, Gold a deep amber, Platinum white touched with blue with a small note beside it that said historical, and at the far end a seventh box with no colour in it at all, only the word Void and a question mark. Down the left side ran the Paths themselves, grouped into families and painted in neat capitals — Movement: Wind, Current, Storm; Hardening: Stone, Iron Skin, Shield, Anchor, Wall; Edge: Blade, Glass — and then Ember and Ash, Force and Pressure, Mire and Tide, and more below those, a long column of names, some of which Cael had only ever seen written.

"This chart is copied from the Compact's own schedule, the list the registry uses," the instructor said. "Every Path an Arbiter can assign is on it. The families are ours, for teaching; the list is theirs. If your Arbiter tells you a Path, it will be one of these. If it isn't on this chart, it isn't a Path." He tapped the top row with a pointer. "Tiers first. You all know the colours. Who can tell me how many ranks are in a tier?"

A dozen hands went up. "Ten," said a boy near the front, without waiting.

"Ten. Rank One to Rank Ten. Almost all of you will start at Copper Rank One, and you earn rank by use, by practice, by working your Path until it grows. And when you reach Rank Ten—"

"You go up," said the same boy.

"You may go up. Rank Ten is the threshold, not the door. To cross from Copper into Iron you need two things, the rank, which you earn yourself, and an evaluation at a registered Arbiter station, which confirms it. Both. Rank without evaluation stays where it is." He pointed down the Copper column. "Most people who Kindle into Copper never reach the threshold at all. They find a level that suits their life, and they stay there. Six of every ten working practitioners in Valdris are Copper, and most adults plateau somewhere in the middle of it."

"My father's Copper Rank Five," said a girl by the window, a little defiantly.

"Then your father is like most fathers," said the instructor mildly. "Copper Rank Five is a good, honest rank. It works a forge. It builds a house." He moved the pointer along. "A quarter of practitioners reach Iron. Those are your journeymen, professional fighters and master tradespeople. One in ten reaches Bronze, and you'll meet a few Bronze instructors here. Silver, perhaps four in a hundred. Gold, fewer than one. Platinum—"

"Nobody," said Oona.

"Nobody living. And Void is a word in stories. You may write it down, but you will not be tested on it."

Cael kept two columns, a habit Ardenmere had given him before he noticed he had it: on the left the thing being taught, and on the right whatever the teaching took for granted. On the left: Ten ranks per tier. Rank Ten is the threshold. Advancement needs rank and a station evaluation, both. Most adults plateau in Copper. On the right: Assumes an Arbiter. Assumes a station that will evaluate you. Assumes your Path is on the chart.

"And who keeps the list?" the instructor asked the room, and answered himself before anyone could guess. "The registry. Every Kindling in every district in Valdris is entered within the week, and in all its history the registry has never once taken an entry out. It is a ledger that has never closed an account." He let that sit. "The list on this canvas has been changed many times, too, by amendment. When you're older, read the amendments. Every one of them is a confession. It tells you what somebody was afraid of, the year they wrote it."

Cael wrote that on the left, and then on the right, after a while: Assumes the registry is the record. Assumes that what it doesn't write down didn't happen. He thought of Vell's ledger folded into his pack, every bout he had fought at the Ironyard and every rating change in her own hand, most of which the Compact's registry had never heard of, all of which had happened anyway.

"Declarations," the instructor said a little later, "are how your Arbiter tells you what your Path has given you."

He described them the way Brom had on the road, a header naming the Path and the tier and the rank, an ability's name in brackets, one or two plain sentences saying what it did and how far it reached. He drew the shape of one on the slate board with blank lines where the words would go. Several of the children copied it carefully.

"Your first declaration comes at Kindling, when your Arbiter gives you your Path and your first ability together. After that, new declarations come as you climb. Not every rank brings one; some do. You'll learn the rhythm of your own Path."

Oona's hand went up. "Do you have to tell people what they say?"

The instructor paused, and the room went quiet in a different way, a listening way, and Cael understood that half the children had wanted to ask the same thing.

"No. You never have to. Your declarations are yours. Your Arbiter shows them to you and to no one else, and nobody — not a parent, not a teacher, not an assessor — has the right to make you share one."

"But people do."

"Sometimes, between people who trust each other a great deal." He set the chalk down. "Showing someone your declaration is a little like letting them read a letter you wrote to yourself. It's intimate. You'll know, when the time comes, whether a person is someone you'd do that for. Most people do it once or twice in their whole lives, if they do it at all."

Oona considered that, then wrote something on her slate and underlined it twice.

Cael was thinking of Brom at the midday rest on the road, refusing Lira for the fifth time with perfect calm — it's more like a receipt — and of Lira, back in Ardenmere, describing her own first declaration to him because he had asked and she had decided to answer. She had not shown it, only described it, and even that, he understood now, had been a gift he hadn't known enough to recognize. Then he thought of his own notices, which no Arbiter had ever shown him because no Arbiter had ever been there. The rule did not reach him at all; there was no one to keep his notices private from except the people he chose to tell, and he had told two. On the right-hand side he wrote: Assumes your declarations are given to you by someone.

Near the end of the block the instructor invited questions about the chart, and there were a great many. Could a Path change families? (No.) Could a person have two Paths? (No.) Was it true that Storm and Wind were really the same Path with different tempers? (A long, patient no, with a diagram.) Why was Glass in the same family as Blade, when glass broke? (Because a thing that breaks well still cuts, and the instructor had a story about a broken bottle that he declined to finish.)

Oona put her hand up last.

"Where's shattered?"

The room did not go quiet at once. Most of the children had no idea what she meant, and they kept rustling and whispering, but the instructor's face went very still for half a moment, and in the back row Cael stopped breathing.

"I'm sorry?"

"Shattered. My uncle says there's one called shattered. He works for the Blade Guild and he says it's in the registry." She frowned at the chart. "It isn't on there."

"No," the instructor said carefully. "It isn't."

"Why not?"

He took a moment before he answered, and Cael watched him choose the words.

"Because it isn't a Path. It's a registry matter, a classification the registry has used, very rarely, in its records. It isn't one of the Paths on the schedule, so it isn't on the chart. The chart only lists Paths." He picked up his chalk again. "It's not something you'll need for your Kindling, Oona. I wouldn't worry about it."

"I'm not worried. I just wanted to know where it went."

"It doesn't go anywhere on this chart."

She accepted that by writing it down.

Cael sat with his pen above the page and wrote nothing. His face felt hot, and that surprised him. He had heard the word said aloud before, by officials, by clerks, once by a man in a market square who had meant it as a warning, but he had not expected to hear it in a classroom from a thirteen-year-old, asked as easily as a question about mud, or to hear the instructor answer it with isn't.

It isn't a Path.

He knew that, of course. He had known it since Denvash, and he had a binder full of evidence that whatever he had, it was not a Path in any way this chart would recognize. It still stung to hear it said in a kind voice to children. He made himself write it on the right-hand side in very small letters — Shattered is not on the chart. Registry matter, not a Path. Said kindly. — and then the bell was ringing, and he closed the binder, because he did not want to think about it any further just then.

The instructor stopped by his bench on the way out and glanced at the open page without any pretense of not reading it.

"Two columns. What's the second one?"

"What the lecture assumes."

The instructor looked at him a moment longer with an expression Cael could not quite read. "Keep it," he said, and went out.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

Oona caught him at the door.

She stood in his way without seeming to mean to, holding her slate to her chest, and looked up at him with frank curiosity.

"You're on the board. Next to me. Observer track."

"I am."

"You're old for an observer."

"I know."

She looked at his tag. Then she held up her own, which hung on a string around her neck. It was the same size as his, and in the middle of it was a hollow circle, a ring with nothing in it.

"Same."

"Same," Cael agreed.

He had known since orientation that she was on the track; he had not, until that moment, thought about what that meant. The category had been built for someone, and it had been built for her, a guild family's daughter who wanted to sit in lectures before her Kindling so that when her Arbiter came she would already know the shape of the chart. That was the real use of the hollow circle. He was the one borrowing it.

"Did you Kindle late? My mother says some people Kindle late."

He thought about how to answer. He did not want to lie to her, and, rather to his surprise, he cared a great deal about not lying to her.

"It's complicated."

She weighed that answer. "That's what grown-ups say when they don't want to tell you."

"Sometimes it's what they say when it's actually complicated."

"How do you know which?"

"You wait and see if they ever tell you."

Oona seemed to find that fair.

"I Kindle in winter. I'll be fourteen. Then I won't be an observer anymore." She said it as if announcing the date of a journey. "Will you still be one?"

"I don't know," said Cael, and it was the truest thing he had said all day.

His first supervised session fell at the fifth bell that afternoon. At the desk he was told to go to section four, and Quenna was there already, standing at the chalk with a slate, and there was no one else in the section and there would be no one else.

"Twice a week. One hour. Under supervision. You may train anything you like within the section. You may not use the open floor, and you may not spar with another student unless an assessor arranges it."

"Has an assessor arranged it?"

"No."

He set his bag against the wall, and it turned out to be a strange hour. He ran the Wind framework against an imagined count, moving through the evasion patterns at half pace and then full pace, reading strikes off a body that was not there. It was harder than it should have been, because the framework did not like empty air: it was built to read an opponent, and without one he had to supply each strike himself out of his own expectations, so that none of them ever surprised him. He did the conditioning circuits Lira had built him in Ardenmere, legs and core and the slow shoulder work that kept the Reydan joint from stiffening. He tried the surface read, and as he had known it would, it had nothing to do. Iron-adjacent needed a body within a few paces, someone whose weight was about to move, and alone it was a sense with nothing to sense.

All the while Quenna stood at the chalk and wrote. He kept shaping the work for her slate, moving a little more cleanly than he needed to, finishing patterns with a flourish he would never have bothered with alone. It took him most of the hour to notice he was doing it and the last ten minutes to stop, and when he stopped and simply worked, she wrote less. It was either coincidence or the most useful thing she had ever told him without saying it.

At the end of the hour she signed the record of the session, tore off the bottom strip, and gave it to him without looking up.

"You could ask for a partner."

"Would I get one?"

"Not yet."

"Then why ask?"

"Asking costs you nothing. Being seen to have asked, early and often, may be worth a great deal one day." She finally looked at him. "Files get read from the front page. I'd like yours to show you knocked from the start."

He wrote the request that evening at the desk in his narrow room, in his most careful hand — The undersigned, enrolled under the demonstration provision, requests that a training partner be assigned for supervised sessions, in order that practice may be conducted against a live opponent — read it over, signed it, and left it at the assessors' desk before the eighth bell. He did not expect it to be granted, and he did not mind. A refusal on paper would at least carry a date and a signature, and most of the doors he had ever stood in front of had offered neither.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On the fourth morning, without meaning to, he watched Lira sign in.

He had come into the training hall early to look at the open-floor roster, and she came in a minute behind him, and he saw her before she saw him. There were two lines at the floor desk. The standard line ran from the near end, where a clerk sat with the big roster and a stamp. The other began at the far end of the same desk, past a small wooden marker, with its own sheet and its own clerk, who did nothing but wait for the few names that belonged there.

Lira went to the far end, and what stayed with him afterward was how well she did it. She did not glance at the standard line or hesitate at the fork. She went straight past the marker and wrote her name, and the slip she took from the clerk would need an assessor's initials before the day was out; then she turned toward the floor with her chin level and her stride unbroken, and if he had not known her he would have thought the whole business meant nothing to her at all. He knew her. He saw her shoulders, a half-second after she passed the desk, come down by about an inch. It was perfect, and it was also labor, and he did not say anything.

There was one other person at the far end of the desk, a woman of perhaps twenty, tall and narrow-shouldered, with ash-pale hair cut short and a training coat patched at both elbows. She signed in after Lira and said something as Lira passed her, and Lira stopped. Cael could not hear them from the roster, but he could read the shape of the minute that followed: the older woman pointing at the slip in Lira's hand, Lira looking down at it and back up, a short dry exchange, Lira almost laughing. When she came over to him she was still half smiling.

"You saw that."

"Some of it."

"That's Gerda. Ash Path. She's been on the track most of a year." Lira held up her slip. "She told me to get the assessor's initials before the sixth bell, every time, or the clerk dates the result the next day, and if three of your results are dated a day late, somebody writes a note in your file asking why you can't keep a schedule."

"That seems unfair."

"That's what I said. She said, 'It isn't unfair. It's procedure. Unfair would be if they hid the rule.'" Lira shook her head slowly. "She's from somewhere south. A different academy. She didn't say which, and I didn't ask."

"Do you like her?"

"I don't know yet." She considered. "She talks to the procedure like it's a dog that might bite. Very calm. Very careful. Never turns her back on it." She glanced toward the floor, where Gerda had gone. "I think she's been bitten before."

At the second bell he went to hear Wray teach the ceiling. He had found the block on the lecture schedule the night before, after Brom's argument about ceilings over the barley — Declaration Efficiency, Hardening Family, Second Years. Instructor Wray. — and since an observer could attend any lecture, he went, though he had not quite believed until he walked into the room that Brom would be there too. Brom was in the back row, sitting very straight with his notebook open and his ribs held carefully to one side.

"You're a first-year," Cael said, sliding in beside him.

"I asked. She said I could sit in as long as I kept my mouth shut until the end."

"Are you going to?"

"I'm going to try very hard."

The twenty students in the room were all of the same family, Stone and Shield and Anchor and Iron Skin, along with one tall boy whose skin went faintly grey and grainy when he was nervous, which was apparently always. Wray stood at the front with a slate board behind her and used no notes. She drew a curve. It started low on the left at a mark labeled Copper One and rose steeply through the early ranks and then began to bend, so that by the middle of Copper it was rising more slowly and by the upper ranks it had nearly flattened.

"Form efficiency. How much more you get out of a declaration, rank by rank, by refining the way you use it. Not by getting stronger. By getting better." She tapped the steep part. "Early on, every hour of form work pays. You learn where your weight goes, you stop wasting motion, and your first declaration does twice what it did at Kindling without your gaining an ounce of raw output." She moved the chalk along the bend. "Then it slows. Somewhere around the middle of a tier, for most people, form work stops paying the way it did. You've learned the big lessons, and the small ones are smaller. And here—" She tapped the flat part. "—is what this school, and every school I know of, calls the ceiling: the point past which refining your form gives you so little that you're better off spending the hours on raw output instead. More force. More endurance. Bigger declarations, earned the slow way through rank."

A Shield girl near the front raised her hand. "Is it the same ceiling for every Path?"

"Roughly. The curve bends at different places for different families; hardening Paths tend to flatten a little later than movement Paths. It's in your reading." Wray wrote a short list of ranks beside the curve. "That's what the doctrine says. That's what I've taught for a long time, and that's what you'll be examined on."

Cael glanced sideways. Brom's jaw had set, and his pen had stopped moving. Wray laid down the chalk.

"There is a first-year sitting in the back of this room," she said, in the same voice she had used for the curve, "who believes the flat part of this line is not real."

Twenty heads turned, and Brom did not move.

"He believes the curve flattens because the people on it believe it will, and stop pushing. He says he has spent two years past where the ceiling ought to be, on his own, without anyone to tell him it was there, and that his form has kept improving every month." She looked at Brom down the length of the room without any expression at all. "I have told him to prove it on the floor. If he does, I will stand here and tell you I was wrong, and I will redraw this line."

The grey-skinned boy went a shade greyer, and somebody near the window whispered something.

"Until he proves it, this is the lecture. Copy the curve."

Twenty heads turned back, and twenty pens moved.

Brom was staring at the board with an expression Cael had never seen on him, a fierce, astonished stillness, as if someone had just set a heavy weight in his hands and told him it was his. He did not say anything for the rest of the block. He copied the curve carefully, exactly as she had drawn it, and then beneath it, in small square strokes, he drew a second line that did not bend. When the bell rang Wray caught his eye on her way out and did not stop; she only said, as she passed, "I meant it," and walked on.

"Meant what?" Cael asked on the stairs.

"The line. If I can show her, she'll redraw it." Brom was holding his ribs and smiling, which seemed to hurt, and he did not stop. "She told twenty people, in her own lecture, that I might be right."

"She told them you think you're right."

"She told them she'd listen. Nobody's ever told a room that about me before."
