He found Lira again at the notice board that afternoon, arms crossed before the roster for the training floor, reading it for longer than reading it could possibly take. He knew what she was looking at before he reached her. Her name was on the roster, and beside it, in the clerk's small hand, sat the same raised dot that was stamped on her tag, the provisional marker, which appeared beside her name and three others, Gerda's among them, and beside no one else on the whole board.

"Before you say anything," she said without turning, "I know it's a clerk's mark. I know it only means somebody checks my results before they count. I've read the rule. Twice."

"I wasn't going to say anything."

"You were going to say something kind and sensible, and I'd have had to agree with it." She kept her eyes on the dot. "Here's the trouble. For two years I've told anyone who'd stand still that Fenmark got me wrong. Then I walked in here and put my name to a page that says Fenmark's record stands, and I did it so I could train, and now there's a mark by my name every morning to remind everyone that my wins need a second signature." She breathed out through her nose. "I was right about Fenmark. I also signed. Both of those are true, and I can't make one of them sit down and let the other have the chair."

"Maybe neither of them has to sit down."

"Maybe." She uncrossed her arms and crossed them again. "I come and look at it every day, as if, if I stare at it long enough, it'll stop being able to sting."

"Does it?"

"Not so far," said Lira, and almost laughed. "I'm very stubborn, though."

She left after that, toward the yard and the floor and the work she trusted more than any board, and Cael stayed a moment longer looking at the dot beside her name. He had been wrong about something, he thought. On the road he had assumed that his own door would be the hard one, the blank board and the borrowed category, and he had braced himself for being the complicated case. He had not thought much at all about what it would cost Lira to walk every single morning through a door that was simple on its face and marked on the inside.

The notice was under his own door when he came back from supper, a single folded sheet slid in flat across the boards with no envelope and no seal, delivered with all the ceremony of a laundry list. He unfolded it standing in the doorway with one hand still on the latch.

Demonstration Assessment. Unclassified Observer Track. First sitting. Training hall, first bell, the eighth day. Closed session. Demonstration at the candidate's own election.

He had seen the date on the public board already, and had known it was coming, but there was a difference between a line on a board in the hall and a sheet of paper on his own floor with his own name at the top, and the difference went through him like cold water. The post had gone down the hill yesterday, and the brown envelope with it, in the same bag as his letter to Hesk. It was somewhere on a road now, getting farther away every hour, toward a desk he would never see. This sheet was the other half of the same thing. Not the signature, not the category, not the hollow circle — all of that only held a door open. This was the first time anyone would walk through the door and look at what was on the other side. It would be written down, and he could no longer be sure that anything written down about him would stay inside this building.

Four mornings, then, to choose what they would see.

He closed the door, sat on the bed, and opened the binder to a clean page.

Chapter 6 — Panel Speed

[Quiet, precise narration; restrained institutional pressure and careful new beginnings]

The morning after the notice, Quenna gave him the rules in the corridor outside the archive, standing, with her folder under her arm and the air of a woman already late for something else, as if the rules were short enough that sitting down for them would have been a waste of a chair.

"There'll be three chairs. Mine in the middle. Wray has the instructor's chair this month. The third goes round the senior faculty in turn, and nobody tells the candidate whose turn it is; we do that on purpose. Spend what's left of your four days on yourself, not on guessing a stranger."

"All right."

"The format is yours to fill. You'll have a training partner, assigned by the instructor's seat, who will strike when he's told to strike and stop when he's told to stop. Nowhere does the provision ask you to name a Path."

"Good. I haven't got one."

"The drafters seem to have foreseen you." Her voice gave the irony nothing at all. "The standard is three words. Consistent, observable practice."

She let them sit in the cold corridor air, so that he heard each one land separately.

"Attend to those three words, because nothing else in the room will matter that morning. Consistent: they must see it more than once, built the same way, ending the same way. Once can be luck. Twice is a pattern. Observable means it happens in the room, at a scale a person holding a slate can see and write down, nothing internal, nothing they have to take your word for. And practice—" She paused a fraction longer than she had on the others. "Practice means it is something you do on purpose. Not something that happens to you."

Cael heard, inside that pause, everything she was not saying. He had told her nothing about how the fragments arrived, and she had never asked, but she had watched him fight for months before she ever spoke to him and she was not a fool, and she had just drawn a line on the floor between a thing he did and a thing that happened to him with the care of a woman marking a boundary she did not intend to step over.

"Read the words for yourself before you decide anything, and notice what isn't in them. Nothing about your best. Nothing about all of it. Whoever wrote that provision knew how far a loose phrase will stretch, and left it loose."

"And whatever I show goes on the record."

"Whatever you show goes on the record, in three hands. Think about that half harder than the first."

She went off down the corridor without saying goodbye, and Cael stood a while outside the archive door, looking at the iron bands on the dark wood without seeing them. He was free to show anything at all, as long as it came out the same twice and a stranger with a pen could follow it and it was his own doing. That was a gift. It was also, he saw a moment later, a trap of the same size, because anything he was free to show he was also free to show too much of, and whatever he showed would be written down and kept.

So he knocked on the frame.

Prynn looked up from a ledger at a high desk just inside, took off her spectacles, and looked at him for exactly as long as it took him to wonder whether he ought to leave.

"The observer."

"I'd like to read the demonstration provision. The academy's copy."

"Would you." She did not move. "Most people ask their assessor to tell them what it says."

"My assessor told me to read it."

Something changed very slightly at the corner of Prynn's mouth. She put her spectacles back on, came down off her stool, and opened the door perhaps two fingers wider than its usual angle, which was not an invitation but the absence of a refusal, and from her that seemed to be the same thing.

The archive was colder than the corridor and much quieter. The shelves ran back in narrow aisles one person wide, and the light came from three high windows and a single lamp on the reading table. Prynn walked him to the end of the nearest aisle, which held the academy's own records, newer than anything else in the room, took down a thick bound book with Statutes and Provisions stamped on its spine in faded gilt, laid it on the table, and opened it without looking to the right page.

"You've done that before."

"Every year or two, for sixty years." She set a weight on the facing page to hold it flat. "Mostly for Quenna. Once for a man who wanted to know if he could use it for his nephew. He couldn't." She looked at him over the spectacles. "Tea?"

He had not expected that. "Yes. Thank you."

She went away between the shelves, and he sat and read. The provision was short; after an afternoon of arguments in a back room he had expected something longer, and it was barely half a page. It said that a candidate without a standard classification issued by an Arbiter might be enrolled for academic exposure and supervised training, that such a candidate would be assessed monthly by demonstration before a panel of three, that the candidate must demonstrate consistent, observable practice, and that the panel's finding should be entered in the candidate's record. That was very nearly all of it. He read it twice, slowly, paying attention to what was not there. There was no word about best, no word about all, no word about naming anything, and no word, he noticed, about how a candidate had come by whatever he practiced. The provision asked what he could do. It did not ask where it came from.

He sat back and let out a breath he had not known he was holding.

Prynn came back with a cup on a saucer and set it at his elbow, well away from the open book. The tea was very strong and very hot and had plainly been stewing in its pot since the morning.

"Don't spill it on the statutes."

"I won't."

"Everyone says that." She returned to her high stool and her ledger and did not look at him again.

He drank the tea, which was terrible, and drank all of it anyway, because she had brought it, and because the room was cold, and because he had a feeling that refusing it would be noticed and remembered for a very long time. When he left he closed the book and set it square on the table exactly where she had laid it, with the weight beside it, and carried the cup and saucer to the end of her desk. Prynn looked at the cup, and then at the book, square and closed, and then at him.

"Hm," she said, and went back to her ledger.

Two days later he saw that she had left the book out for him. It was still on the table, closed, with the weight beside it, when he next came in. Nobody had reshelved it, and he was fairly sure that nobody in that room did anything Prynn had not decided they should.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

That night he sat on his bed with the binder and began, as he began most decisions that mattered, by writing down everything he could show and then striking through most of it, until what was left would fit in the palm of his hand. Then he made himself do something harder, which was to imagine the record being read.

Not by Quenna and not by Wray. They would be in the room, and whatever they wrote would be honest. He imagined it being read a year from now, in some office he had never seen, by somebody who had never been in the room at all. He built that reader carefully, because a careless version would be useless. Not a villain; a villain would make mistakes out of spite, and spite could be planned for. He built a clerk instead, patient and thorough and correct in every procedure, with a long file of notes on him and no particular feeling about him either way, who would sit at a plain desk under a plain lamp and read the panel's entry line by line, looking not for what it said but for what it implied. How fast had the observer grown? Where was his ceiling? What could he do that a child who had not yet Kindled could not possibly do? What, in short, made it harder to call him an unclassified observer and keep a straight face?

He had met people like that, a man in a market square with careful questions and a careful voice, officials who had looked at him across desks and written things he never got to read. He let them blur into one patient figure under a lamp, at a desk somewhere at the end of the road the brown envelope had gone down. He sat across the desk from that figure in his imagination and went through what he could show one capability at a time, and watched what the reader did with each. He hated every minute of it. He was fairly sure it was the best use of his time all week.

When he was done, he wrote the rule across the top of a clean page in the slow, square hand he kept for things he meant to obey.

Show enough to pass. Bank everything that matters.

Then he went through the binder section by section, and decided.

Wind-adjacent first: Lira's framework, drilled through every bout he had fought since she had taught it to him, neither of them knowing at the time what was being taught. Its range was the length of a fight. It read a strike off an opponent's body a half-beat before the strike arrived and let him step, slip or turn into the space the strike would not occupy. Its price was fatigue over long exchanges and one structural weakness, which was that he had to choose his direction before he moved, so that a sharp opponent who saw the choice could close the door behind it. Against faster opponents it read less. He had shown it on the Ardenmere circuit a hundred times in front of crowds and judges and at least one man from the Compact, and it was not a secret anymore. It was simply skill.

Show.

Iron-adjacent, Brom's gift: a pressure-sense along the skin that told him where a body's weight was about to go, at contact and out to a few paces. Its range was short and speed thinned it, so that against a fast opponent at distance it gave him almost nothing. Its price was close attention, a listening with the whole body that tired the mind more than the muscles. It had been on the circuit too, more quietly, visible to anyone watching only as a boy who was very rarely surprised.

Show.

Pressure-adjacent, Feryn's redirect: three clean uses mapped across a long, careful year, each paid for in the right shoulder at a price he knew to the ounce. Contact only. It took force aimed at him and turned it, the way a door on a good hinge turns a shove into a swing. It had never been shown to any judge or panel or official. Lira and Brom knew, and no one else.

Bank.

Compression-adjacent: days old, a quarter of a slow push caught on a good try, paid for through the shoulder and breastbone, with a habit of draining into the nearest joint whenever he forgot to choose a road for it first. It was the youngest thing he owned and the least understood. If he showed it badly, the record would say erratic; if he showed it well, the record would say something far worse.

Bank.

And under all four, the thing that was not a fragment at all: how any of them had come to him. Each had a name beside it in the binder, the person it had come from, Lira and Feryn and Brom and Reydan, and beyond that he did not know anything. They had arrived without asking and without explaining, and he had spent long hours learning the shape of each one after it came and none at all understanding why it had. The binder had a section for each, and a page for each notice, and between its lines a quiet suspicion that the list was not finished. That was not something a person demonstrated. It was the ground every demonstration stood on, and the provision asked for practice; it said nothing about digging.

Never.

Two shown, two banked, and one thing never. Written down that way it looked almost tidy, and because the log was the one place he never lied, he added a line at the bottom: Iron-equivalent by Vell's ledger. That means I can beat Iron-tier fighters. It does not mean I have a tier. It does not mean the panel will believe either.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On the sixth morning Oona found him in front of the assessment board.

He had not meant to stop there. He kept doing it anyway. His line was still there in the same ink as everybody else's — Eighth day. First bell. — and Oona stood beside him with her slate under her arm and read it too, moving her lips.

"That's yours. The demonstration."

"Yes."

"I don't have one of those."

"No."

"Why do you?"

He thought about how to answer. He had decided at the classroom door that he would not lie to her. He was finding that a promise like that was much harder to keep with a thirteen-year-old than with anyone else, because she asked the questions everyone else was too polite to.

"Because I'm older, and they want to see what I can do."

"Can you do things?"

"Some."

"Are you scared?"

He opened his mouth to say no, the way he would have said it to Naveth or the gate clerk or anyone who asked across a desk. Then he looked at her, small and solemn with her slate, and found he did not want to give her a grown-up's answer.

"A little."

"I'm scared about my Kindling. Not very. A little. My mother says it doesn't hurt. My uncle says it's like being hit by a door you didn't know was there." She frowned. "I don't know which one is lying."

"Neither of them, probably. It's different for everyone."

"What was yours like?"

He thought of the certification office in Denvash, the scrubbed floor and the clerk's gentle voice and the silence that had gone on far too long, and the word in brackets afterward that had followed him across half the continent.

"Short," he said at last. "And then very long."

Oona turned the answer over, and Cael braced himself for the next question. It did not come. She looked up at him with something that, on an adult, he would have called sympathy.

"That sounds like a bad one."

"It wasn't a good one."

"Mine will be ordinary," she announced. "I've decided."

"I hope it is."

"It will be. Good luck on the eighth day. I hope you're not boring."

She went off down the hall before he could tell her that boring was the entire plan. He stood in front of the board a while longer, smiling, and the small cold knot he had been carrying under his breastbone since the notice slid under his door had loosened by about a thread.

The refusal came that same afternoon. It was waiting in the narrow wooden box with his name on it at the assessors' desk, folded once, written in a clerk's hand under a printed heading.

Request for assignment of training partner, supervised sessions, demonstration provision. Request declined at this time. The provision does not presently authorize regular partnered practice for candidates in the observer category. The request has been entered in the candidate's file.

At the bottom were two sets of initials, and one of them was Quenna's.

He read it in the corridor, and was surprised by what he felt, which was not disappointment but something much closer to satisfaction. It said no, and not yet, and we have written down that you asked, and he had spent most of his life in front of doors that said nothing at all; a no with a date and two sets of initials was better company than any silence. He took it up to his room and slid it into the pocket inside the binder's back cover, behind the stranger's note from Ardenmere and Vell's folded sheaf, where he kept the papers that proved things.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

That night after the eighth bell he knocked on Brom's door. Brom opened it already in his shirtsleeves, looked at Cael's face, and stepped back without a word to let him in.

The room was the mirror of Cael's own, narrow and whitewashed, with the one difference that Brom had already arranged everything he owned in neat rows on the shelf, as if he expected an inspection, and had set his enrollment tag in the very centre of the row, crest up.

"Compression," said Cael.

"Before an assessment?"

"Not for the assessment. It isn't going anywhere near the assessment." He sat on the floor with his back against the bed. "But it's the only one that still gets worse when I leave it alone. Two days without practice and the timing slides."

Brom lowered himself onto the floor opposite, slowly, keeping his right side stiff. The ribs the broad Stone student had found four days ago had gone a deep, spreading purple. He had shown them to Lira, who had said something sharp about Stone Path students and then fetched him a cold cloth from the kitchens.

"Left hand. The right side still doesn't like leaning."

"Left's fine."

They worked quietly, the way they had on the road. Brom set his left palm against Cael's braced forearm and hardened it, a little Iron Skin coming up under the skin like frost forming on a window, and leaned. Cael waited until the force was in the bone, and chose the road before it could choose for itself — out, back along the line it came in — and reached.

The first try failed; he had been early, and the fragment simply did not answer, and the push came and went like any push. The second caught, and he sent it back, and a quarter of Brom's weight knocked against Brom's own wrist with that small solid sound. Then the bill arrived, the hot bar laid across his collarbones and the two breaths he could not take, and he sat with his eyes shut and waited them out while Brom waited with him.

They did ten. Four caught. None went to a joint, and each one that caught cost exactly the same, down to the breath.

"Four in ten," Brom said at the end. "On the road it was three in twelve."

"Same size, though. A quarter. Every time."

"The size is a different problem. You've fixed the timing." Brom turned his left hand over and looked at it. "When you started, you were reaching early and hoping. Now you wait, and you wait well. I could feel you waiting."

"What does waiting feel like, from your side?"

Brom thought about it seriously. "Like pushing on a door and knowing someone's standing on the other side of it, deciding whether to open it."

Cael wrote that down, not knowing yet what it was evidence of, only that it felt like evidence. He did not reach for the Pressure redirect, though he thought about it. His right shoulder had spent its credit on the road, and it would be asked for nothing in two days' time, and he wanted it quiet and unbothered and dull. Some things were banked in the binder, he decided. Some were banked in the body.

When they were done, Brom sat back against the desk leg and looked at the ceiling.

"She had me on the floor again today. Same partner. He still hasn't told me his name, and I haven't asked." His mouth twitched. "It's started to feel like a rule, as if asking would spoil something."

"What did she have you do?"

"Fetch." He said the word with a kind of rueful respect. "He held back, and I had to make him give me something without opening myself up to get it. I couldn't. I opened myself up eleven times, and every time she stopped it and showed me where." He touched his ribs very lightly. "She didn't let him hit me again, though. She's careful about that. She said the bruise had already taught me everything a bruise could teach."

"Did it help?"

"Not yet." He did not sound discouraged. He sounded, if anything, pleased, the way he had sounded at the end of their first fight in Ardenmere, when he had found the whole result interesting. "But I know what I'm bad at now. Two years I didn't know. That's not nothing."

Cael thought of the page in the binder with its four headings, and of Brom spending four days filling in the cost column for himself and being happy about it.

"No. It isn't nothing."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

On the seventh evening Lira took the whole question away from him and turned it into a training session, because whatever she could not settle by arguing she settled with her hands.

She had found a way around the refusal. Cael was not entirely sure how; he suspected she had gone straight to Quenna and asked a question shaped very precisely to fit the rules, and he suspected Quenna had enjoyed it. The training-hall roster for the last supervised block that evening now carried a new line in a clerk's hand — Assessment preparation. Observer track. Demonstrator: Lira, re-certification track. — on a different form from the one he had filled out, a form that said nothing at all about a partner.

"I'm not your partner," Lira said, signing in at her end of the desk while he signed in at his. "I'm a demonstrator. I'm here to demonstrate strikes so you can demonstrate getting out of their way. It's completely different."

"It's exactly the same."

"It's on a different form," she said serenely, "which makes it different."

An assessor Cael did not know sat on a stool by the wall with a slate on his knee, pretending not to find them interesting, and Lira took her mark in the chalk ring.

"Framework. Half speed."

He ran it, and she struck, clean and simple, from a dozen angles, and he read each strike off her body a half-beat early and stepped where it would not be.

"Again. Demonstration speed."

He ran it faster.

"Stop," she said after the fourth pass. "Second strike. You went out too far."

"I corrected."

"You corrected halfway through the step. You were making up your mind on the move." She reset her feet. "Listen. In a fight, deciding while you move is the whole point; that's what the framework is for. But in that room tomorrow a choice made mid-step reads as reflex, and reflex reads as something that happens to you, and that's the last thing you want on their slates."

He stopped, thinking of Quenna in the corridor. Practice means it is something you do on purpose.

"Let them see a skill somebody chose. A choice made beforehand looks finished. So finish every choice out here, tonight, where the only slate belongs to him, and he doesn't count."

The assessor by the wall went on pretending not to listen.

"How fast?"

Lira considered, and then invented a speed on the spot, as she invented most useful things.

"Panel speed. Quick enough that nobody thinks you're pretending. Slow enough that a pen can keep up."

They ran it eleven more times. The first three were bad, because his body knew the framework at full speed and kept trying to use it that way in the middle of the pattern. Lira stopped him each time with a single raised hand and a flat look. On the fourth he found the pace, and it felt wrong in his legs, slower than anything he had ever done for real; on the fifth it felt less wrong; by the seventh he had stopped thinking about it. Somewhere around the eighth, something changed in the work. It stopped being a framework he was holding back and became one that had been built to a certain height beforehand, so that he was no longer catching himself mid-step and reining in, because the limits were already there, set before he moved, like the depth of a channel cut before the water came, and there was nothing left to flex and nothing for a watching eye to catch adjusting. He felt the change before he understood it, and on the ninth pass he understood it and nearly laughed out loud, because it was the same lesson the Compression fragment had been teaching him all week — choose first, always choose first — and Lira was teaching it to him in a completely different language, and he had not noticed until now that they were the same sentence.

On the eleventh pass Lira lowered her hands and stepped back. "There."

She tossed him his water, and he drank while she watched him with her head on one side.

"That's a fence. You've built it to the provision's height and not a finger over." She took the water back and drank herself. "Whatever's on the other side of it, keep your eyes off it tomorrow."

"That's your professional advice?"

"I'm a demonstrator. It's on the form."

Brom was at the rail. Cael had not seen him come in; he had simply become part of the room at some point in the second half of the drill, leaning on his good side with the patient interest he gave to most things worth watching. He fell in beside them as they left the hall.

"The surface read. Do the last part with your eyes closed."

"Why?"

"It's true, and it reads as restraint." Brom shrugged, carefully, minding his ribs. "You don't need your eyes for it; you never did. But they don't know that. If you shut them at the end, they'll see you aren't watching the partner's hands or his face or his feet. They'll know you're reading something they can't see you read."

"That sounds like the opposite of what I want."

"No. Listen." Brom stopped on the path and turned to face him, which was how he signalled that a thing mattered. "Somebody with a slate is always hunting for one word, and it's the word that tells them you won't hurt anyone. Controlled. Give them a reason to write it, and it goes with you everywhere that file goes." He started walking again. "Shut your eyes for the last one."

Lira looked at Brom with open admiration. "When did you get good at evaluators?"

"Velmere," said Brom shortly. "I spent my whole childhood learning what evaluators liked so I could stop giving it to them." He considered. "Turns out it's still useful the other way round."

He lay awake that night in the narrow room and ran the morning through the way he used to run fight preparation the night before a circuit bout: the framework first, four times, at panel speed, the same structure each time and only the angle varied. Then the surface read, four calls, eyes open for three and closed for the last; and nothing else, no Pressure, no Compression, nothing about where any of it had come from. Small. The same every time. Dull, with any luck. Dull would get him a second month, and a third. On the circuit he had learned to make crowds lean forward, and tomorrow the whole skill would be to make three people with slates sit back in their chairs.

Across the corridor Brom shifted in his sleep and grunted at his ribs. Two doors down there was no sound at all, which meant Lira was awake and lying very still.

He was not afraid, he found when he looked. He was nervous, which was different. Afraid would have meant he did not know what was going to happen; nervous only meant he did. He thought of the sentence across the top of the clean page, and of his line on the board in the main hall in the same ink as everyone else's. He fell asleep somewhere between the two, and did not dream.

Chapter 7 — Consistent, Observable Practice

[Quiet, precise narration; restrained institutional pressure and careful new beginnings]

The training hall at first bell was a room he had never seen before, though he had walked through it every day for a week.

Someone had cleared it. The chalk lines of the six sections had been swept away, leaving only faint pale ghosts on the boards, and a single fresh ring had been drawn at the centre of the floor. The high windows let in a thin grey morning, and the air smelled of new chalk and cold stone and, faintly, of the lamp oil someone had burned before dawn to see by while they swept. At the far end stood three chairs in a row facing the ring, each the same distance from the next, with a faint chalk tick on the boards beside each leg to tell him somebody had used a rule, and in front of the middle chair a small table with an inkwell on it. There was nothing else: no benches, no rail, no crowd. He had fought in front of six hundred people at the Ironyard. He had never once walked into a room this quiet to be looked at.

Quenna sat in the centre chair with a slate on her knee. To her left sat Wray, upright and still in her brown coat buttoned to the throat, watching him come in with the same level attention she had given Brom on the defensive floor. To Quenna's right sat a man Cael had never met, older than both women, white-haired and spare, who sat as a heron stands in a shallow, ready to wait all morning for one thing worth noticing. He had a slate too, and had already written something on it. The rotating seat, the one he could not prepare for. Cael did not try. He looked at the man once, noted his age and his stillness and the loose way he held his pen, as if he had held a great many pens and broken none of them, and then let him go.

The training partner was waiting in the ring, and Cael knew him at once: the broad student from Brom's floor, the Stone Path fourth-year with forearms like fence posts and a face of perfect patience. He stood easily at his mark with his feet a shoulder-width apart and regarded Cael without any curiosity at all. Wray rose, crossed to him, and bent to his ear; the boy nodded once, and Wray returned to her chair. Then he settled his weight and waited, without glancing at the panel or at Cael's tag, simply standing there being furniture, and whatever he had been lent for, he plainly meant to be that and nothing more. Cael felt a rush of gratitude toward him so strong that it embarrassed him.

"For the record," said Quenna.

Her voice had dropped into a slower, flatter cadence, each word set down separately, and Cael understood that from this moment everything she said was being written as she said it.

"Demonstration assessment. Unclassified observer track. First sitting. Present: the presiding assessor, the instructor's seat, the rotating faculty seat. The candidate demonstrates at his own election, under the panel's observation; the instructor's seat will direct the exercise partner." She looked up. "Begin when you choose."

She said it the way a clerk says next, and he suspected she had practiced that.

He walked into the ring and took his mark across from the partner at the distance Lira had drilled into his legs the night before. He set his feet and let his shoulders drop, and he chose. That was the whole of the preparation now, and he did it before anything moved: the framework would run at panel speed, four passes, the same structure each time, its ceiling already built and its height already set, the channel already cut before the water came. Whatever happened in the next quarter of an hour, he would not decide it while moving.

"Framework," he told the panel. "Evasion. Four passes, same structure, varied angle."

Wray lifted a finger to the partner, and the partner struck.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

It was an honest strike with nothing theatrical in it. The boy came in on a straight line from the left with his weight committed exactly as far as a textbook recommended, a solid, workmanlike blow aimed at the centre of Cael's chest. Cael read it off his body before it had properly begun. The read came the way it always came, not from the fist but from the hip, from the small settling of weight into the boy's front foot and the quarter-inch drop of his shoulder as it loaded, so that a half-beat before the strike had any speed in it Cael already knew where it was going to be. The framework moved him out of that place and into the space beside it.

He did not hurry, and that was the hard part. Every muscle that had fought on the Ardenmere circuit wanted to slip the strike at full speed and come back around inside it with a counter, as he had a thousand times against fighters who meant to hurt him, and instead he moved at the speed he and Lira had set the night before, quick enough to be real and slow enough for a pen, and stepped half a pace to his right with his weight already set for the next.

The second strike came from the right. He read it and moved.

The third came low, a short hooking blow at the ribs, and he turned his hip away from it a half-beat before it arrived and let it pass through the air where his side had been.

The fourth came high. He sank under it, rose behind it, and stood still.

Four strikes, four reads, the same structure from beginning to end with only the angles changed. He reset to his mark and waited, and three pens moved at the far end of the hall.

"Second pass," said Quenna.

He ran it again. The partner came in from a new set of angles, each called by Wray with a small movement of her fingers that Cael could see from the corner of his eye and did not try to read, because it made no difference what she called. The framework did not care where a strike came from, only that a body was about to send one. Read, move. Read, move. When he came back to his mark he was breathing a little harder than he would have liked, not from tiredness but from the effort of holding a thing at a pace it did not want to go.

Between the second pass and the third, Wray raised a finger and held it there. She did not speak. She looked at the partner, and something passed between them that Cael could not read, and then she lowered her finger halfway and held it again, and lowered it the rest of the way at a moment that was not on the rhythm she had used before.

The partner struck early.

He came a quarter-beat ahead of where the count would have put him, and on the next strike half a beat behind, and on the third with almost no gap at all between two blows. Wray had broken the count. Whatever she had told him at the start, it had included this, to be done when she gave the sign: abandon the pattern and see what happened to a fighter who had been fed it.

Cael knew within the first strike what she was testing. If his framework ran on the count, if over two passes he had learned the panel's rhythm and was moving on the beat rather than on the body, then breaking the count would break him. He would step into a strike he had expected later, or away from one that came sooner than he thought. But the framework did not run on the count and never had. It ran off the boy's hips and shoulders and the weight in his front foot, and those told the truth whatever rhythm Wray chose, so that the first early strike came at him and he read it off the boy's body as easily as the others and moved at panel speed into the space beside it, and the late one he read too.

The double came fast, two blows almost on top of each other, and for a fraction of a second he felt the old circuit hunger leap up in him, wanting full speed, wanting to slip both and come back around. He did not let it. The ceiling was built. He moved at the speed he had chosen the night before and took the second strike, not cleanly, on the outside of his left forearm.

It landed solid. A Stone Path fourth-year, even holding back, hit like a dropped sack of grain.

And something in Cael's chest woke up.

It was low and tight and familiar, the gathering he had felt every morning on the road and every evening in Brom's room. The force of the blow was already in the bone of his forearm, already his. The Compression fragment had felt it arrive and was reaching toward it, closing on it as a hand closes on something dropped into it. For one breath a road opened, and he could feel exactly where it went: out, back along the line the strike had come in, a quarter of the boy's own weight sent home into the boy's braced arm with that small solid sound like a door shutting in another room.

Three people with slates would hear it.

He chose.

He chose nothing. He gave the gathered force no road at all, and he let it go. It spilled out of him harmlessly, as it had on the last road morning when he felt it sliding toward his knee. His forearm took the blow the ordinary way that any forearm takes a blow, with a dull flat ache that would be a bruise by supper.

He finished the pass — read, move — and came back to his mark.

His heart was going hard. He kept his face still and his breathing slow and his hands loose at his sides. Nothing had happened; that was the whole point. Nothing at all had happened, and anyone at the far end of the hall would have seen a boy take one strike on the forearm out of a dozen and keep his form.

Wray lowered her finger and wrote.

The fourth pass he ran on her ordinary count again. It came out the same as the first, the same structure and the same four reads, and nothing in it showed the broken rhythm, or the strike, or the road he had not taken.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The rotating seat spoke for the first time.

"Your lead." His voice was mild and dry and addressed to the room in general. "The half-beat. Is it the same against any partner, or does it change when the partner is faster?"

Cael had prepared for many questions and not for that one, and he was glad, because it meant he had to answer it honestly instead of well.

"It changes."

Then, because the room ran on exactness and he wanted his own words in the record to be exact: "It has limits. It reads the opponent's body. The quicker someone is, the less of his body I have to read from. Their weight shifts later, and for less time, and the faster they get, the less there is to go on. I haven't found where it stops working. I know which direction that is."

The rotating seat wrote for a long time, and when he finally looked up he looked faintly, modestly pleased, like a man who has been handed exactly the right tool without having to describe it twice. Cael understood why after a moment. He had handed the man an edge, and an edge could be measured, and a thing that could be measured sounded studied rather than boasted about; boasting was what got underlined later, by people under lamps.

"Thank you," said the rotating seat.

"Second demonstration," said Cael. "Surface read."

It was simpler to show and stranger to watch. Through Wray he asked the partner to stand at the edge of reach and shift his weight in any direction he chose, whenever he chose, doing nothing to hide it, and then he stood still two paces off and let the read open. It came in through the skin, as it always did — not through his eyes, though he kept them open, but as a kind of pressure along his forearms and the backs of his hands and the front of his body, as if the air between them had grown thicker on one side than the other. A big body carried a great deal of weight, and weight that was about to move leaned on the world a moment before it went.

"Left. Heel."

The partner's weight went to his left heel.

"Forward. Right foot."

It went forward onto the right foot.

"Back. Both."

The partner rocked back onto both heels, a fraction late this time, as if he had begun to suspect something and wanted to see whether he could beat the call. He couldn't; Cael had named it before the boy had properly decided.

For the fourth call he closed his eyes. He did it as Brom had told him to, simply and without any show. The hall went dark and the pressure along his skin did not change at all. It had never needed his eyes. It had only let him think it did. The big body in front of him leaned very slightly toward the right and went still, then leaned toward the right again with more weight in it, as if gathering itself.

"Right. Toes."

He opened his eyes in time to see the boy's weight settle forward onto the ball of his right foot.

The partner huffed through his nose, startled, like a man who has just heard someone finish his sentence, and for the first time all morning he looked at Cael properly, a long, flat, measuring look. Then he looked back at Wray and waited for his next instruction. Wray gave him nothing. She wrote.

Cael stepped back to his mark. "That's the demonstration."

The panel withdrew to the end of the hall farthest from him and stood close together by the wall with their slates, speaking too low for him to follow. He read what he could anyway, because he could not help it. Wray spoke first and briefly and then folded her arms. The rotating seat spoke longer and used his hands, sketching something in the air with one finger that might have been a curve. Quenna said almost nothing; she listened with her pen still, and twice she nodded before the speaker had finished, and he guessed from that that her mind was already made up.

The partner stood easy in the ring throughout. He did not sit, though nothing stopped him, and he did not wander or stretch or look over at the panel. He simply stood where he had been told to stand, feet planted and hands loose, showing not the slightest interest in the verdict, and waited to be told he could go. Cael's eyes rested on him. He had watched this boy put Brom on one knee on their second day here, and now had been hit by him himself, once, on the forearm, and he still did not know his name. Brom had said that not asking had started to feel like a rule. Cael did not think asking would spoil anything. He thought the boy had probably stood in for other people's tests so often that nobody had thought to ask him anything at all, and that was not a rule. It was only a habit everyone had fallen into without noticing. He decided, standing there, that he would learn the boy's name before the month was out, and find a proper moment to thank him — for the patience, for the honest strikes, for being exactly as useful as he was asked to be on a morning when being interesting was the most dangerous thing in the room. He did not say any of this. He put it away somewhere he would not lose it.

The panel returned to their chairs. Quenna made a note on her slate and glanced to her left, and Wray spoke without any change in her voice, as if she were reading a measurement off a gauge.

"Unorthodox architecture. Consistent execution. No safety concerns."

Quenna wrote it down word for word, and Cael watched her pen form each phrase, and watched the rotating seat nod once, very slightly.

"Assessment satisfied," said Quenna, and set down her pen.

Nobody moved. The hall had the stillness of a sum that has come out right and needs no checking.

Cael stood in the swept ring and waited to feel something enormous. For four days he had built this morning in his head into a far larger and more dangerous room than the one he was standing in, and now that it was over the room felt almost small — not unimportant, but small: three chairs, a ring of chalk, a few sentences in ink. The distance between the room he had feared and the room he got seemed like a lesson worth keeping.

The rotating seat was the first to go, slate under his arm, with nothing more to say. Wray stood, looked at Cael, and nodded once, the same nod he had seen her give Brom, which meant that something had held when she leaned on it. Then she went to the partner, spoke a word, and walked out with him a step behind her.

The door closed. Quenna stayed.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Quenna laid her slate on the little table and turned it over, so that the writing faced the wood. The tap of it was the only sound in the hall.

"That satisfies today," she said.

It was not the voice she had used for the record. The record voice was flat and slow and built for clerks. This one sat lower and came at him more directly, and Cael had begun to notice that she kept it for things she wanted left off every page.

"Before your shoulders come down, hear what today was."

He nodded, and stayed on his mark.

"Today proves you're real." She folded her hands. "Nothing more than that. It's the first line in your record. From this morning on, the file holds a candidate under this provision who did what the provision asks, in the provision's own terms, and gave a hostile reader nothing to take hold of. That was the whole task. You did it, and you did it well."

He could hear that she had more.

"The sittings that matter are later ones. Those are the ones a person will read who wants you gone. This morning we were the writers. One day the reader will be somebody who has never sat in any of these chairs, and every line we put down from here on has to stand up in front of that somebody."

Cael thought of the reader he had imagined under lamplight, a patient shape at the bottom of the hill road where the brown envelope had gone. He thought of the third pass, and the road he had refused to open, and how near it had been.

"I'll be ready."

"I know." She stood and took up the slate, still face down. "You being ready has never been what keeps me up."

She gave no reason, and he did not ask for one. Hesk had handed him sentences like that, and so had Vell; some things were meant to be carried shut. Her footsteps went away along the hall, and the door closed after them.

He did not leave at once. The quiet a panel left behind it was its own particular quiet, and he let it work on him until his shoulders came down by themselves. His left forearm had begun to throb where the third pass had caught it, and along the outer edge the bruise was rising already, dull red with blue underneath. He had paid for a road he never took, and the log had a column for that kind of price. In the chalk ring the morning was still written out: the scuffs his own feet had made, two deep marks where the partner's heels had dug in, a smear where he had dropped low under the last strike of the first pass. Somebody with a broom would take all of it before the fifth bell. After that, the only place the morning would exist was a folder on a shelf in a school that ran on paper. They had written him down for an hour, and every word they had been allowed to write was a word he had chosen: two things shown, two held back, and one never reached for at all. It had gone well. He meant to keep it going well.

On his way out he crouched at the ring's edge and set two fingers in the smear, as someone leaving a house touches the doorframe. Then he got up and went to find the others.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

Nobody outside the hall knew what had happened in it. That did not slow anyone down. By the fourth bell the whole academy had decided something had, and was busy deciding what.

He felt it in small changes, as a fighter feels a crowd turn behind him. A conversation on the stair paused as he passed and started again behind him. A first-year looked at his tag, saw the hollow circle where every other tag had a crest, and became suddenly fascinated by the ceiling. Two older girls from the lecture wing, who had not once looked at him all week, wished him good morning on the stair in careful, bright voices, as if they were putting a coin in a box against a rainy day.

Lira slid onto the bench across from him at the midday meal with the bright, contented face of a circuit veteran reporting on a district she understood perfectly.

"Current theories. In order of popularity."

"Please don't."

"First." She held up a finger. "You're a late Kindler and your classification's been sealed by a court, and nobody's allowed to say what it is. Very popular with the second-years. They like the word sealed."

Brom, beside her, was eating barley with the slow, devoted attention of a man who did not intend to be distracted by anything as minor as his friend's reputation.

"Second. You're the son of some important family in the north. They've had a scandal and hidden you here until it blows over. That one's mostly the girls on the third floor. They've given you a tragic past, and you should be flattered; it's very detailed."

"What is it?"

"I didn't stay for all of it. There's a river involved." A third finger. "Third. You're from the Compact, sent to watch the faculty and report on whether Greyvane is fit to keep its charter. That one's spreading fastest. People are being very nice to you because of it."

"That's why the girls on the stair said good morning."

"That's why the girls on the stair said good morning." Lira looked deeply satisfied. "And there's a fourth, very small, mostly among the first-years, that you can't fight at all, and you spent the closed session reading poetry to the panel, and they passed you out of pity."

Cael put down his spoon. "Where did that come from?"

"The first-years," said Lira with enormous dignity, "came up with that entirely by themselves. I only told a few of them that you'd asked me how to spell sonnet." She reached across the table and took the better half of his bread without asking. "It's my favourite. It's the only one where you lose."

"Not one of them is anywhere near."

"Isn't it lovely? Four stories, all wrong, all pulling different ways, and everyone's so busy arguing with each other that nobody's looking at you." She tore the bread in half again and gave one piece back. "Worry when they start to agree."

Brom looked up from his bowl for the first time. "How did it go?"

It was such a plain question, after Lira's market, that Cael laughed.

"Satisfied. Wray said three things, and Quenna wrote them down."

"What three things?"

He told them. Unorthodox architecture. Consistent execution. No safety concerns.

Brom chewed slowly, testing each phrase with his teeth.

"No safety concerns. That's the one. That's the best one." He went back to his barley. "That's controlled in a different coat."

Lira was looking at Cael's forearm, where his sleeve had ridden up and the bruise was beginning to show its colours. "And that?"

"The partner broke the count. I took one."

She studied the mark with the professional eye of a woman who had given and received a great many bruises. "You took it on purpose." It was not a question.

He thought of the road opening in his chest, and three pens.

"I took it instead of something else."

Lira said nothing. Then she nodded slowly, as she did when an opponent did something she would have done herself, and pushed the rest of the bread back across the table to him.

"Eat. You've earned the crust."

Chapter 8 — Vantage

[Quiet, precise narration; restrained institutional pressure and careful new beginnings]

By the time he crossed the yard that afternoon, the rumors had found a face to hang themselves on, and it was his.

He had first noticed Edran three days earlier, from the rail of the open floor, where an observer was allowed to stand and watch as long as he did not step over the chalk. Edran had been the easiest person in the hall to pick out, because everyone else on the floor moved around him like water around a post, without seeming to think about it, and because he fought with the settled ease of someone who had been at the top of a board for so long that he no longer checked whether he was still there. Glass Path. Iron Rank Two. First on the standings.

Cael had watched him for most of an hour, filling a page. Glass was not what he had expected; he had always thought of glass as the thing that broke. Edran's declarations broke, certainly, and Cael watched a bright, hard shell of something like crystal form along his forearm to take a strike and then burst into a glitter that hung for a heartbeat in the air before it vanished. But the shell did not break because it failed. It broke because breaking was what it was for: the burst carried the strike's force away with it in a hundred directions at once, and before the glitter had faded a new shell was already forming in the next place Edran expected to be hit. By the end of that first bout Cael had crossed out a page of his own notes about brittleness and started again.

Somewhere in the middle of the second bout, between exchanges, Edran had looked up at the rail. His eyes had gone first to the open binder, Cael was nearly sure, and only afterward to the person holding it. He held the look a beat longer than a glance needed, his face showing nothing at all, before he turned back to his opponent and finished the bout a little sharper than he had begun it, as if he had tightened a screw. Sharper with an audience, Cael had written under the page, and then, because the log was the one place he did not let himself be generous: Or he minds being taken down in ink. Find out which.

Now Edran was waiting near the yard's north gate, as a man waits when he has decided where another man will have to walk.

He was not alone. Three or four students were nearby, doing other things very slowly; one was retying a boot that had not come untied, and two were talking with the particular attention of people listening to a different conversation. Cael saw the shape of it before he was close enough to see faces. It was not an ambush. It was an audience.

"Observers don't demonstrate."

Edran said it to the yard in general, in a clear, level voice that carried without being raised, but he never once took his eyes off Cael, and Cael stopped walking.

"That's not what the category is for. I've read the provision. I've sat beside observers in lectures since my first year. Observers watch. They take notes. They don't get a panel and a closed hall and a training partner at first bell." He tilted his head very slightly. "So either the faculty spent a morning watching you do nothing, which I don't believe, or somebody wrote a form that says one thing and means another."

The boy retying his boot had stopped pretending.

"What exactly are you?"

It was not hostile, and that was the hard part. Cael had faced hostile questions all his life, and hostile questions were easy in their way, because they told you what the person wanted and you could refuse to give it. This was something else. Edran sounded genuinely curious, almost academic, like a student who has found a hole in a rule and would like to know how deep it goes. Anger burned out. Curiosity kept a notebook.

Cael felt the yard around him the way he felt a crowd before a bout, the loose half-ring of listeners, the boy with the boot. He knew that whatever he said in the next breath would be in every common room by the seventh bell, word for word, and improved on by the eighth. He went through what he had: a form that said a thing its signers knew was not so; a binder in his pack that no one here would ever read; and nothing between the two that he could say out loud and keep. He would not lie. He had decided that long ago, on a different road.

"I'm enrolled."

Every word of it was true, and none of it was the thing Edran had asked.

Edran looked at him, weighing it as Cael had watched him weigh an opponent between exchanges. Cael saw him consider pressing and decide against it, not out of kindness but out of something more like respect for a guard that had been put up properly.

"That isn't an answer."

"No."

"It's the one you're giving, though."

"Yes."

Edran nodded once, slowly, and left for the training hall without saying anything else. The boy with the boot went after him, and the others drifted apart, already talking. Cael stayed where he was by the north gate, his own shadow stretched long beside him on the packed earth, and understood that the question had not been answered. It had only been put down, carefully, where both of them could see it.

He told Brom that evening in the stable, over barley, because by now it would have felt stranger not to. Brom heard it out as he heard out any fight, which was what it had been, and asked two questions — where the other students had been standing, and whether Edran had raised his voice — and then ate without speaking, turning it over.

He's sat at the top of them since he came, and he thinks they're true. Then this morning the faculty spent first bell on somebody who isn't on them at all, and nobody will say why." He wrote the day up that night by the narrow window with the lamp turned low, in the four headings, because the four headings were where it belonged.

First assessment. Function shown: Wind framework, four passes at panel speed, one with the count broken; surface read, four calls, eyes closed on the last. Benefit: assessment satisfied. Wray's words, on the record: Unorthodox architecture. Consistent execution. No safety concerns. Cost: one strike taken, left forearm, third pass. He sat with that. It was true, and it frightened him a little, and he could not entirely say why.

He told Hesk the assessment had passed, that three people had watched, that one of them had asked a good question and he had answered it with a limit in it and the man had looked pleased. He did not mention the strike or the fragment that had reached for it; some things were for the binder. He signed it, folded it, and set it ready for Lira's next trip down the hill.

His supervised hour on the third day of the second week was the one he would remember, though nothing much happened in it.

It was section four again, and Quenna again, standing at the chalk with her slate, and nobody else. He ran the framework against no one at half pace and then full, supplying his own strikes out of the air, and did Lira's circuits, and at some point in the first quarter of an hour he realized he had stopped shaping any of it for the slate. He had not decided to stop. He had simply forgotten she was there. The work had become his own again, plain and repetitive and a little dull, the shoulder rolls slow and careful, the footwork patterns walked through over and over until his legs stopped asking his head for directions. Twice he glanced up and found her pen still, and once he found her not looking at him at all but out of the high window. He understood that she had stopped needing to watch him closely, which might have been the most useful thing that had happened to him all week.

At the end she signed the session record, and then, instead of handing him only the strip, she took a second slip from inside her folder and held it out between two fingers.

It was small and stiff, printed on a thin grey card, with a date stamped across one corner in purple ink and a set of initials he did not know in the margin. The printing said Received for Notation and beneath it, in a clerk's hand, his name, and the name of the academy, and a long reference number.

"It came back up the hill yesterday," Quenna said. "The regional office acknowledges what it's sent. They always do."

He turned the card over. The back was blank.

"So someone has it now."

"Someone has entered a line in a book, and initialed a card, and put the card in the post." She took it back from him and slid it into the folder. "Whether anyone reads the line is another question, and not one the card can answer."

"Usually," said Cael, "a clerk files it."

She looked at him, and he could not tell whether she was amused.

"Usually." She closed the folder. "You're learning the language. Keep your assessments clean, Cael. That's the whole of our part. Theirs is theirs."

He walked back across the yard with the date on the card fixed in his head, a purple stamp on a grey corner, the first thing that had come back up the road the brown envelope had gone down. It did not frighten him. It was more like hearing, from inside a quiet house, a door close somewhere at the far end of it, and knowing that someone else was home.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

In every other free hour of that second week, he watched.

That was what an observer was allowed to do, so he did it from the rail of the open floor, from the edge of the formal yard during standings bouts, and from the back of the defensive branch's drill hall, with the binder open on his knee and his pen moving. He could not fight anyone, and he was not eligible for the open bouts where most of the real learning of the place seemed to happen, the unscheduled matches between friends and rivals that filled the late afternoons. But nobody had ever said he could not stand at the edge and look. By the fourth day he was building a page format without having decided to. Across the top went the declaration structure, as far as he could see it from outside — what came up, where, how fast, how it faded — and down the left margin went the tells, the small things a body did before its Path did anything, and the middle held timing, and at the bottom of each page, after some days of trying other headings, he wrote a single line under the words What this Path believes. He had come to think that every Path held an opinion, not only a set of abilities but a settled view of what a fight was for and how one ought to be won, and that you could see the view in how its people stood long before they threw anything.

Glass believes you can afford to break if you break first and on purpose.

The Stone Path page was the broad student's. Cael had watched him three times now, on Brom's floor, across a chalk ring at first bell, and once more on the fifth day of the second week, drilling alone in a corner of the defensive hall while Wray worked with someone else. Alone, with no one to be furniture for, the boy moved differently — slower than Cael had expected, and lower, his feet barely seeming to leave the floor, though every shift of his weight went down through his heels and came back up a fraction stronger, as if the ground were lending him something each time he touched it. Watching, Cael realized that the boy had been solving the same problem Brom solved, how to take a strike and survive it, from the opposite direction entirely. Brom gave and borrowed. This boy refused to be moved at all, and let the ground do the arguing.

Stone believes that if you refuse to move, the other person has to.

The defensive branch posted its drill pairings on a board outside the hall. Cael had walked past it every day for a week without reading it, because it had nothing to do with him, and that afternoon he stopped and read it. Brom's name was there three times in the week, and each time, paired beside it in the same clerk's hand, was a single short name.

Hobb. Stone. Fourth year.

He said it under his breath once, to fix it. Hobb. It was a plain name for a plain, patient person who stood where he was told and hit exactly as hard as he was asked. Cael did not go and find him. A thank-you shouted across a drill hall would be worth nothing, and he did not want it to look like an observer currying favor with the partner who had been lent to him. He wanted a quiet moment, and he thought he would know it when it came. He wrote the name under the Stone Path page and left the debt where he could see it.

That evening he told Brom. "His name's Hobb."

Brom put his hand up flat, like a man stopping a cart. "Don't."

"Don't what?"

"Don't tell me any more. I'm going to ask him myself." Brom looked faintly embarrassed, and then faintly stubborn. "It's been two weeks. He's hit me harder than anyone in my life. The least I can do is hear his name from his own mouth."

"You already know it now."

"I'll forget it," said Brom firmly. "Watch me."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Lira's standings bout fell on the sixth day of the second week.

It was not an assessment, not exactly. The re-certification track required its candidates to fight a set number of recorded bouts each month against students from the standard roster, with the results entered in the candidate's file beside an assessor's initials, and it was meant to be routine. The clerk who scheduled it had paired her, by the luck of the roster, with a third-year standing high on the Copper side of the board: a Force Path, tall and long-armed, Copper Rank Eight by the board, with a clean record and a reputation, Cael learned from the rail, for pushing opponents out of the ring before they had properly set their feet. He had no dot beside his name anywhere. He came into the formal yard with the easy, half-bored air of somebody keeping an appointment.

Twenty or so students had drifted in to watch, not for him but for the dot.

Cael stood at the rail. Gerda came and stood two places along, arms folded, her ash-pale hair bright in the cold sun, and nodded to him without speaking, and a minute later Brom arrived, still moving carefully on his right side, and leaned on the rail between them.

"She's going to go hard," Brom said quietly.

"I know."

"She shouldn't."

"I know. She's going to anyway."

Gerda glanced at them both and said nothing, and then said, to no one in particular, "The assessor will initial it either way. The procedure doesn't care how she wins."

"Lira cares," said Brom.

Gerda considered that, and something passed over her face that Cael could not quite read.

"Yes," she said. "I used to."

The ring in the formal yard was wider than the training-hall sections, eight long paces across, and the chalk around its edge had been freshly laid, white against the packed brown earth. The Force Path took his mark on the north side with his back to the benches. Lira took hers on the south with the low sun behind her, which Cael suspected she had arranged by being first to the ring.

The first exchange went the way a procedural bout was supposed to go. The Force Path opened at the textbook distance and tested her with two straight pushes, each carrying a thickening of the air in front of his palm, a shove made solid. Lira slipped the first and let the second brush past her shoulder without committing to anything. She was measuring him. Cael could see it in her feet, which never quite settled, and in the way her eyes went to his hips and not his hands. The third push she let come all the way in before stepping off its line at the last instant, the Wind in her moving her a half-pace sideways as easily as a door swinging, so that the push went past her into empty air and the Force Path's weight followed it a little too far. She did not punish it. She stepped back to the centre, and the crowd made a small, satisfied sound, because that was what a procedural bout looked like: careful, polite, a testing of edges.

Then the second exchange began, and Lira stopped being polite.

She came off her mark before he had finished setting his feet, not at the textbook distance but inside it, fast, the way she had fought on the Ardenmere circuit when the rent was due, in a style no academy had ever taught her and Fenmark's records had never once managed to describe. The Force Path threw a push to drive her back out, and it was a good push, a real one, the air in front of his palm going thick and hard as a wall. She could have slipped it. Cael saw the space where she could have slipped it.

She didn't. She took it on the left shoulder.

It knocked her a full step sideways, and Cael heard Brom draw breath beside him. But she had turned with it, so that the step sideways became a step around, and before the Force Path had brought his arm back she was inside his reach on the side he had just opened and had hit him twice, short and hard, once under the ribs and once on the point of the shoulder that had pushed. He gasped and went back a pace, and the yard went very quiet. Cael had seen this before, on the circuit, many times: Lira had paid for those two strikes with a hit she could have avoided, deliberately, in front of everyone, so that everyone would see the price and see that she did not care about it.

The Force Path was not a fool, and in the third exchange he tried to take the fight back to where he wanted it. He reset to the textbook distance, five paces, and set himself properly, rear foot planted, and when she came in again he was ready for her and threw a push low and wide at her legs to take away her footing. She jumped it, the Wind lifting her a hand's width higher than her legs alone could have managed, and landed already moving, and he had read that too. His second push was waiting for her landing, high this time, aimed at the place her shoulders would be when her feet touched down. It caught her half-turned and drove her back across the ring toward the south chalk, three paces, four, until her rear heel came down a finger's width from the line and she stopped there with her arms out like someone on a wall.

The crowd drew a breath. Gerda's arms came unfolded.

Lira stood on the edge for a heartbeat, breathing, and Cael watched her look not at the Force Path's hands but at his feet. He saw what she saw, because he had been watching the same thing from the rail. Before every full push, the tall boy planted his rear foot. It was a small thing, the heel going down flat and the knee softening, the body asking the ground for something to push from, and it came a clear half-beat before the palm opened. She had found the tell. The next push came, and his rear heel went down. She was already gone, stepping off the line on the plant rather than the palm, so that the push went through the space where she had been and out over the chalk into empty yard. She came back along the edge of the ring and in at his side, and he had to turn to find her.

He learned. Cael saw him learn it, and liked him a little for it. For the rest of the third exchange the tall boy stopped planting, pushing instead from wherever his feet happened to be, short, quick shoves with less weight behind them, which she could no longer read early but which no longer had the weight to move her far. The exchange ended with the two of them back near the centre, his chest heaving and her shoulder beginning to stiffen, neither ahead.

The fourth exchange was the one Cael drew afterward in the binder, as a map, with arrows.

She did not let him have distance. A Force Path's push needed room between palm and target to gather itself, the way a door needs room to swing. She simply refused him that room: she came in and stayed in, inside his elbows, so close that any push he threw had nowhere to travel before it reached her and arrived as little more than a shove. He stepped back to make space. She followed, and slightly to his left. He stepped back again. She followed, a little more to his left. Each step he took to find room for his arm she turned into a curve, so that without ever once hitting him she walked him in a slow arc across the ring. Cael, at the rail, watched the chalk come up behind the tall boy's heels a foot at a time and saw that he could not see it, because he was looking at her.

At the last he understood where he was. Cael saw it in his shoulders. He planted, once, hard, for one big push to clear her off him and buy back the ring — and she ducked under it, so that his own weight carried him forward over his planted foot. She put two fingers flat against his breastbone as he came, not a strike, hardly a touch, and he stepped back to keep his balance as anyone would.

His heel came down on the chalk.

The assessor called it.

She did not celebrate. She collected her water from the bench, drank, and walked off the formal ground toward the rail with the look of someone who has said what she came to say and does not intend to say it twice. The crowd did not leave at once. She left before either of them could answer, and Cael watched her walk away across the yard, tall and narrow and very straight, and wondered what Gerda's own file said, and what she had done the last time a floor had watched her and a box had not.

They sat on the wall outside the residence wing at dusk, the three of them, as they had sat on walls in a dozen towns. Lira had a cold cloth from the kitchens folded over her shoulder, where the push had landed, and the bruise underneath had come up dark and broad, and she did not seem to mind it. "The assessor initialed it," she said at last. "Before the sixth bell. Gerda was right. He looked at the time when I handed him the slip. He actually looked."

"So it's dated today," said Brom.

"It's dated today. It's in the file." She tilted her head back against the wall. "With a dot next to it."

Cael waited. He had learned long ago that Lira's thoughts arrived in their own time and did not like to be fetched.

"I still hate the dot. I want you both to know that. I'm not going to wake up one morning and like it."

"Nobody asked you to like it," said Brom.

"I know." She was quiet a moment. "But I signed the page, and I'm glad I signed it. I'm glad I'm here. Today I stood on their floor and did what I do, and twenty people saw it, and a clerk wrote it down with the date on it." She turned the cold cloth over on her shoulder. "Both of those are true. "What happened to the fight between them?"

Lira gave it the care she gave an opponent's footwork.
