The sky over the hill town went from gold to grey while the three of them sat on the wall outside the residence wing, and Cael spent most of it thinking about a satchel.

By now the bundle would be on the road in the courier's bag, wrapped in its oiled cloth. In a day or two it would come to rest on a desk. A knife would go through the string. Someone would read the six words Wray had given the second sitting and the two Quenna had given both, and the rotating seat's long, careful paragraph about an anticipation that grew thinner as opponents grew quicker.

"My name went into their books in Denvash," he said, not really to anyone. "They've had it every day since. That part's no different this month."

"Then what is?" said Lira.

It was a fair question, so he gave it time.

"The ground I'm standing on. Denvash's walls were Denvash's; nobody else had a key. The circuit wasn't anyone's at all, not so they could come and rap on it. Greyvane's different. It answers to them. They can tell it what to do, and it has to listen." He watched the town. "They never lost me. They knew where I was the whole time. All I've done is stand somewhere with a door they're allowed to knock on."

Brom had been watching the colour leave the sky, with the slow patience he gave most things now. When he spoke he did not turn his head.

"When I was little, my family kept a steward for the debts. The ones people owed us." He seemed to be counting the first lamps below. "He used to say that a man who writes before he sends the cart means to be paid in the end, and means to be paid quietly. The ones to fear, he said, were the ones whose cart came first."

"And this one?" said Lira.

"Wrote." Brom lifted his shoulders the smallest amount, the spare little shrug that Cael had learned meant the words under it had been a long time in the making. "If you write for papers first, you want it done according to the book. So there's a book. And Cael reads books."

Lira snorted, then laughed outright, and knocked Brom's knee with hers. "That's the most comforting thing you've ever said, and it was about collecting debts."

"Velmere was very good at collecting debts," Brom said, without any bitterness. "It's one of the few things I learned there that I still use."

Cael laughed with them, and then sat between them in the dusk without talking. Before the light went he opened the binder and wrote, slowly, in his squarest hand. A thing that would stay written ought to be written exactly, even when being exact did not make it any easier to read.

They know where I am. They always knew where I was. What's changed is that where I am now has walls they think they own.

He shut the binder. Down in the town the lamps were coming on, one after another, along the one street worth walking. Somewhere past the last of them a courier's horse was carrying three certified signatures and two sittings' worth of record down a road whose end Cael would never see, toward a desk where he would never sit, for a reader who had asked.

Chapter 15 — Public Draft

[Curious, analytical narration; keep consent, records, and trust sharply distinct]

Karis climbed the standings like floodwater coming up a stair, without any visible effort and without stopping.

She had full standing as a transfer, and a scheduled bout every few days like anyone else, and in her first fortnight on the board she fought three of them. She won all three, none in more than three exchanges, and after each one the clerk who kept the board climbed his little ladder with his chalk and his rag and moved her name up a section. By the end of the fifth week it sat second, directly beneath a name that had not moved in longer than anyone could remember. The schedule paired the top two of each cohort at the turn of the half-term. Everybody at Greyvane could count, and everybody knew what the next pairing would be some days before it went up on the board.

Cael did not spend those days watching her. He spent them, mostly, on the floor of Brom's room after the eighth bell, with his left forearm braced across his chest.

"Again," said Brom.

The road was a long way behind them now, and the work had moved indoors with them. Brom knelt with his left palm on Cael's forearm, Iron Skin coming up under the skin, and leaned, slow and steady, the weight arriving the way a tide arrives. Cael waited for the force to settle into the bone, chose its road before it could choose its own, out, back along the line it came in, and reached.

He had been catching a quarter of the push for a month. It had become almost reliable; he caught it four times in ten, sometimes five, and the price had stayed the same through all of it, a hot bar laid across the collarbones and two breaths he could not take. He had begun to think of the quarter as a floor he stood on. Tonight he was trying to find out whether it was also a ceiling.

The first six tries went as they usually went. Two caught at a quarter. Four did nothing. On the seventh he reached for more than he had chosen, greedily, a fraction too late, and the gathered force slid sideways off the road he had laid for it and went down into his left wrist. It did not hurt at once. Then it hurt a great deal, a deep, hot throb in the joint, and he sat back on his heels and held the wrist against his chest while Brom waited.

"Joint," said Brom.

"Wrist." Cael flexed the fingers, carefully. They moved. "I tried to take more than I'd decided to take. It went somewhere I hadn't decided."

"So decide more."

"That's the whole problem."

"No," said Brom, who had said this before, on a hillside in the pine needles, and seemed to enjoy saying it again. "That's the whole answer. Decide first, and decide bigger. Again."

The eighth try did nothing at all.

On the ninth, Cael did something he had not tried before. He did not reach harder. He chose a wider road. Before the force arrived he laid the line back out along Brom's arm and imagined it twice as broad, a channel cut for twice the water, and only then, when the push had settled fully into the bone, did he reach. The fragment gathered. It gathered further than it had ever gathered for him, a long, tightening pull that ran from his forearm up into his chest, and for a moment he held half of Brom's push in him like a breath he had taken too deep. Then he sent it home.

It went back into Brom's wrist with a sound like a fist on a table. Brom's arm jerked back a full hand's width. Under the Iron Skin his eyebrows went up and stayed up.

And then the bill came, and it was not the same bill.

It ran up through his right shoulder and across his breastbone as it always had, but it was twice as broad and twice as heavy, a bar laid on him that had become a beam. He could not breathe for two breaths, and then three, and then four. On the fifth he got air into himself and it came back out as a cough so hard it brought water to his eyes, and he coughed again, bent over his knees on Brom's floor, until the bar slowly lifted. His right shoulder had locked. He could not raise the arm past his chest.

"Half," said Brom quietly. He was turning his own wrist over, looking at it. "That was half. I felt it come back."

"Half," Cael managed.

"What does it cost?"

"Double." He tried the shoulder again, and it refused him. "It doesn't give discounts. Twice the catch, twice the bill. Possibly more than twice. I'll know in the morning."

He knew in the morning. The shoulder had loosened by the first bell, grudgingly, but his breastbone was sore to the touch, a deep ache under the bone as if he had been struck there from the inside, and the left wrist was swollen enough that he wrapped it before the lecture so nobody would ask. He wrote it up that night under the four headings, slowly, because it was the first time in a month the Compression section had needed new lines.

Compression-adjacent. Brom's room. Function: half a slow push caught and returned, once, on the ninth try. Done by choosing a wider road before the force arrived, not by reaching harder. Benefit: none in a real fight yet. Twice what I had. Cost: twice what it was. Four breaths gone and a cough, the right shoulder locked for an hour, the breastbone still sore. Seventh try misrouted into the left wrist when I reached for more than I'd chosen. Integration: partial. Half, once.

Underneath, in smaller letters:

The price grows with the catch. Choose first, always. Choose the size first, too.

Lira's second recorded bout of the month fell two days later, against a Current Path third-year with quick feet and a habit of circling left, and Cael watched it from the rail of the formal yard with his wrist wrapped under his sleeve.

It was not the bout she had fought in the second week. That one had been an argument, made in public, for the benefit of everyone watching. This one was work. Karis was at the rail too. Cael had not seen her come. She was standing a few places along, with her notebook shut under her arm, and when Lira came back she turned and waited until Lira had finished drinking.

"No." Karis said it at once. "The seven clauses are about him. This is about you, and you can tell me to go away."

She looked at Karis directly for the first time. "That isn't for your notebook."

The pairing went up on the first morning of the sixth week, and by the fifth bell the formal yard was fuller than Cael had ever seen it.

It was, Cael realized, the longest speech he had ever heard Hobb make, and it had ended in a tactical note, freely given. He wrote Hobb: he'll press with a crowd in the margin of the binder and felt he had been handed something more than the note.

Edran took the north mark with his back to the benches, as the higher-ranked fighter was allowed to, and settled into the easy, upright stance of a man who had stood at the top of a board so long that he no longer checked whether he was still there. Karis took the south mark with nothing in her hands and nothing in her face. Hobb was right. Edran pressed.

He came off his mark almost at once, faster than the textbook distance, and Cael saw in the first three steps why he had held first place for so long. His Glass came up along his forearms as he moved, bright hard shells like ice forming in a stream, and he led with them, forward and forward, inviting her to hit them. Glass was not afraid of being struck. It wanted to be struck, because a struck shell burst outward in a glittering spray that carried the force away with it, and before the glitter had faded a new shell was already forming in the next place he expected to be hit. He fought like a man walking through rain he had dressed for.

Karis gave ground.

She went back across the ring in short, neat steps, her weight even, her eyes on his chest. Edran's answer in the third exchange was the right answer, and Cael admired him for finding it so quickly.

He stopped pressing her and went straight at the points instead. He came off his mark at an angle, not at Karis but at the crescent behind her, and drove through it on a line that would cross three points before she could do anything with them. It was a brave and sensible thing to do. A point was only a small heat. A man with Glass on his shins could take a small heat and burst it and keep going. If he broke up her crescent before she could use it, she would have spent two exchanges laying nothing.

The first point bloomed under his shin, and his shell burst in a spray of light, and he went on. Karis let the third point go before he reached it. Cael saw the shimmer of its release, that third of a breath of lingering warmth, and saw Edran see it too and decide, in the space of one step, to plant his foot right through the shimmer while it was still dying, betting the lag would be shorter than it looked.

It was not shorter. It was exactly as long as it looked. His foot came down in the last of the warmth, and the heat caught the edge of his boot, and he hissed through his teeth and stumbled a half-step. Wray's pen moved.

He learned. Cael watched him learn it. For the rest of the exchange Edran waited out every shimmer before he stepped through it, a third of a breath each time, and the waiting cost him speed, and the speed cost him the crescent. Wray called it.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

For a moment the yard was silent. Then the benches broke into noise all at once, the voices of forty people trying to work out how to tell it to someone who had missed it, and the channels faded and the points went out one by one, each leaving its third of a breath of shimmer on the air, until the ring was only chalk and packed earth again with a few faint scorch marks on it that the broom would take by morning.

Karis walked to the edge of the ring and drank from her flask. She did it as a person drinks after a walk, not after a fight, and Cael wrote that down.

He had written a great deal. He looked at the page now, while the yard emptied round him, and read it back.

Exchange 1: two points, both at contact, both against shells. Footwork only otherwise. Measuring shell timing.

Exchange 2: six points laid behind her, one per step back. Looks like retreat. Edran sees them at the end.

Exchange 3: he goes for the points. Right answer. She lets three go. Lag on every release, a third of a breath, every time. He tries to step through the lag and gets burned once. Learns. She lays five more on the far side while he's breaking the first lot. Nine on the floor at the end.

Exchange 4: channels. Five that I could count. Two places to stand. He yields rather than cross.

Off hand still before every point. Lag after every release. Never more than nine points at once. Breathing never changed. Hands never flushed. She finished the way she started.

He looked at that last line, and then wrote the one under it that mattered.

She didn't spend anything she couldn't spare. Whatever she has in reserve, nobody in this yard saw any of it today.

Beside him, Lira had finished her apple and was looking at the ring with an expression he could not quite read.

"She's going to be trouble for somebody," she said at last. "I'd like it not to be us."

"She signed a page with us."

"I know. That's why I'd like it not to be us." Lira tossed the core over the wall into the kitchen garden. "Did you see her let him take that shoulder? In the third. She could have slipped it."

"I saw."

"So did I." Lira was quiet for a moment. "I do that. When I want people to see something not matter."

Brom said nothing. He was looking at the north side of the yard, where Edran had gone to stand by the standings board.

The clerk was already up his little ladder with his chalk and his rag. Cael watched him rub out the name that had sat at the top of the cohort for longer than anyone could remember, and write Karis, and then write the old name one line beneath it, in the same hand, at the same size.

Edran stood and watched him do it. He did not look angry. Cael had expected anger, or the tight polite smile of a man pretending not to mind, and there was neither. There was something stranger in Edran's face, a kind of stillness, like a man standing on a deck who has just felt it move under him and is waiting to find out whether it will move again.

Then Edran turned his head, and his eyes went across the yard to the rail, and found Cael there with the binder open on his arm and the pen still in his hand.

He held the look. His face showed nothing at all. Cael thought he understood it anyway. In the space of a month the best fighter in the building had watched a boy with no Path walk into two closed sittings and come out satisfied both times, with nothing anyone could see to show for it but a hollow circle on his tag, and now he had watched a transfer who had been at Greyvane barely a month take the place he had spent three years earning, without spending, so far as anyone could see, a single thing she could not spare. The ground had moved twice. He had felt it both times.

Edran looked away. He went out through the north gate alone, without hurrying, and the students who would once have fallen in round him like water round a post let him go.

Cael closed the binder slowly. He was not glad, though he had every reason to think he would be. He had spent a month watching Edran and had filled three pages on him, and the line at the bottom of the Glass page was about breaking first and on purpose, with a question under it that he still could not answer. He had not, until this afternoon, seen Edran choose not to break at all.

By supper the rumor market had already rebuilt itself around the afternoon, and Lira delivered the new theories in the stable with the brisk competence of a woman reporting on a district she had always understood.

"First," she said, holding up a finger. "She's a Compact inspector, sent to see whether Greyvane is fit to keep its charter. That one used to be yours. It's moved."

"I'm hurt," said Cael.

"You should be. It was your best one." A second finger. "Second, Ternhall sent her to beat everybody here as a lesson, and she'll go home at midwinter with the board in her pocket. Mostly the third-years. They don't like that one, but they keep telling it." A third. "Third, Edran yielded on purpose, because his family owes hers money. That one is very stupid, and very popular on the stairs."

"And the fourth?" asked Brom, who never asked and always listened.

"The fourth is mine." Lira tore her bread in half and gave Cael the larger piece without being asked, which told him how she felt about the afternoon better than anything she might have said. "Nobody's started it yet. It's that she came here because of somebody, and that the somebody is sitting at this table eating barley." She looked at Cael. "I'm not going to start it. But it's the only true one, and somebody's going to work it out before the month's over."

"Then what do we do?" said Cael.

"Nothing." Lira shrugged. "Same as always. Four stories pulling different ways and everybody arguing. Worry when they start to agree."

He laughed, because she meant him to, and ate the bread, and did not tell her that of the four, the true one was the only one that worried him.

Chapter 16 — Three Pages

[Curious, analytical narration; keep consent, records, and trust sharply distinct]

It was Brom's turn to be the witness, and he took it as seriously as everything else he did.

He came into section four two minutes after the fifth bell, unannounced, as the second clause allowed, and stood at the rail with his feet set and his hands clasped behind his back like a man attending a funeral he had been told was important. Karis looked up from her borrowed stool, nodded to him, and changed nothing. Quenna, at the chalk with her slate, went on writing.

"I'd like to do the read today," Cael said. "Not the framework."

"The read needs a body," said Quenna.

"Brom has one."

Quenna looked at Brom over the top of her slate, and Cael could see her turning the request over against the written refusal in the back of his binder, the one with her own initials on it. The provision does not presently authorize regular partnered practice.

"Standing still is not sparring," she said at last. "He may stand at the edge of reach and shift his weight. He may not strike, and you may not touch him. If either of you forgets that, the session ends and I write down why." She made a note on the slate. "Go on."

So Brom came over the rail into the section and stood two paces from Cael and shifted his weight wherever he liked, whenever he liked, doing nothing to hide it, and Cael stood still and let the read open and called it.

"Left. Heel."

"Forward. Both."

"Right. Toes."

Brom was a better body for it than Hobb had been, because Cael had read Brom for most of a year and knew the grain of him, and a worse one, because Brom also knew what Cael was doing and kept trying, with a scowl of deep concentration, to beat it. He leaned one way and went the other. He started forward and stopped and went back. He stood perfectly still for a long count and then shifted with no warning at all. Cael called every one of them, and called most of them before Brom had properly decided, and after the twentieth Brom straightened up and said, with real indignation, "That isn't fair," and Lira was not there to laugh at him, so Cael did it for her.

Karis wrote throughout.

He had grown used to the sound of her pen in the weeks since the first session. It ran in long, even passages while he worked and stopped the moment he stopped, every time, as reliably as a mill wheel stops when the race is shut. He had stopped listening to it, just as he had stopped hearing the pipes in the residence wing.

So he noticed at once when it stopped while he was still working.

It happened on the twenty-sixth call. Brom had gone forward onto his left foot and Cael had named it, and somewhere in the naming the pen at the edge of the section went quiet. Cael called the next shift, and the next, and the pen stayed quiet, and then it started again in mid-phrase as if nothing had happened. He kept working. Eleven calls later it happened a second time, at no moment he could identify as special, and again it held still for the space of two calls and then went on.

When the session was done and Quenna had signed the strip, he went over to the stool.

"Clause six," he said.

Karis turned the notebook toward him without a word.

The page was dense with her small upright hand, columns of calls and times and Brom's weight in a shorthand he could not quite read. In the margin, at two places, she had drawn a short vertical stroke. Beside the first stroke was a page number, and beside the second the same number again.

"Your pen stopped," he said. "Twice. Not when I stopped."

"Yes."

"Why?"

She looked at the two strokes, as if deciding how much of the true answer was observable from outside.

"It stops when something I'm seeing now agrees with something I wrote down before," she said. "It doesn't happen very often. When it does, I stop writing for a moment so that I don't write down what I expect instead of what I see." She touched the page number. "That's the page I wrote at your first session, when you ran the framework with nobody striking. You make up your own strikes out of the air. So I timed the gap between your eyes settling on where a strike would come from and your feet going. Today I timed how far ahead of Brom's weight you called it." She turned the notebook back toward herself. "It's the same amount. A quarter of a breath, near enough. Two different things you do, with two different results, and they both lead by the same margin."

"What does that mean?"

"I don't know yet." She capped the pen, with the small definite click. "That's why the pen stopped instead of writing a theory. Clause five. I can write that the margins match. I can't write why."

He looked at her, and she looked back, entirely calm, and he understood that she was telling him the truth, all of it, as far as it went.

"It fits something," he said.

"It fits something," she agreed. "When I know what, you'll read it first."

They walked out together, with Brom a little ahead of them, still muttering about fairness.

The afternoon had turned cold. The leaves on the hill below the wall had gone yellow at the edges in the last week, and the wind coming up over the training yard smelled of smoke from the town and of the first frost that had not arrived yet. Karis walked with her notebook held against her chest and her free hand in her pocket, and neither of them said anything.

"You let him take your shoulder," Cael said at last. "Edran. In the third exchange."

"Yes."

"You could have slipped it."

"I could have." She did not seem to mind being asked. "In a standings bout, a clean hit taken costs one touch. If I'd slipped it, I'd have had to step north, and I'd been laying the north side for a whole exchange. A touch was cheaper than the side." She considered. "And I wanted to know how hard Glass hits when the shell's already formed. Now I do."

"And when he yielded?"

Karis was quiet for several steps.

"He read the floor correctly," she said. "Every line of it. He's very good." She looked out at the yellowing hill. "I'd rather he'd crossed."

"You wanted him burned?"

"No." She said it quickly and firmly, and turned her head to make sure he had heard it. "I wanted to know what Glass does to a channel. Whether a shell bursting outward breaks the line or only breaks itself. I'll never find out from him now, because he was sensible." She frowned faintly. "I wanted the result. I didn't want him hurt. Both of those are true at once. I'm not sure what to do with that, except write it down."

"Is that in the second notebook?"

"It will be tonight."

They reached the corner of the residence wing, where their ways divided. She stopped. She had carried the question the whole length of the yard, and now she asked it.

"You charted the bout. I saw you."

"Yes."

"May I see it?" She held up one hand before he could answer. "You can say no. None of the clauses cover what you write about me. I'm only asking."

He thought about it. The binder was the one thing the first clause kept from her, and she had promised never to ask for it, and he did not mean to make her break the promise by accident. So he opened it at the page, kept it turned toward himself, and read the chart aloud to her, line by line.

She listened standing in the cold, with her lips pressed together, all the way down: the two points at contact, the six behind her, the lag on every release, the nine on the floor, the channels, the yield, and at the bottom, She didn't spend anything she couldn't spare. She asked him to read the last line again, and he did. Then he closed the binder.

"That's accurate," she said. Something in her voice had changed, very slightly. "All of it. Even the lag."

"Is the lag a flaw?"

"Ternhall thought so." She looked at him with an expression he could not read at all. "You count the way I count," she said. "I didn't know anyone else did."

She went into the wing without another word, and he stood at the corner in the cold with the binder under his arm and the odd sense that he had been handed a compliment by someone who had never once in her life wasted one.

He wrote it up that night in a single line, because it was a single fact.

Her pen has started stopping. Not when I stop. When something fits.

Edran came to the rail the next afternoon.

Cael watched him go, and then opened the binder at the Glass page and wrote one line in the space he had left there, under the question of what Edran believed.

He's not asking what I am anymore. He's asking what the board is.

Brom came back from the defensive floor that afternoon with chalk to his elbows and Karis's sixth notebook under his arm, and sat down on the end of Cael's bed without being asked, which he had never done before.

"I showed it to Wray."

There is one now. Prove it. W.

It went up the next morning, before the first bell.

Cael saw the crowd before he saw the paper. The main hall was full of students who should have been at assembly, standing three and four deep in front of the board where the public assessment calendar hung, and the noise they made was the low, busy noise of people reading something aloud to each other in pieces. Several of them turned as he came in. Then more did, and a space opened in front of the board, not because anyone stepped back on purpose but because nobody wanted to be standing in the place where he would have to stand.

He stood in it.

The petition was three pages, pinned in a row with brass tacks beside the calendar, written in a clear, careful hand that did not shake. Across the top of the first page, in capitals:

Petition of Standing. Filed by Edran, Glass Path, Iron Rank Two, third year. Concerning the supervised floor access of the candidate enrolled under the demonstration provision.

He read it all, from the first line to the last, before he let himself think anything about it.

The first page set out the provision. It did so accurately. It quoted the half page Cael had read more times than he had counted in the archive, and then explained, in plain sentences, what the provision was for: the academic exposure and supervised training of candidates still waiting on their formal Kindling assessment, which was to say, in nearly every case, children. It noted that such candidates were assessed monthly by demonstration, and that the standard was consistent, observable practice. It observed, correctly, that a child who had not yet Kindled would ordinarily have very little to practise.

The second page set out the record. It did that accurately too. It noted the dates of two closed sittings and the finding of each, assessment satisfied, which the public calendar had recorded. It noted that the candidate had been seen at the rail of every floor in the building, filling a binder, and had been present at the standings bouts of the cohort's leading students. It said, without any heat at all, that whatever the candidate had demonstrated to the panel in closed session, it could not have been the practice of a child without a Path, because the panel had found it consistent and observable and the provision did not reward nothing. And then it drew its conclusion, in a sentence Cael read three times.

The petitioner therefore submits that the candidate is evidently a practitioner of some classification, which the faculty has elected not to disclose, and that his enrollment under a provision designed for those without one places him outside the framework by which every other student's standing is measured.

The third page made the request. It asked that the candidate's supervised floor access under the provision be suspended pending a review of his enrollment; or, in the alternative, that the candidate be assessed under the same framework as students of full standing, in public, so that the academy's standings might continue to mean what every enrolled student had been told they meant. And then, beneath it, in a last paragraph that Cael could hear in Edran's voice as clearly as if he had been standing at the rail, the real grievance, where petitions always put it.

The petitioner has earned his standing at this academy in public, over three years, under its framework, and does not dispute any result that framework has produced. He asks only whether the framework is still the measure. If a student may stand outside it and be found satisfactory, then every student who has met it honestly is entitled to know by what measure they now stand.

It was signed at the bottom of the third page, Edran, in the same hand that did not shake, with the date.

Somebody small pushed in at his elbow. He looked down, and it was Oona, with her tag on its string, reading the first page with her lips moving.

"Is that about you?"

"Yes."

She read on. She was a slow and thorough reader, and he waited for her. Somewhere behind the lecture wing the first bell began to ring, slow and unhurried, and the crowd came apart reluctantly round them, in twos and threes, still talking, until the hall had nearly emptied and the two of them stood alone at the board with the brass tacks. When she reached the bottom of the third page she frowned at it.

"Is it true?"

He thought about it. He had told her he would not lie to her, and he found, standing there in the emptying hall, that the promise was easier to keep than he had feared, because the honest answer was the simplest one.

"Nearly all of it."

"Which part isn't?"

He put one finger beside the sentence on the second page, not on it, as Prynn had put her finger beside the routing code.

"That part. Where he thinks the faculty is hiding what my Path is."

Oona read the sentence again. "Aren't they?"

"No," said Cael. "There isn't one to hide."

Oona looked at the sentence, and then up at him, and he watched her work it through, as she had worked through shattered in the taxonomy lecture: where it went, why it wasn't on the chart.

"Oh," she said at last. "Then he's asking the wrong question."

"No. He's asking a fair question." Cael looked at the three pages, at the careful hand and the brass tacks and the signature at the bottom. "He's only got one fact wrong in the middle of it. Everything else is right."

"Will you tell him?"

The bell had stopped. Somewhere above them a door shut, and feet went quickly along a corridor toward assembly, late.

Cael did not answer her straight away. He read the conclusion on the second page one more time, the way he had once read a category line three times over a cup of tea going cold, and did not resent a word of it. Edran had asked in the open, in the yard, in front of a dozen people. Now he had asked again, in ink, in front of everyone, with his own name signed at the bottom, by the book and in daylight. It was the most honest thing anyone at Greyvane had done about him, apart from a girl who had walked into an archive to ask permission. It was right about the provision, and right about the children, and right about the board, and right about him in every particular but one.

The one was the only one that mattered, and nobody had ever written it down.

"I think I'll have to," he said.

Chapter 17 — Three Audiences

[Measured, public-facing narration; let each challenge expose character as well as skill]

He was the last one into assembly, and everybody in the room knew why.

The assembly room sat at the end of the lecture wing's ground floor, a long plain hall with benches in rows and a lectern at the front that nobody used. By the time Cael came through the door the benches were full and the instructor reading the day's notices had reached the second of them. He did not stop reading, and nobody said anything, but a ripple went along the back rows as Cael found a space at the end of the last bench. It was the small, collective adjustment of two hundred people who had just been reading about him on the board in the main hall and now had to pretend they had not.

He sat down, folded his hands on the binder and looked at the lectern.

The notices were ordinary: a change to the lamp oil allowance in the residence wing, a lecture on Current Path footwork moved from the third bell to the second, a reminder that the kitchen garden was not a shortcut. The instructor read each one in the same patient voice, and Cael listened to every word as if it mattered, because the alternative was to feel the backs of two hundred heads deciding not to turn around.

Lira was three rows ahead, and she did not turn either. But halfway through the notice about the garden she lifted one hand, as if to scratch her neck, held up two fingers where only he could see them, and put the hand down again.

Two fingers was a circuit sign. In Ardenmere it had meant I see you, stay where you are, I'll come round after, and he had not known until that moment how badly he had wanted somebody to make it.

Assembly ended on the fourth notice. The room came apart into noise at once, and he stayed where he was on the end of the bench while it emptied, because getting up in the middle of it would have meant walking through it.

Brom found him first. He said nothing about the petition; he sat down on the bench beside Cael with his elbows on his knees and looked at the empty lectern.

"Lira's gone to find out who saw Edran go in to the clerk. She thinks there was a witness to the filing. She's furious she didn't know yesterday."

"There's nothing to find out. He signed it."

"I know. I told her." Brom considered the lectern. "She said finding out was for her, not for you."

Cael almost laughed. It came out as a breath.

"You read it?"

"All of it."

"And?"

"It's right," said Cael. "Nearly all of it. He's got the provision right and the record right. He's got the children right." He turned the binder over on his knees. "He's only got one thing wrong, and it's the thing in the middle that the rest stands on."

Brom nodded slowly. It was his nod for a fight that had gone as he expected and not as he wished.

"It's a very good petition."

"That's worse."

"I know."

They sat a while longer in the empty room. Then the second bell rang for lectures, and Cael went to the registry history block, because it was on his schedule and because walking into a lecture hall on time was one of the few things he was sure he could still do correctly that morning.

He did not take a single note. He sat in the back row with the binder open to a clean page and the pen in his hand while the thin woman at the front talked about the third revision of the station fees. Twice he caught himself reciting the conclusion on Edran's second page from memory. Evidently a practitioner of some classification, which the faculty has elected not to disclose. It was a good sentence, careful in all the right places, and he would have been proud to write it if it had been true.

At the end of the block a junior clerk was waiting outside the lecture hall door with her hands folded.

"The provost would like a word," she said. "Now, if you can."

She said it in the tone of somebody who had been told to make it sound less important than it was, and she did not quite manage it.

Naveth's door was shut.

Cael had climbed the worn stair to that office three times now, and every time before the door had stood open. He stopped on the top step and looked at the plain dark panel with its iron latch, and understood that this conversation had been made private before he was ever sent for.

He knocked.

"Come."

There were four chairs this time. Somebody had carried two more up the narrow stair and set them against the wall, and two of the four were already taken. Quenna sat by the window with her folder on her knee. Wray sat beside her in the brown coat buttoned to the throat, her hands resting flat on her thighs, as still as she had been on the panel at both sittings.

Naveth sat behind his desk. The three pages of the petition lay squared on the blotter in front of him, and Cael saw at once that they were not the originals, which were still downstairs on the board under their brass tacks where the rule said they must stay. These were copies in a clerk's hand. Naveth had had the petition copied before he read it, so that he could read it as often as he liked without once being seen standing in front of the board.

"Sit. This concerns you more than anyone, and I'd rather you heard all of it than the useful parts."

Cael sat in the fourth chair, the one facing the desk.

"You've read it."

"Yes."

"Then I won't read it to you." Naveth laid one long hand flat on the pages. "I'll tell you what I can and can't do with it, and then Quenna will tell you what she thinks I should do instead, and then Wray will tell us both whether it's possible. That's the order we agreed on the stair."

He raised one finger, as he had on the first morning with the alumni ledger.

"I can't dismiss it. It's clean. Every clause is in the right place and every date is correct, and the young man who wrote it has three years of standing behind him and the right to file. If I set it aside because it's inconvenient, I tell every student in this building that a petition is a thing the provost answers when he likes the question." He paused. "A good many of the students in this building came here because some other place answered their questions that way. A petition that gets posted and then answered is the only protection some of them have ever had. I won't spend it on you. You wouldn't thank me if I did."

"No," said Cael.

A second finger.

"I can't grant it either. Suspending a student's floor access pending review of his enrollment isn't a thing a provost can do alone; it needs a formal review of the enrollment itself." He looked at Cael over the copied pages. "And a formal review of your enrollment, a week after a sealed bundle of your assessment records went down the hill to the Compact, is the one thing in the world I least want to sign. Whatever that review wrote would be the first thing anyone read."

"And doing nothing," said Quenna, from the window.

"Doing nothing is a decision." Naveth did not look round at her; it had the sound of a line they had already said to each other once that morning. "It's the worst one I have. Silence from this office reads as weakness to one half of the building and favour to the other, and both halves would be partly right. I need an answer that's public, lawful and true, and I need it today."

He took his hand off the pages and leaned back, and the chair gave its worn creak.

"That's all I've got. Quenna has something better."

Quenna did not stand up. She turned a little on her chair so that she faced Cael directly and put her folder down on the floor beside her, which he had never once seen her do.

"The petition asks two things. Suspend him, or assess him in public under the same framework as students of full standing. Naveth can't do the first. So read the second one again."

Cael did not need to read it again; he had it by heart. That the candidate be assessed under the same framework as students of full standing, in public, so that the academy's standings might continue to mean what every enrolled student had been told they meant.

"He's asked for a public assessment," he said slowly.

"He has. In writing, signed and posted." Quenna's voice had taken on the flat, careful cadence of the sittings, each word set down on its own. "Your sittings have been closed: formal, recorded and closed. That was right for the first two. It isn't right now, because now the closed door is the thing being argued about. So we open it."

She held up one hand, palm out, and laid the plan on it one piece at a time.

"An exhibition bout, held in the formal yard, under standings rules, with the full faculty seats present and the school free to watch. Consistent, observable practice: the provision's own three words, and the bout goes into the record under them as this month's sitting. We don't grant his petition and we don't refuse it." She closed the hand. "The petition asked a question. We let the whole school watch it answered." She opened the hand again, as if there were one more piece on it. "It isn't a standings bout. It carries no rank and no tier, and it can't move him or you a single line on the board. A demonstration assessment says one of two things, satisfied or not, and that is all it will say. But it will say it in front of the whole school."

"Against Edran," said Naveth. It was not really a question; he had heard this on the stair.

"Against Edran. He filed it. If anyone is going to find out, it should be the boy who asked."

Cael sat with it.

He did what he always did with a plan that was not his own, which was to walk around it looking for the place where it would break, as he walked around an opponent in the first exchange. He found the place at once, because nobody had hidden it.

"If I lose, his petition is answered the way he wanted. I'll have shown the whole school that he was right."

"Yes."

"Not partly. In front of everybody. In the record."

"Yes." Quenna did not soften it, and she did not hurry past it. "If you lose, the record will say that the candidate under the demonstration provision was assessed in public against a student of full standing, an Iron Rank Two, and was beaten, and the petition will stand on that page for as long as the page exists. I would not be proposing this if I thought you would lose. But I want you to walk into it with the stakes named, not with the stakes I'd like them to be."

She held his eyes.

"I've watched Edran train since he came here at fifteen. He has a seam, as everyone does. The question isn't whether it's there. What I don't know is whether you'll find it before he's said everything he came to say."

Cael looked down at his hands. He thought of the board in the main hall with its three pages pinned in a row, and of Oona's face working through Then he's asking the wrong question. He remembered his own answer to her, that it was a fair question with one fact wrong in the middle of it. A fair question deserved to be answered where it had been asked. Edran had asked in the yard, and then in ink, and answering him now in a closed hall with three people and a slate would only be one more door shut in his face.

"Schedule it."

Wray had not spoken. She spoke now, without moving her hands from her thighs, in the voice she used to read a measurement off a gauge.

"He's the best I have on the Edge floor, better than his rank. He will press early, because there will be a crowd, and he always presses with a crowd. And he learns inside a bout. Most people learn between bouts; he changes his timing mid-exchange when something fails." She looked at Cael. "Whatever you find on him, find it twice. He won't leave it lying where it was."

"I'll find it twice."

"Then I'll assess it." She turned her head toward Quenna. "Standings rules. Exchanges called on my count. A touch is a touch, a yield is a yield, the ring is the ring. No allowance either way for the category."

"No allowance," Quenna agreed.

Naveth reached for a blank posting form from the drawer of his desk, then stopped with it half out and held up his other hand.

"Before that, one thing. I want it said here, with the door shut."

He looked at Cael as he had on the first morning, with the joiner's look that decided whether a beam would carry a floor.

"You understand what Quenna has turned this into. Eight days from now most of this school will be round that ring watching you, and whatever you show them goes into the assessment record with two hundred witnesses to it. Lose to Edran and we're in difficulty." He paused. "If you beat him by too much, I'm not sure the problem we'd have instead is any smaller."

Cael said nothing. He had been thinking the same thing since the word public, and he had been waiting to see whether anyone else would say it aloud.

"I'm not telling you how to fight. I wouldn't know how. I'm telling you that this fight has three audiences. The students on the benches, who want to know whether the standings still mean anything. The panel, who will write down what they see. And a file, which will be read some day by people who were never in the yard and don't care how the morning felt." He folded the posting form flat on the blotter. "Only one of the three will be standing across the chalk from you. Don't fight for that one alone."

"I know."

Then, because the man had shut his door to say it and had earned more than two words, Cael said the rest.

"It's what I've been doing since Ardenmere. Every bout on the circuit, I had to win in front of people without showing them more than they'd already seen. Winning at a chosen size." He looked at the copied petition on the blotter. "I've forgotten how to win any other way."

Naveth looked at him, and something moved in the old weathered face that Cael could not read. Then he uncapped his pen.

"Winning at a chosen size," he repeated, writing nothing. "That tells me more about you than your intake file did." He turned to Quenna. "The first bell, eight days from today, in the formal yard. Write me the wording and I'll sign it before the fifth bell."

Quenna was already writing.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The answer went up beside the petition before the fifth bell, as Naveth had promised, on a single sheet in Quenna's hand with his signature beneath, pinned with the same brass tacks.

Answer to the Petition of Standing filed by Edran, Glass Path, Iron Rank Two. The petition's alternative request is granted in the following form. The candidate enrolled under the demonstration provision will be assessed in public, in the formal yard, at the first bell on the eighth day from this posting, in an exhibition bout under standings rules against the petitioner. The bout will be logged as the candidate's demonstration assessment for the month, under the standard of the provision. The faculty seats will sit. The academy may attend.

That was all of it. It was shorter than any one page of the petition.

Cael saw the crowd in front of the board from the far end of the main hall at the change of bells, thicker and noisier than the morning's, and he did not go to it. He stood by the archive passage with the binder against his chest and watched the reading change as it moved through the crowd from back to front. In the morning the hall had been full of the low, careful noise of a verdict being handed round in pieces. At the front of the crowd now, where people had finished, it had already become something louder and quicker, with laughter in it here and there. At the back two second-years were arguing and one of them was holding up fingers.

Gerda came out of the crowd on its near side, with her patched coat buttoned and her slip for the floor already in her hand. She saw him by the passage, changed course, and stopped two paces off.

"Answered."

"Yes."

"The same day it was posted." She looked back at the board, at the single sheet beside the three. "That's the good kind. They didn't put it in a drawer and let it go cold. They didn't refuse it in a sentence. They gave him what he asked for, in a shape they could live with." She looked at him again. "Now it's yours to answer properly."

"You've seen one answered badly."

Gerda considered him.

"I've seen one answered correctly. That isn't always the same thing."

She went on toward the floor without another word, checking the clock above the door as she passed it.

Edran was not at the board, and Cael had not expected him to be. He had already been once, early, before anybody else, to read his own petition pinned up in his own hand, and he would not go and stand in front of it now with a crowd watching him read the answer. But at the change of the sixth bell, crossing the formal yard, Cael saw him on the far side by the standings board, where his name now sat second, in the same clerk's hand at the same size, one line below Karis's.

He was not looking at the standings. He was looking across the yard at the main hall door, where a few students were still coming out from the board in twos and threes, talking with their hands, and then his eyes moved and found Cael. He did not come over. He lifted his chin very slightly, a single small movement that meant, as plainly as if he had said it across the chalk, I've read it. Accepted.

Cael lifted his own in return.

Edran turned away and went through the north gate toward the open floor, and Cael stood in the yard and understood that the conversation he had told Oona he would have to have was now a great deal harder. He had meant to go to Edran and tell him the one wrong thing on the second page. Now the yard stood between them, and the answer on the board, and eight days, and anything he said before the first bell on the eighth would look like what it was not. He thought about that all the way to supper.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Lira had read the answer by the time he reached the stable. He could tell from the far end of the long room by how she sat, very upright at the scarred table under the bricked-up hay door, with her bread untouched in front of her.

"They've put you in a ring," she said, before he had sat down. "For the whole school to stand round and look at."

"Yes."

"Two hundred people. On a calendar. With a date." She pushed the bread away. "Ever since Ardenmere I've watched people look at you as if you were something on a table to be weighed, and now they've sold tickets."

"Nobody's selling tickets."

"Somebody will." She looked at him with her jaw set, the small muscle working at the hinge of it. "Wasn't there anything else? Anything at all, that didn't mean standing you up in front of everybody?"

Brom set down his spoon.

"They've put him in a ring with rules. Wray's count. A touch is a touch. That isn't a market square, and it isn't a back room with a man asking careful questions. It's the floor." He looked at Lira steadily. "You walked a Force Path off the edge of that same ring in the second week because you wanted twenty people to see it. You said so on the wall."

Lira opened her mouth, and shut it.

"That was different."

"It was the same. Except he's got two hundred, and you only got twenty."

For a moment Cael thought she was going to throw the bread at him. Then something in her shoulders gave, very slightly, and she pulled the bread back toward her and tore it in half.

"I hate it when you do that."

"I know."

"I hate it more when you're right." She looked at Cael across the table, and the anger had gone out of her face, and what was left under it was the thing the anger had been standing in front of. "All right. It's a ring. I know rings." She lowered her voice, though the two second-years playing tiles by the fire were nowhere near. "What are you going to show them?"

"The framework."

"And?"

"Nothing else."

"Not the read?"

"Not even the read." He turned his bowl a quarter-turn on the table. "The Iron-adjacent read is on the record twice already, so it's safe. But a fight won with one fragment is smaller on paper than a fight won with two."

Lira considered him in silence, and then gave him the single nod she gave an opponent who had done something she would have done herself.

"Good." She pushed half of it across to him. "Eat. You've got eight days of being looked at, and you can't do it hungry."
