He went anyway, the next morning, because he had told Oona he would, and because a thing being harder had never once in his life been the same as a thing being wrong.

He found Edran where Brom had said he would be, on the open floor before the first bell, alone, drilling in the far corner by the high windows. Nobody else was in the hall. The light came in grey and level through the glass and lay along the boards while Edran moved through it in short, exact sequences, shell after shell forming along his forearms and bursting outward in a glitter that hung for a heartbeat in the grey air before it was gone.

Cael stopped at the rail and waited.

Edran finished the sequence he was in, all the way to the end, without hurrying it. Then he let his arms drop and turned.

"You're early for the rail."

"I didn't come for the rail."

Edran looked at him, and at the empty hall, and back. He did not come any closer; he stood in the middle of the floor with chalk on his hands and his breathing settling, and waited.

"There's one thing in your petition that's wrong," said Cael. "On the second page. I wanted you to hear it from me, before the eighth day, so that you'd know I wasn't hiding behind the bout."

Edran did not move.

"Don't," he said.

It was quiet and quite firm, and it stopped Cael where he stood.

"I mean it. Don't tell me." Edran wiped his palms down the front of his training shirt, slowly, one and then the other. "If you tell me now, I'll have your word for it. And I'll probably believe you. You don't seem to lie much, and I've watched you a while." He looked at the floor between them, at the chalk and the grey light. "Then I'll go into that yard knowing something nobody earned in front of anybody. One more thing on the board that didn't come from the board."

"It isn't about the board."

"Everything I've asked has been about the board." Edran's voice did not rise. "I didn't file it to find out what you are. I filed it to find out whether the framework can still tell. If it can't, I'd rather know that from the floor than from you."

Cael stood at the rail with the thing he had come to say still in his mouth, and could not argue with one word of it.

"All right."

Edran nodded once.

"For what it's worth," said Cael, "it was a fair question. Both times."

Something passed over Edran's face, not quite surprise and not quite pleasure, and it was gone before Cael could name it.

"I know it was. I'm still not sorry I asked it in ink." He turned back toward the high windows and set his feet. "Eight days. Go and watch somebody else. I'll be here every morning, and you're allowed the rail, and I won't change anything for you." He paused with his hands half raised. "I'd think less of you if you didn't come."

He began the next sequence. Cael watched the first shell form and burst. Then he did what he had been told and went to watch somebody else, because the first bell was ringing and because he understood that he had just been given permission to study the man for six days, by the man himself, in daylight, in the open.

Oona was at the board when he came back through the main hall, in front of the answer. She had been waiting for him, and she did not pretend otherwise.

"Did you tell him?"

"I tried."

She turned round. "What happened?"

"He told me not to." Cael looked at the four sheets on the board, the three in Edran's hand and the one in Quenna's. "He said if I told him, he'd have my word for it, and he didn't want my word. He wanted the floor to tell him. In front of everybody. The way he asked."

Oona thought about that with the whole of her face, while students went past behind them toward the second bell.

"Then he's not asking the wrong question anymore."

"No?"

"No. Before, he was asking what you are. That's the one he had wrong." She looked at the answer on the board, Quenna's short square paragraph. "Now he's asking if the board can tell. He's allowed to ask that. That's his. And you can't answer that one with words anyway. It's not a words one."

He looked down at her. She was thirteen and had been at Greyvane for six weeks, and she had just said in four sentences the thing it had taken him a whole night to understand.

"No. It's not a words one."

"So you have to win," said Oona. "Or lose. Either one answers it." She considered him. "I'd rather you won."

"So would I."

"Then you should," she said, and went off toward the lecture wing.

That night he wrote the whole of it down under the four headings, because the four headings were where a fight began.

Exhibition. Eighth day from posting. Formal yard. Standings rules, Wray's count. Edran, Glass, Iron Rank Two, second on the standings, first for most of three years. Function: answer the petition in public, with the Wind-adjacent framework and nothing else. Benefit: if it goes well, the question gets answered where it was asked. Cost, if I lose: the petition stands, in the record, for as long as the record does. Cost, if I win too well: whatever the record says I did, somebody will read it who wasn't there.

He let that last line stand.

Three audiences. Only one across the chalk.

Then, beneath it, on its own line, because he wanted it where he would see it every night for a week:

He told me not to tell him. He wants the floor to say it. I owe him the floor.

Chapter 18 — Odds

[Measured, public-facing narration; let each challenge expose character as well as skill]

By the next evening the whole academy had decided the exhibition was the best thing that had happened to it all term.

Cael had braced himself for something else. He had spent the night after the posting lying awake in the narrow room, building the week ahead as he had once built the reader under the lamp, carefully and out of every unkind thing he remembered. He had expected the low, sidelong noise of the first week, the conversations that stopped on the stair as he passed, the people who looked at the hollow circle on his tag and then very carefully did not look at his face. None of it came. What came instead took him most of three days to recognize, because he had not been on the receiving end of it since Ardenmere.

People asked him things, plainly, to his face, in corridors and at the meal hatch.

A Storm Path fourth-year he had never once spoken to stopped him on the stair outside the lecture wing and asked whether he meant to fight Edran close or at range. A pair of Copper first-years from the movement floor asked, very politely, whether observers were allowed to wear gloves. A girl from the hardening family asked if it was true that he had fought on the Ardenmere circuit, and when he said it was, she said, "Then you've done this before, with people watching," and went away looking reassured on his behalf.

On the second day, in the line for barley at the seventh bell, a second-year from the movement floor fell in beside him and began, without any introduction at all, to talk odds.

He was a thin, quick boy with ink on his thumb, and he talked like the circuit touts on the stairs of the Ironyard, fast and pleasant and entirely without shame. He had grown up, he said, in a river town with a fighting pit behind the tannery, and he had been taking wagers on things since he could count. Not money, he added quickly, because Greyvane didn't hold with money, but crusts and kitchen duty and the good seat by the stable fire.

"Edran's the favourite," he said, as if this were news. "Three to one, on the stairs. Five to two in the hardening hall, because they like an underdog in there. The Edge floor won't take a wager against him at all." He lowered his voice. "I'd be very grateful for anything you could tell me. Not much. A word."

"What sort of word?"

"Whether you've got something you haven't shown."

Cael looked at him, and the boy looked back, bright and hopeful, with his bowl held out for barley he had forgotten about.

"No."

"No, you haven't?"

"No, I won't tell you."

The boy considered this, and then, to Cael's surprise, his whole face split into a delighted grin.

"That's the right answer. That's exactly what a real fighter says. I'll put a crust on you myself." He took his barley and went off down the long room toward the fire. A moment later Cael heard him announcing to a table of second-years that the observer had refused to give inside information, and that this was the best sign yet.

Lira, at the end of the bench, had watched the whole thing with her chin on her fist.

"You've made his week."

"He wanted me to tell him what I can do."

"He wanted you to refuse. Touts never want the answer." She pushed half her bread across the table to him. "Three to one on the stairs. I've been asking. It was four to one this morning, and then somebody found out you fought on the Ardenmere circuit and it came in."

"You've been asking?"

"I've been listening. That's different." She looked down the long room at the fire, where the second-year was holding up fingers. "It's nice, isn't it."

"What is?"

"This." She waved her bread at the room. "Nobody's whispering. They're betting crusts. A week ago they were making up stories about rivers and sealed courts." She ate. "It's a fight now. Everybody knows how to talk about a fight."

He wrote it down that night, because it had taken him three days to find the shape and he did not want to lose it.

Sport. That's how they're taking it, not as a verdict. I keep bracing for the dread, and every time it's a boy wanting to know whether I'll fight close or at range instead. So this is a school asking its question out loud, I think, instead of passing it round behind me.

He read it over and added one more line.

Three to one. Lira says that's fair.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He spent the six days on Edran.

He had done this before, many times, in a city where the cost of getting it wrong had been a split lip and a long walk home. He had spent six days on Feryn once and lost to him anyway, and the losing had taught him more than the six days had; he had spent longer than six days on Reydan. He knew how to do it. The only new thing was the size of the price, and he wrote that down on the first night so that he would not pretend otherwise.

Ardenmere, losing cost me a bruise and some pride. This costs the provision. Study accordingly.

Edran trained on the open floor every morning before the first bell, in the far corner by the high windows, as he had said he would, and he did not change anything for the rail. He nodded to Cael on the first morning when Cael came in, and after that he never looked at the rail at all, because he did not need to: Cael was always there.

The first three days taught him the Path before they taught him anything about the man.

Glass ran on discrete commitments. Cael had known that in outline since his second week, when he crossed out a page of notes about brittleness and started again, but now he watched it close enough to see the grain. A Glass declaration did not grow or bend. When Edran called a shell along his forearm it came up all at once, bright and hard and finished, like ice that had decided to be ice everywhere in the same instant. Once it was there, it could not be changed. He could not thicken it on one side or thin it on another, or turn its edge a little further round as a strike came in. If he wanted a different shape, he had to let the first one go and call a new one, and letting go meant bursting: the shell broke outward in that glittering spray that carried force away with it, and then it was gone.

It was the exact opposite of Lira's Path. Wind could be feathered; Lira could start moving one way and change her mind halfway through the motion, and the wind in her went with her, adjusting as she went. It was the opposite of Brom's, too, because Iron Skin could be laid on late and pressed harder as the blow arrived. Glass did neither. A Glass fighter chose before he moved, committed everything to the choice, and lived with it until it broke.

Choose first, Cael wrote in the margin, and then stopped and looked at the words, because they were his own rule, the one the Compression fragment had beaten into him on the road and Lira had beaten into him again before the first sitting. Glass was a whole Path built on the lesson he was still learning.

There was a second rule underneath the first, and it took him the whole of the second morning to see it, because it was a rule about the inside of a person and he could only watch the outside.

Edran could hold two structures at once, one on each forearm, and no more. He always went into a sequence with both already up: a shell on his left forearm for taking a blow, and on his right an edge, a thin hard ridge along the outside of the bone, so that a strike with that arm was also a cut. Glass sat in the Edge family with Blade, and now Cael saw why. The taxonomy instructor had refused to finish his story about a broken bottle, but Cael thought he understood it now. A thing that broke well still cut.

What he could not do was build a new one quickly while another still stood. Each structure took the whole of his attention to make, and Cael watched him make the opening pair every morning, slowly, one and then the other, before he moved at all, with his eyes half shut, like a man threading a needle. A Glass fighter could not give his whole mind to a new structure while some of it was still holding up an old one. So the pair he started with was ready and waiting, built at leisure, and everything after them had to be made fresh in the middle of the fight, from nothing, after the last one had gone.

Edran ran his sequences in sets of two and three and four, against the empty air, without a partner, and every one of them was clean. Cael began to understand the shape of the training, and then the shape of the person who had chosen it. A Glass fighter could not waste a motion, because every motion was a commitment he could not take back, and a Glass fighter who trained sloppily would fight sloppily, with no feathering to save him. So Edran did not train sloppily, ever. He had come to Greyvane at fifteen and drilled this way, Cael was willing to bet, every single morning for three years, until there was nothing left in him that had not been chosen.

Glass doesn't forgive, he wrote on the second night. So neither does he. Not himself, anyway.

On the third day, in the afternoon, he went to the archive and asked Prynn for the standings record.

"Which year?"

"All of his."

Prynn looked at him over her spectacles, then climbed down off her stool without a word and walked him to the end of the nearest aisle, where the academy's own records were kept. She took down a tall narrow book with a cloth spine and laid it on the long table.

"Standings bouts. Every one, every term, as the assessor entered them. Public record. Anyone may read it."

"Does anyone?"

"Almost nobody." She set a weight beside it. "Tea?"

"Please."

She went away between the shelves, and Cael opened the book.

It was a plain record, kept in columns like Vell's ledger: the date, the names, the assessor, the number of exchanges, the result, and a short line in the assessor's hand. He found Edran's first entry near the front of the section three years back, a Copper first-year of fifteen beating another Copper first-year in five exchanges, and beside it the assessor had written Glass. Over-commits. Will learn. The next entries said the same thing in shorter words and then stopped saying it, and by the end of the first year the line beside Edran's name said only Clean.

He followed the name forward through three years. It climbed the columns as it had climbed the board, steadily and without any great leaps, through the Copper ranks and over the threshold into Iron, and it lost only four times in the whole record. Every one of the four losses was in a bout that went past the third exchange.

Cael sat up.

He read the four entries again, and then went back and read every bout Edran had won in more than three exchanges, and there were only eleven of those. Edran won early, in two exchanges or three; he pressed from the first count and finished things while they were still going his way. When a bout ran long, the record began to say other things in the assessors' small hands. Late in the fourth. Lost his line after the third. And once, in Wray's square hand, Tires in the sequence, not the body.

Prynn came back with the cup and saucer and set it at his elbow, well away from the book.

"You've found something." It was not a question.

"I don't know yet."

"Then you've found something worth not knowing about properly." She went back to her stool. "Don't spill it on the standings."

He drank the tea, which was as bad as ever, and copied Wray's line into the binder exactly. Tires in the sequence, not the body.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Karis found him that evening on the wall outside the residence wing, where he had gone to sit with the binder and the cold.

She did not sit down. She stood at the end of the wall with her notebook shut under her arm and her other hand in her coat pocket, at the distance she always chose, neither near nor far.

"May I ask you something that isn't covered?"

"Go on."

"The exhibition is public. Anyone may watch, and anyone may write down what they see." She paused. "I'd like to chart it. The way I charted your sessions. I don't need your permission, because it isn't a session and the clauses don't reach it. I'm asking anyway."

In the half-light the yard had gone grey behind her, and the hill town's first lamps had come on below.

"Why ask, if you don't need to?"

"Because you'd know I was doing it, and you'd wonder whether you'd agreed to it." She said it simply. "I'd rather you didn't spend any of the eighth morning wondering about me."

"Chart it. Clause six still applies. I read it first."

"Of course." She nodded once, and he thought that was the end of it. Then she did not go.

"There's something else. I'm going to tell you that I won't tell you something. That's an odd thing to say, so I'll be exact about it." She looked out at the yard. "I fought him, not a week ago. I've charted him, and I have pages on him you've never seen. You haven't asked me what's on them."

"No."

"I'm glad." She seemed to mean it. "I've been waiting all week to find out whether you would. If you'd asked, I'd have had to decide whether answering was fair to him. He doesn't know what's in my notebook. He'd never agree to me handing it across a table to the person he's fighting." She turned the notebook over under her arm. "It would be a little like reading his declarations to you."

"That's why I didn't ask."

She looked at him properly then, and he saw her take that and set it down somewhere careful.

"Noted."

She went in. He sat on the wall and watched the lamps come on down the hill, and wrote one line before he lost the light.

K. has pages on him. Didn't ask. She was glad I didn't. That's the second thing this week somebody has been glad I didn't do.

Oona was at the board the next morning, in front of the answer, reading it for what he suspected was the fifth or sixth time. He came up beside her, and she kept her eyes on the paper. She only said, as if they had been in the middle of a conversation, "They keep asking me."

"Who does?"

"The second-years. The ones with the crusts." She frowned at the posted sheet. "Because I'm on your track. They think I'd know if you had something."

"What do you tell them?"

"I tell them to ask you." She turned at last and looked up at him. "I'm not telling anybody what you told me. At the board. About the second page."

He had not asked her to keep it, and he realized, standing there, that he had not even thought to. He had told a thirteen-year-old the most important true thing he owned and then walked away to assembly, and she had carried it for two days through a building full of people who were trying to find out that one thing.

"Thank you."

"It's yours," said Oona. "You get to say it. Not me." She looked back at the board. "Are you going to win?"

"I don't know."

She weighed that.

"That's a true one. You'd have said yes if it wasn't."

"Would I?"

"Grown-ups always say yes about winning. To make you feel better. I'm coming to watch. Everybody is. My uncle says you should watch a good fight even if you don't know anybody in it, and I know somebody in this one."

She went off toward the lecture wing before he could answer. He stood in front of the board with the answer and the petition side by side and was smiling in a way he would not have wanted Edran to see.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He found the seam on the fourth morning.

Waiting for a mistake would have been no use; Edran hardly ever made one. What Cael hunted instead was the spot where all that precision sent in its own bill, and it was slow to show itself, because it lived in a gap so small that only the shape of the whole sequence showed it.

Edran ran a set of four. The shell on his left forearm and the edge on his right were both up before he moved, waiting like a held breath. The first two went one after the other, the shell bursting on an imagined blow and the edge sweeping through an imagined strike, so fast that the two seemed to be one long motion. Cael had watched that a hundred times now and it never stopped being beautiful.

The third did not come so fast.

It came a sliver later: not much, a tenth of a breath, perhaps less. But in that sliver, after the edge had burst and before the third structure had formed, both of Edran's forearms were bare, and his weight sat on the commitment that had just ended with nothing new yet to carry it.

Cael watched him run the set again, and the sliver was there again, in the same place, between the second and the third. He watched the set of three, and the set of five, and the sliver sat in every one of them, always after the second, always before the third.

He understood it on the walk back across the yard, with the binder held flat against his chest in the cold. The first two were the ready pair, built at leisure with the whole of Edran's attention before the fight asked anything of him, and they cost him nothing to spend. The third had nothing behind it. It had to be built from nothing in the middle of everything, and building a full structure took the whole of a Glass fighter's mind, which was not free until the last of the ready pair had gone. Every Glass sequence of three or more had to pass through that one moment when the ready structures were spent and the next was not yet made.

It was not Edran's mistake. Any Glass fighter alive would carry that sliver in a sequence of three or more, and the better trained they were the smaller it would be, but it would always be there, because it came out of the Path itself. Edran had narrowed it as far as three years of perfect mornings could narrow it. He could not close it, not without paying for the closing somewhere else.

The record had said it too, in Wray's square hand. Tires in the sequence, not the body.

He wrote it in the binder that night in the plainest words he had.

The gap sits between the second and the third. He didn't put it there; the Path did. There's nothing in him to fix. Patience, not correction.

He did not sleep much.

On the fifth and sixth days he confirmed it from three directions, because one direction was a guess and two was a coincidence. He watched Edran drill alone in the mornings, and the gap held. He watched him spar in the afternoons against two partners Wray put across from him, a Blade fourth-year with very fast hands, and Hobb, who stood like a wall and made Edran come to him, so that every sequence had to run long. Against the Blade student the gap hardly mattered, because the bouts ended early. Against Hobb, who refused to be moved, Edran's sequences ran to four and five, and the gap opened after the second every single time, and Hobb, who was not looking for it, never used it. Hobb nodded to Cael at the rail afterward on his way out and said nothing at all, and Cael was almost certain that Hobb knew what he had been watching.

The third direction was the record. He went back to the archive on the sixth afternoon and read the four losses again with Prynn's terrible tea at his elbow, and this time he knew what to look for. Every one of the four had been lost to a fighter who outlasted the ready pair in an exchange, and every one had been lost after the third exchange, when Edran was pressing to finish. The gap held from every direction. It was structural, not incidental, and it was there whether Edran was fresh or tired, alone or watched.

He did not train against it.

He wanted to, very badly. He wanted to go into section four in his supervised hour and run the framework against an imagined Glass sequence, timing a step into the sliver over and over until his legs knew it. He did not. Edran had said he would not change anything for the rail, and Cael did not doubt it. But Wray would be in that hall for one of his hours and Quenna for the other, and a seam that anyone could watch him rehearsing stopped being a seam the moment it was seen. He had learned that on the circuit, from the wrong end, more than once.

So he ran Lira's circuits in his supervised hour, and the framework against nothing, and the slow shoulder work for the Reydan joint, and Quenna wrote less than usual on her slate. Once she looked up at him across the section with an expression he could not read at all, and then looked back down.

The one thing he did train, those six nights, had nothing to do with Edran at all.

"Compression," he said on the fifth night, on Brom's floor after the eighth bell. "Quarter only. I'm not reaching for half this week."

Brom lowered himself onto the boards opposite with care; his own left wrist still remembered the night a half push had knocked it back. "Why not?"

"Because half costs four breaths and a locked shoulder, and I want both shoulders on the eighth." Cael set his left forearm across his chest and braced it. His own wrist, the one he had misrouted a fortnight ago, had gone from swollen to stiff to nothing, and he flexed it once to make sure it stayed nothing. "And because it gets worse when I leave it. Two days without practice and the timing slides. If I let it slide this week, it'll wake on the eighth with bad manners."

"It'll wake anyway. If he puts a shell on you."

"I know. I want it to wake the way it's used to waking. Quietly. So I can tell it no."

Brom looked at him, and then set his left palm on Cael's forearm without any further argument. Iron Skin came up under the skin, and he leaned.

They did ten. Each time Cael waited for the force to settle into the bone and chose the road before the fragment could choose one, out and back along the line it came in, a quarter's width and no wider. He did not let himself imagine the channel any broader than that. Five of the ten caught. Each of the five went home into Brom's wrist with the small solid knock he knew by now. Each one cost exactly what the quarter had always cost, the hot bar across the collarbones and two breaths he could not take, and none of them went into a joint.

On the sixth try he did something new, and he did it on purpose.

The force arrived, and the fragment woke and gathered and reached for it, and the road was laid and open. He let it gather all the way, until he could feel the quarter held in him like water in cupped hands, ready to go home.

And then he let it go.

He did not send it anywhere. He opened his hands, as it were, and let it spill out harmlessly, as he had at the first sitting with three pens moving, and his forearm took the rest of the push the ordinary way, with a dull flat ache.

Brom eased off and looked at him.

"You had that one."

"I had it."

"Then why—"

"Because on the eighth I'll have to have it and not use it. In front of everybody. I've only done it once in my life when it counted, and that was half by surprise. I wanted to do it when I'd decided to."

Brom sat back against the leg of his desk and looked at him, and then he laughed, low.

"Most people practise catching. You're practising dropping."

"Lira says I've always done everything backward."

"Lira's right." Brom turned his left wrist over and looked at it, as if it might have something to report. "Again. Catch four. Drop the fifth. I'll count."

They did ten more. Four caught and went home, and two did nothing, and four times Cael gathered a quarter and held it and then let it go. The fourth time it went so quietly that Brom, with his palm on the forearm, could not tell from his side whether anything had been caught at all.

"That last one. Did you have it?"

"Yes."

"I couldn't feel it go out." Brom took his hand away. "That's either very good or very strange."

Cael wrote it up that night under the four headings. Compression-adjacent. Quarter only, by choice. Five of ten caught. Then four caught and dropped on purpose, after the gather, before the send. The last one so quiet Brom couldn't feel it leave. Cost of a drop: none found yet. Integration: partial. Learning to put it down.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

Lira found him on the sixth night in the stable after supper, when the long room had nearly emptied.

He had the binder open on the end of the scarred table under the bricked-up hay door, and he was not writing in it. He was reading the Glass page from the top for perhaps the tenth time. She came down the long room with a mug of something hot in each hand, set one by his elbow, read the page over his shoulder without asking, as she had read every page of that binder since Ardenmere. Then she sat down across from him and wrapped both hands round her own mug.

"You've had it since the fourth day."

It was not a question.

"I wanted to be sure."

"You're always sure by the fourth day." She blew across the top of the mug. "You've just stopped believing yourself that early. You used to. In Ardenmere you'd come home on the fourth night and say, it's his left foot, and you'd be right, and we'd go and eat."

"Being wrong on the fourth day used to be cheaper."

She did not argue with that. She drank, and looked at him over the rim, and he could see her decide not to say three different things before she said the fourth.

"It's a good seam. I read it. It's real."

"I know it's real."

"Then stop reading the page." She reached across and closed the binder for him, gently, with two fingers on the cover. "You've read it ten times. I counted from the door. There's nothing on it tonight that wasn't on it at supper."

He let her close it, and sat with his hands flat on the cover and the hot mug steaming beside them, and for a while neither of them said anything at all. The fire at the far end of the room was down to its last coals, and two second-years playing tiles beside it had very carefully not looked up when Lira came in, and somewhere upstairs a door closed. It was the kind of quiet the two of them had got good at, on more nights like this than either of them could have counted, across a table in some building that did not belong to them.

"Brom's done his numbers," Lira said eventually. "Fetch. Eight today."

"Eight."

"He told me at the hatch as if he were reporting a death in the family, and then went away looking pleased." She smiled into her mug. "He's started carrying the sheet in his coat. He takes it out when he thinks nobody's watching and looks at it."

"Like Edran with his shells."

"Like you with that." She nodded at the closed binder. "Everybody in this building has a thing they take out when they think nobody's watching. Mine's the dot." She drank. "Karis has two notebooks. Gerda checks the clock."

"What does Edran take out?"

Lira thought about it with the same care she gave an opponent's feet.

"The board. He goes and looks at the board."

They sat until the coals were nearly black and the tile players had packed up and gone and the lamp at the end of the table had burned down so far that there was no reason left to sit on. Then Lira stood and took both mugs, and put her free hand on his shoulder as she passed, the way she always had.

"Sleep. Tomorrow's the seventh. You get one more day of being sure."

He slept better than he had all week.

Chapter 19 — The Observer's Floor

[Measured, public-facing narration; let each challenge expose character as well as skill]

The formal yard had never held so many people, and it had not been built to.

Its benches were meant for forty. By the time Cael came through the gate from the main hall, a quarter-hour before the first bell, the benches had stopped meaning anything. Students sat on them two to a space and stood on them behind the sitters. They lined the low wall along the open side three deep and sat along the top of it with their heels hanging down. A row of first-years had climbed onto the roof of the little tool shed in the corner and were being ignored by every instructor in the yard, which was a thing Cael had never seen at Greyvane before and suspected he never would again.

It was cold. The first frost had come in the night at last, and the packed earth of the yard was grey with it except inside the ring, where somebody had swept it bare before dawn and laid fresh chalk. Two hundred people breathed out white into the morning, and the yard smelled of frost and chalk and wool coats, and under all of it, faintly, of the kitchen's bread.

He stopped at the edge of the ring and let himself take the crowd in one piece at a time, because the alternative was to take it all at once.

The three chairs stood at the north end with their chalk ticks and the little table and its inkwell. Quenna sat in the middle with the assessment ledger open. Wray sat on her left in the brown coat, upright and still. The rotating seat this month was the lean old instructor who took the heat Paths, the one with scorched cuffs, who had watched Karis lay six practice points on her second afternoon at Greyvane and said only Ternhall. He had a slate on his knee and a pen held loosely, and he was looking at the crowd with the mild, appraising interest of someone who had sat before plenty of crowds and expected this one to disappoint him a little.

Lira and Brom were at the front of the rail on the open side, near the south mark, where they had plainly been since before the frost lifted. Lira had her arms folded and her chin up. Brom stood beside her with his feet planted and his hands clasped behind his back, as he had stood at the rail of section four for his witness session.

Karis was three places along from them with her notebook already open and her pen already moving. She was not charting him yet. She was charting the crowd.

Hobb was at the far corner of the rail, alone, with his hands in his pockets. Gerda was near the gate with her arms folded and her patched coat buttoned to the chin. And on the front bench, squeezed between two first-years who were both taller than her, sat Oona, with her slate on her knees and both hands pressed flat on top of it.

Past fifty faces he made himself quit counting and simply breathe.

Then he did the thing he had come to do, before anything moved, because that was the rule.

He chose.

The framework, and only the framework. Wind-adjacent, the evasion he had shown at both sittings and on the circuit a hundred times, at whatever speed the fight asked of it, and nothing under it. He would not open the surface read. It was safe to show, it was on the record twice already, and he would not use it, because he did not need it, and because a fight won with one thing was a smaller fight on paper than a fight won with two. The Pressure redirect stayed banked where it had been banked for a year. The Compression fragment stayed in his chest where it belonged, and if anything Edran did woke it, he would give it no road.

The size was chosen. He set it as Lira had taught him to set panel speed, the walls built before the water came.

"For the record," said Quenna.

Her voice dropped into its slow, flat cadence, each word set down separately, and the yard went quiet from the front backward like a field going still in front of a wind.

"Demonstration assessment, unclassified observer track. Third sitting, held in public, in answer to the Petition of Standing posted on this term's board. Present: the presiding assessor, the instructor's seat, the rotating faculty seat. The bout is an exhibition under standings rules, three exchanges on the instructor's count, against the petitioner." She looked up from the ledger. "The candidate takes the south mark. The petitioner takes the north."

Edran was already there.

He stood on the north mark with his back to the chairs and his hands loose at his sides. Up close he looked as he did every morning in the corner by the high windows, rested and exact, with nothing in his face that Cael could use. He was not hostile. He had the look of someone about to learn the answer to a thing, who needed very badly to know which answer it would be.

Cael took the south mark. Eight paces of swept earth lay between them, and the chalk.

"I said I wouldn't change anything," Edran said, very quietly, so that only Cael could hear it under the noise of two hundred people settling. "I haven't."

"I know. I watched."

Edran's mouth moved, very slightly. Allowed to continue, it could have become a smile.

Wray rose from her chair, came to the edge of the ring, and raised one finger.

She lowered it.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Edran came at once.

Wray had said behind Naveth's shut door that he always pressed with a crowd, and Hobb had said it at the rail before her, and he pressed now, off his mark before Wray's hand had finished falling, faster than any morning in the corner. Cael had known he would be faster. Everyone was faster at a fight than at a drill. He had still not been ready for how much.

Both of the ready pair were up before he had taken two steps, built at his mark before Wray's hand ever fell. The shell on his left forearm caught the low winter sun and threw it, a bright hard sheath along the bone, and the edge ran along the outside of his right. He came in behind the two of them like a man walking into weather he had dressed for.

The first strike came high, at the line of Cael's jaw. Cael read it off the shoulder before it had any speed, and the framework moved him half a pace to the left and the edge went past his ear. He heard it go. A Glass edge in motion made a small thin sound, like a wet finger round the rim of a cup, and a chill came off it as it passed, sharp as the frost on the ground.

The second came low, a kick at his knee with nothing on the shin but cloth. He stepped back off it. The third came across, the left forearm swinging round flat at his ribs, and he slipped inside it and out the far side, and found himself four paces from the south chalk with Edran already turning.

He gave ground where ground was cheap. He held where it cost. He watched.

Edran was not trying to finish anything yet. Cael saw that by the fourth strike. He was asking questions, quick ones, one after another. How far did the observer give? How did he move when he was pressed toward the chalk? Did he go left or right when he had the choice? Would he panic, with two hundred people watching and a ledger open? Each strike was a question, thrown whole and finished and impossible to take back, and between them the ready pair stayed whole and unspent, because Edran was not yet spending anything.

At the sixth strike Edran drove the left shell straight at his chest, a short hard push meant to move him, and Cael had nowhere clean to go and took it on his raised forearms.

The shell burst against them.

It went outward in a spray of glitter, bright as a handful of ice thrown into sunlight, and the force of the push went with it in a hundred directions, but not all of it. Enough arrived to drive his forearms back against his own chest and put the weight into the bone.

Something low and tight in his chest woke and reached for it.

He had felt it every morning on the road and every night on Brom's floor and once, in this same cold month, in a closed hall with three pens moving. The force was already his. The fragment closed on it, the way a hand closes on something dropped into it, and a road opened back along the line the shell had come in.

He gave it nothing.

He let the gathered force go as he had let it go at the first sitting, and it spilled out of him harmlessly, and his forearms took the push the ordinary way, with a dull flat ache. Nobody in the yard saw anything. A boy had taken a shell on his guard and stepped back from it. That was all.

The framework moved him off the line before the next strike. He let the breath out slowly.

Edran pressed him for the rest of the exchange with the edge alone, and did not spend it, and Cael gave ground and took it back and did not once let his heels near the chalk. He did not try to draw a sequence out of him to see the seam better. He had six days of mornings behind him. He did not need to see it today, not yet.

Wray called the exchange.

There was no touch. The crowd made a sound that was half a breath let out and half disappointment, because nothing had happened that anyone could tell anyone else about. On the north side, the Edge floor students who stood together on the benches looked satisfied. Their man had owned the ring, start to finish. The observer had spent the whole exchange stepping out of the way.

Cael walked back to the south mark and breathed, and looked at Edran across eight paces, and Edran looked back at him with exactly the same face as before.

Edran was faster than the mornings by about a quarter. Cael wrote it in his head, because he could not write it anywhere else. A quarter faster. Same shape.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Lira had decided before the first bell that she was not going to shout. She lasted the whole first exchange, which she considered a personal triumph.

"He's slow," said somebody on the bench behind her. A third-year from the Edge floor, by the sound, all collar and opinion. "He's just running away."

"He's measuring," said Lira, without turning round.

"He's running away and calling it measuring."

She did turn round then, and looked at the third-year until he discovered something interesting about his own boots. Then she turned back to the ring. Beside her, Brom had not moved at all. He had planted himself for the whole day, hands behind his back and weight in his heels, and only his eyes were going.

"The shell," Brom said, very low. "On his arms. Sixth strike."

"I saw."

"Did he—"

"No." Lira kept her eyes on the south mark, where Cael was standing with his hands loose and his breathing slow, looking at nothing. "He felt it go for it. I saw his shoulders. He let it go."

Brom let out a breath that came out white and hung in front of him in the cold.

She had been watching for that since the frost lifted, if she was honest. Not for the framework, because she had taught him the framework without knowing it and could read it in her sleep. Not for Edran, because she had watched Edran fight three times this term and knew roughly what he would do. She had been watching Cael's chest. A shell bursting against his guard was a push arriving in the bone, and the thing he had taken from Reydan on the last night in Ardenmere lived in that place, and woke for exactly that. She had seen it wake on Brom's floor, and she had read in the binder what it cost him to catch half of a slow push and seen him the morning after, holding his shoulder. If it woke in front of two hundred people and three slates and he let it go home, the whole yard would hear the knock.

It had woken. He had let it go. She could breathe now, for one exchange.

Wray raised her finger for the second.

Lira read it before Wray's hand came down, which was a thing she could do with Cael and nobody else in the world, and had been able to do since the second month in Ardenmere. She read it in how he set his feet on the south mark: a fraction narrower than in the first exchange, his weight a little forward. He was not going to give ground this time. He was going to stand closer than was sensible, inside the reach of a sequence, and stay there.

"He's going to take one," she said.

Brom's eyes came round to her. "Where?"

"Left arm." She was already sure. "He'll want it where he can see it."

Wray's hand fell.

Edran came in harder than the first time, because the first time had told him the observer would give ground, and a fighter who gives ground can be pressed to the chalk. He came in with a fresh pair built at his mark, shell up on the left and edge on the right, and a sequence already running, and Lira saw Cael not give.

He stepped in.

Not far. Half a pace, when everything about the first exchange said half a pace back. It put him inside the arc of Edran's right arm, close enough that the first strike, the left shell driven at his chest, had to come short and cramped, and the framework took him round it by a finger's width as it burst on empty air. The second came down from above, the edge on the right forearm, the other half of the ready pair. Cael slipped it too. He slipped it by less than he could have, Lira saw. He could have gone out wide, out of the sequence altogether, and the third would have cut nothing but air.

He stayed.

Lira's hands closed on the rail. She did not mean them to.

He stayed for the third. She could see him wait for it, see the stillness come over his face that she had seen on him across a hundred circuit rings, when he had stopped trying to do anything and was only looking. The edge burst on Edran's right arm in its spray of light. For a sliver of a moment, so short she would not have seen it if she had not been watching Cael's eyes instead of Edran's arms, there was nothing on either of Edran's forearms at all.

Cael's eyes were on the bare right forearm, where the third would have to come. Not on Edran's face, or his feet, or the space the next strike would cut. On the empty arm.

Then the third edge came up on that arm, made cold, and arrived, and Cael moved a fraction late off it, on purpose, because he had been watching it form instead of watching it come, on purpose, and the edge went across the outside of his left forearm.

It did not go deep. Lira saw that at once, with the part of her that had stitched cuts on the Ardenmere circuit. A graze. A thin line opened across the outside of the arm a hand's width below the elbow, and a few beads of red came up along it, bright in the cold. But it had connected, cleanly, in front of three slates.

"Touch," said Wray. "Petitioner."

The north benches came up off their seats with a noise like a flock of birds lifting. The Edge floor students were shouting, and the second-year tout on the end of the near bench put his face in his hands, and somebody on the wall whistled.

Lira did not hear most of it. She was watching Cael.

He walked back to the south mark holding his forearm away from his body. He did not look at the cut. Not once. He walked with his eyes on Edran's forearms, where Edran was building a new pair at his mark, and he had the faint, distant look that she knew better than her own face in a glass.

He had found it. Whatever he had spent six mornings at the rail looking for, he had just paid a strip of skin to see it once from the inside, and he had seen it.

"He paid for something he already owned," Lira said.

Brom turned his head. "What?"

"He knew it was there. He's known for four days." She heard the edge in her own voice and did not try to take it out. "He just wanted to see it from where Edran's fist was. Because he doesn't trust the fourth day anymore."

"That's not stupid," said Brom slowly.

"I didn't say it was stupid." She let go of the rail and found her palms had gone white where it pressed them. "I said it cost him skin to learn something for the second time. That's him all over. Everybody else pays to learn a thing once."

Brom considered that, and then nodded, which from Brom was a long speech of agreement.

Along the rail, Lira saw that Karis's pen had stopped. It had been moving the whole time, through the first exchange and into the second, in long even passages. Now it had stopped, with the nib resting on the page, and Karis was not looking at the cut either. She was looking at Edran's right forearm, with her lips pressed together, where Cael had looked.

Lira watched her and felt something she did not have time to name, part annoyance and part the thing that came after annoyance when it turned out the other person was right. Karis had seen it too. Of course she had. She had laid nine points on that boy not a fortnight ago and walked him into a drawing of a ring, and she would have laid them exactly so that he never reached his third.

Further along, at the gate, Gerda had unfolded her arms.

"He let it land," Gerda said, to nobody, in her flat procedural voice. "The edge. He could have gone wide."

"Yes," said Lira.

Gerda looked at her down the rail. "You knew he would."

"Before Wray dropped her hand."

Gerda considered that, and then folded her arms again and looked back at the ring. "Then he's not losing," she said. "He's buying."

Lira decided, in that moment, that she liked Gerda a great deal and would tell her so some other day when nobody's skin was involved.

On the front bench, Oona had both fists pressed into her slate so hard that her knuckles had gone white, and the first-year on her left was trying to tell her something, and she was not listening to him either. Her eyes were on Cael, on his arm and then his face.

A second-year leaned down from the bench above her. Lira knew him: one of the crust-wagering crowd from the stable fire. He said something to Oona, quick and wheedling, and Oona turned round on the bench and looked up at him.

"Ask him," said Oona clearly, in a voice that carried three rows. "Not me."

The second-year straightened up and went pink, and the girls on either side of him laughed, and Lira grinned for the first time since the frost.

In the middle of the ring, Wray had come forward to look at the cut. She took it in as she took in everything, as a measurement, and then asked Cael something too quietly to carry. Cael shook his head. Wray looked at him a moment longer, then stepped back to the edge of the ring and wrote on her slate, and Lira understood that she had asked whether he wanted it bound before the third and he had said no.

Of course he had. He wanted the arm where he could feel it.

Lira looked at her own hands on the rail, at the white marks fading from her palms. Somewhere on the calendar in the main hall there was a line with her name on it and a date not very far off. A formal reassessment, two bouts, a panel, a file. She had not thought about it once all morning. She noticed that now, standing at the rail with the frost going off the ground round her boots, and decided that she would think about it tomorrow.

Today she had a different fight to read one exchange ahead.

She looked at how Cael was standing on the south mark, the cut forearm held a little away from his side and his weight perfectly even, and she knew what the third exchange was going to look like before Wray had even risen from her chair.

"He's going to stop running away now," she said to the third-year on the bench behind her, without turning round.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Edran pressed to finish.

Cael had known he would. Four losses in three years, every one after the third exchange, every one because he had pressed to finish a bout that was going his way. He had a touch. He had two hundred people who had just seen him take it. He had the Edge floor on its feet. A fighter like Edran did not wait with all that in his hands.

Wray's finger fell, and Edran came across the ring with a full sequence called.

Four structures. Cael could see it in the set of his shoulders before the first was even up: the long sequence, the one meant to end things rather than ask questions. The ready pair first, rebuilt at his mark between exchanges: the shell on the left and the edge on the right, the held breath. Then the third, made cold. Then the fourth.

Cael let the first one land where it had to land.

It came at his chest, the same hard short push that had woken the fragment in the first exchange, and he did not try to slip it clean. He took it on the outside of his right forearm, angled, so that the shell burst along his arm instead of into it. The glitter went past his face like sleet, and most of the force went with it, and what was left he let go before anything in his chest had time to reach for it.

The second came from above, the edge on the right, down at his collarbone. The framework read it off Edran's shoulder and moved him inside it, half a pace to the right, and the edge went down past his left shoulder close enough to feel the chill.

Then it burst. Edran had to let it go to call the third, and it went in its spray of light, and for the length of a sliver, between the second breaking and the third forming, both of Edran's forearms were bare and his weight sat on a commitment that had just ended.

Cael was already moving.

He had not decided to move when the sliver opened. He had decided six mornings ago. The framework read the shoulder that was meant to carry the third structure, read that it had nothing yet to carry, and moved him in along the line it would have taken, into the space where Edran's arm was empty. It was the same thing the framework had done with every strike since Lira taught it to him without knowing. It read where something was about to be and put him beside it. Only this time the something was not a strike. It was the absence of one.

He put his right palm flat on Edran's breastbone.

He did not strike. He laid the hand there, firm, the way Lira had laid two fingers on the Force Path's chest at the edge of a ring in the second week, a touch that was not a blow and could not be mistaken for anything but a touch. Under his palm he felt Edran's heart going hard, and the third structure forming on Edran's forearm a sliver too late, bright and cold and finished, with nothing left in the world for it to do.

He stepped back out.

"Touch," said Wray. "Candidate."

For a moment the yard did not make any sound at all.

It was not spectacular. Cael had made sure of that, as he had made sure of everything that morning. No fragment had been shown beyond the framework the panel had logged twice. Nothing had flared or knocked or burst except the Glass. A boy had stepped into a gap and put his hand on another boy's chest and stepped out again. That was all anybody on the benches had seen, and most of them could not have said how he had got there.

Then the noise came, all at once, from every direction, and it was not like the noise after the second exchange. That had been a cheer for one side. This was the sound of two hundred people turning to the person beside them at the same moment with the same question.

Cael walked back to the south mark. His left forearm stung where the edge had crossed it, a thin cold line of heat. His heart was going nearly as hard as Edran's had been under his palm. He did not look at the crowd. He looked at Edran.

Edran stood where Cael had left him in the middle of the ring, with the third structure still on his right forearm, bright and useless. He was looking at it. He looked at the shell he had called a sliver too late as if it were a page in his own handwriting with an error on it he had never seen before.

Then he let it go, and it burst into glitter and was gone.

At the table, Quenna had lifted her pen from the ledger. "One touch each," she said. "Three exchanges are concluded. The bout stands—"

"A fourth."

Edran had not raised his voice. He did not need to. The whole yard was listening to him.

He had turned from the middle of the ring to face the three chairs, and he stood very straight, as he had stood at the rail beside Cael on the open floor when he asked what the board was for. "The petitioner requests a fourth exchange, if the presiding assessor allows it."

Quenna looked at him across the frost-grey earth for a long moment. Then she looked at Wray, and Wray looked back at her and gave the very smallest nod, and Quenna looked at Cael.

Cael nodded too.

"A fourth exchange is allowed," said Quenna, "at the request of the petitioner, on the instructor's count." She wrote it down. "Take your marks."

Cael went back to the south mark and understood, as he went, that he had just learned more about Edran from those four words than from six mornings at the rail.

Most fighters, watching their best sequence fail against a gap they had not known they carried, would have needed a moment. They would have taken the draw Quenna was offering and walked away to think about it, and come back next term with the gap narrowed. Edran had not taken the moment. He had asked for another exchange at once, in front of everybody, with the gap still open in him and the whole school knowing it was there.

He wanted to fix it now. On the floor. While it was still costing him.

Cael set his feet.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Wray's finger fell, and Edran came across the chalk, and Cael saw at once that something had changed.

It was the timing of the shoulders. Six mornings of watching had taught him the rhythm of a sequence of four the way he knew the rhythm of the bells, and this one was wrong. The ready pair was up, rebuilt at the north mark, the shell on the left and the edge on the right. The shell went first, at his guard, and burst. The edge came next. And before it had burst, while it was still whole on Edran's right arm, Cael saw the left shoulder begin to load.

Edran was calling the third early. On the other arm. While the second still stood.

It was so simple that Cael almost laughed, and so expensive that he saw at once why three years of mornings had never tried it. The sliver lived where it lived because a full structure needed the whole of a Glass fighter's mind, and nobody had a whole mind to spare while another structure still stood. So Edran had stopped waiting for a whole one. He was building the third on his free left arm while the edge still held on the right, so that by the time the edge burst, the third was already half made. In the space of four words and one walk back to the north mark, he had found a way to fold the gap in on itself, and had decided to pay for it.

It narrowed the sliver to almost nothing.

Almost.

The framework had already read the shoulder and moved him out of the line of the second edge, and he saw, as he went, the cost of what Edran had done. A third structure called while the second still stood was a structure called with half a mind. It was coming up on Edran's left forearm thinner than the others, paler, not quite finished. It would be there sooner. It would not be as strong.

The second burst.

The gap opened, and it was half the width it had been in the third exchange, and there was a thin pale edge already rising in it on the left arm, where no third had ever come before.

A seam did not have to stay wide once you knew exactly where it lived.

Cael went in earlier than he had in the third exchange and lower, under the line of the half-made edge instead of beside it. He did not wait to see whether it would finish forming. He knew it would, a hair too late to stop him and a hair too soon to miss him entirely.

It finished forming as he passed it. The thin new edge came round with Edran's arm and caught him low on the right side, across the ribs, as he went by. It was a glancing thing, half formed and fast, and it did not cut so much as rake. It still hurt, a sudden hot line under the coat that drove the breath out of him.

His right palm was already on Edran's breastbone.

He held it there for a heartbeat, flat, firm, and felt Edran's heart under it, going as hard as ever. Then he stepped back.

Wray did not answer at once. She came to the edge of the ring and looked at Edran's half-formed edge, and at the line it had left in Cael's coat, and at Cael's hand, and her face did not change.

"Touch," she said. "Candidate. The petitioner's edge was unformed at contact. Glancing."

Quenna's hand came up from the ledger before Edran could open his mouth.

"That's the bout," she said. "Logged."

For a breath the yard was silent, with the silence of two hundred people who had come to see one particular thing and had not truly expected to be shown it.

Then the quiet broke, and it did not break into cheering, because Greyvane was not a place that cheered. It broke into the enormous, churning noise of two hundred people who all needed to say something to the person beside them at once. The Edge floor was on its feet and silent. The second-year tout was on his feet and not silent at all. The first-years on the tool shed roof were pounding it with their heels. Somebody on the wall was explaining the third exchange with both arms.

Cael stood at the centre of all that noise, ribs on fire, hands hanging loose, breath coming hard and white, and let it roll past him without trying to sort any of it.

He found, when he looked, that in the whole loud yard there were exactly three things that were still.

Wray, at the edge of the ring, writing on her slate as if the noise were weather.

Karis at the rail, with her pen stopped on the page, looking at him the way she looked at a timing that agreed with something she had written down before.

And Edran.

Chapter 20 — Witness

[Measured, public-facing narration; let each challenge expose character as well as skill]

Edran did not walk away.

Cael had half expected him to. He had expected, without ever quite letting himself think it, the thing that had happened once before in another city, on another floor. An opponent had beaten him there and then sat down beside him afterward wanting to know how the third exchange had worked, and that question had turned into the best friendship Cael had ever been given. Brom had done that. Some old, hopeful part of Cael had been waiting all week for a version of it. He caught himself waiting for it now, standing on the frosted earth with his ribs burning, and understood as he caught himself that it was a mistake. One ending did not have to look like another. This one was shaped differently, and he would have to let it keep its own shape.

Edran stood in the middle of the ring and breathed. He was not breathing as hard as Cael was, because Glass did not tire the lungs as Wind did; it tired something further in. But his hands had a fine tremor in them at his sides, and his face, which had shown nothing all morning, showed something now that was not anger and was not quite anything Cael had a page for.

Then he turned, not to Cael but to the three chairs, and the yard began to go quiet again from the front backward, because people could see that he was about to speak.

"For the record," said Edran.

Quenna looked up from the ledger with her pen already in her hand.

Edran turned back to Cael and looked at him across the two paces of swept earth with the flat, plain honesty of someone reading a finding off a page rather than conceding a fight.

"Whatever you are," he said, "it's real."

A breath. The yard was silent now, all of it, two hundred people and the first-years on the tool shed roof.

"I withdraw the petition."

Quenna wrote it down. Cael could hear the pen in the silence, every stroke of it. He watched her write, and watched the rotating seat turn his head to look at Edran with his mild old eyes suddenly not mild at all. He watched Wray, at the edge of the ring, give Edran the same single nod she had given Brom on the defensive floor and Cael after his first sitting, the nod that meant something had held when she leaned on it.

Edran did not offer his hand. He did not smile, or sit down on the bench beside Cael, or ask how any of it had worked. He nodded once to Cael, the slow, deliberate nod he had given at the north gate and at the rail and at the end of every question he had ever set down, and then walked out of the ring by the north side and across the yard toward the gate. The Edge floor students on the benches stood up to let him pass, and did not follow him.

It was not friendship, and Cael, still blowing hard in the cold, knew that very clearly. It was a narrower thing. In its own way it was worth as much. A student of full standing, Iron Rank Two, first on the standings for most of three years, had stood across a chalk ring from him in front of the whole school. Then he had said aloud, for the record, that the thing the observer category had no word for was something real. Nobody had told him to. He had filed the question himself, and now he had answered it himself, in the same daylight.

It was a witness.

Cael did not know yet what a witness was worth. He suspected it would be worth a great deal one day, and that he would find out how much at a time he would not have chosen, and he put the word away somewhere careful, where he would be able to find it again.

"The record," said Quenna.

She had not moved from her chair. The formal cadence was back in her voice, flat and slow, each word set down by itself, and the yard, which had begun to talk again, fell quiet once more to hear it.

"Demonstration assessment, third sitting, held in public. The instructor's seat."

Wray did not consult her slate. She spoke as she always did.

"Evasion framework under live opposition. Consistent with prior record. No safety concerns."

Cael counted the words without meaning to, as he had at the second sitting. Twelve, more than last month, and he understood that the new words were under live opposition: Wray had written down, in the plainest language her dialect allowed, that this time somebody had been trying to hit him.

"The rotating seat."

The lean old man with the scorched cuffs looked at his slate, on which he had written a great deal, and then looked up and said only, "Entered at length." He paused. "I'll add that the candidate fought the petitioner's sequence rather than the petitioner. I've seen that done twice in thirty years. Both times by people who'd watched a very long while first."

"Entered." Quenna wrote, and then set down her pen and looked at Cael across the frosted earth. "Assessment satisfied."

She closed the ledger with the same economy she had opened it with, as if a public reckoning in front of the whole school had been only the day's next line. The yard came apart into noise again, louder now, and students began to climb down off the benches and the wall and the roof of the tool shed. Cael stood in the ring and could not quite make his feet move.

Quenna rose, gathered the ledger under her arm and came round the end of the little table toward him. She did not lower her voice; in the noise there was no need.

"That satisfies this month." Then, as he turned to go: "Soon, I'd like to try something with more structure to it."

He waited. He had learned to wait out her silences, because there was usually something at the end of them.

Quenna glanced along the rail on the open side, and he followed her eyes. Karis was standing where she had stood all morning, three places down from where Lira and Brom had been, with her notebook still open in her hands and her pen resting on the page. She was not writing. She was watching him with an expression he had not seen on her before. It was not satisfaction, though there was some of that in it. It was closer to the look on a person's face when a sum she had not dared write down has just come out right on somebody else's slate.

"She's already asked," said Quenna.

There was something underneath the flatness of it that was almost warm.

Cael looked across the yard at Karis, and Karis looked back and did not look away, and he understood, standing there with his ribs on fire and his forearm stinging in the cold, that the next question would not be the kind Edran had asked. Edran had asked what. Whatever Karis had asked Quenna would be nearer to how. He was not sure yet that he was ready for that question, and he was fairly sure, looking at Karis, that it was going to be asked anyway.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Lira got to him first. After a fight she always did. It was among the few things in his life he no longer needed to check.

She came straight across the ring without waiting for the chalk to be cleared and ran her eyes over him in the quick two-second count she had taken of him after every bout since Ardenmere. Eyes first, then the forearm, which she took by the wrist and turned to the light without asking, then the line across his coat on the right side, low on the ribs, where the half-made edge had raked him. She put two fingers flat against it, quite gently, and he flinched before he could stop himself.

"Bruised. Not cracked. You'd have made a different noise." She let go. "The arm's nothing. It'll sting for a week and you'll pick at it."

"I won't pick at it."

"You'll pick at it." She stood back and looked at his face, and he saw her decide, and then she gave him her reading of the bout. "You let him have the fourth exchange."

"He asked for it."

"He earned it. That isn't the same thing. You paid him with all your attention, every scrap of it, and tonight when he goes back over the bout he'll know that. That was the right coin. "And he withdrew, standing in the ring with the whole school watching, in words he chose himself, every one of them written down. Losing cost him less than that did. Remember it about him."

"I'll remember."

Brom had come up behind her while she talked, at his own pace, and stood with his hands still clasped behind his back. His review was shorter. It always was.

"Fourth exchange. He narrowed the gap in the middle of the fight."

Brom left a space after it, to let it land.

"He moved the third to the other arm, between your third and your fourth, in about the time it takes to walk back to a mark. I've known people train for years and never once change a thing like that during a bout." Brom looked at Cael steadily. "You beat a very good one today. When you write it up, write that down as well. "I will."

"I mean it. Seams are easy to write down. People are harder, and they matter more later."

Wray arrived as he finished, crossing the ring with her slate under her arm. She took Cael's left wrist as Lira had and looked at the graze along his forearm, measuring it, and then pressed two fingers into his right side where Lira had, and this time he managed not to flinch.

"Kitchen. Cold cloth for the ribs, clean water for the arm. Breathe deep tonight, all the way down, even though you won't want to. If you breathe shallow to spare them, they'll stiffen and you'll lose two more days than you need to." She let go of his wrist. "Two days. You'll feel it on the stair."

"Thank you."

"You chose a small fight." It was the first thing she had ever said to him that was neither an instruction nor a record. "You kept it the size you chose all the way through, with two hundred people and that boy asking you to make it bigger. That's harder than winning. She went off toward the gate. Cael looked after her, and then at Lira, who had raised her eyebrows nearly to her hair.

"With Wray," said Brom, "that's the same thing."

He did not get to the kitchen for nearly half an hour, because the yard would not let him go. People did not crowd him, because Greyvane was not that sort of place. But they came up one or two at a time while he stood at the rail with Lira and Brom, said things, and went away again, and every time he thought it had finished someone else arrived. The Storm Path fourth-year who had asked whether he meant to fight close or at range came up, said, "Close, then," nodded, and left. Two girls from the hardening family, who had wished him good morning on the stair in the first week for entirely the wrong reasons, said good morning again now, and he thought they might have meant it this time.

Hobb came past on his way to the gate, alone, with his hands in his pockets. Naveth was in the passage outside the kitchen when Cael came out of it, with a cold wet cloth held against his ribs under his coat and the graze on his forearm washed clean and smarting.

The provost was not waiting for him, exactly. He was standing at the passage window with his hands behind his back, looking down at the formal yard, where the last students were still drifting out in twos and threes and a clerk with a broom had begun sweeping the frost and the chalk from the ring.

"I watched from my window," Naveth said, without turning round. "The glass is old and the angle is poor. I saw most of it."

The paragraph would last longer than any of them.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The withdrawal went up on the board in the main hall that afternoon, before the fifth bell, as the rule said it must. It was a single sheet in Edran's own hand, the same clear hand that did not shake, pinned with one brass tack beside the three pages of the petition and Quenna's answer. Cael went to read it at the change of bells, when the hall was busiest, because he had decided on the way down from the kitchen that he would not wait for it to be quiet.

Withdrawal of Petition of Standing. The petitioner, Edran, Glass Path, Iron Rank Two, withdraws the petition posted on this term's board concerning the candidate enrolled under the demonstration provision. The petitioner states that the question the petition asked has been answered on the floor, in public, under the framework, in a form he accepts.

It was signed, and dated, and that was all.

Cael read it through. He noticed the word framework, and he noticed that Edran had written a form he accepts and not a form that satisfies him, and he thought he understood the difference. Edran was not satisfied, and was not sure he ever would be, but he had asked whether the standings could still tell, and they had told, and he had put his name to that.

Gerda was at the board too, a few people along, reading the withdrawal with her slip for the floor in her hand.

"Posted," she said, when she saw him. "Answered. Withdrawn." She said each word as if laying down a card. "All three, in daylight, inside a week, every one with a signature. I've never seen one end like that."

"How do they usually end?"

Gerda turned to look at him, and for a moment he thought she would tell him. Then she glanced at the clock above the door, as she always did, and he saw the moment go.

"Correctly," she said, and went to the floor.

The rumor market had rebuilt itself before supper, and Lira delivered the new theories at the stable table with less relish than usual, because, as she said, most of them were true, and there was no sport in that.

"First. You've got a Path nobody's allowed to name, and it's a very good one. That's the most popular. Second, you've been trained in secret by a Silver-tier master in the north." She glanced at Brom. "That's you, by the way. Somebody saw you at the rail looking serious."

"I'm always serious," said Brom.

"That's why it worked." She held up a third finger and then put it down again. "Third, there isn't a third. It's gone. Nobody's saying you're a Compact spy anymore, and nobody's saying you read poetry to the panel." She sounded faintly mournful. "The poetry one was my favourite."

"What happened to it?"

"You won a fight in front of two hundred people." She tore her bread. "Poetry doesn't survive that. Nothing silly does. Everybody saw the same thing at the same time, so now they all half agree, and the whole market's going quiet." She looked at him across the table. "That's the bad part, if you want one."

"Worry when they start to agree."

"They've started. Not about what you are. About whether you're real. That one's settled." She pushed one half across to him. "Eat. You've earned the crust twice today."

He wrote the day up that night in the narrow room with the window open an inch, because the cold helped him breathe all the way down, as Wray had said he must, even though it hurt. He wrote it plainly, without ornament, under the headings the binder had taught him.

Third sitting, public, the formal yard. Assessment satisfied. Wray: evasion framework under live opposition, consistent with prior record, no safety concerns. Function shown: the Wind-adjacent framework and nothing else. The Compression fragment woke for a shell on my guard in the first exchange. Gave it no road. Third time I've chosen that, counting Brom's floor. It's getting quieter to do.

Cost: a graze on the left forearm, second exchange, taken on purpose to see the gap from inside. Lira says I paid for something I already owned. She's right. A rake across the right ribs in the fourth, from a third structure called early on the other arm. Two days, says Wray.

Edran withdrew. He did it in the ring, in front of everyone, in words of his own, and they're in the record now. Whatever you are, it's real. Not friendship. A witness. I don't know yet what that's worth.

He stopped there, remembered Brom, and turned back to the Glass page. Under the line he had written in his second week, Glass believes you can afford to break if you break first and on purpose, he had left a question with a space beneath it, And what does he believe?, and the space had been empty for a month. He wrote in it now.

He believes the board ought to be able to tell. He would rather lose to it than win around it. When he found a gap in himself, in front of everybody, he asked for another exchange so he could close it while it still cost him. He narrowed it by half in the time it takes to walk to a mark.

He looked at that, and then added one more line, because Brom had told him to and because it was true.

I beat a very good one today.

He closed the binder and lay back on the bed with his right side held carefully off the mattress and breathed all the way down, slowly, three times, as he had been told, and it hurt every time. Across the corridor Brom was snoring, and two doors down Lira was quiet, and somewhere in the residence wing Karis was almost certainly still awake, writing in the second notebook by a low lamp. Somewhere on the far side of the yard Edran was almost certainly awake too, with his own sheet of paper and his own pen, working out how to make a third structure on the other arm come up a little less thin. Cael hoped he managed it. He fell asleep before he could decide what it meant that he hoped so.
