The first opponent was a third-year from the movement floor, Current Path, Copper Rank Seven by the board, a solid square boy with a reputation for doing everything the way the lecture said to do it. Current moved like water down a slope, a long gliding step that seemed to carry a body further than its legs had any right to. The boy had a textbook advance built on it. Two glides in, the second one curving, and a strike off the end of the curve while his opponent was still working out which way the water was going.

Wray lowered her finger.

Lira gave him the first exchange. She always gave the first exchange; Cael had watched her give it to fighters in Ardenmere who had not deserved the courtesy. She gave ground in short neat steps and let him show her everything. He glided in, and in again with the curve, and struck off the end of it, and she was not there, and he glided back out to the textbook distance and set himself and came again in exactly the same shape. She let him. Cael watched her watching. Her eyes were on his hips, where the glide began, and on his back foot, where it began a moment before that.

Wray called the exchange with no touch.

The second exchange lasted perhaps four breaths.

The third-year came off his mark into his first glide, and Lira came off hers at the same moment, straight at him, not to the side as the textbook said an evading fighter must but along his own line, inside it. She was there before the second glide had finished loading. He had committed to a curve, and the curve had nowhere to go. She put two fingers flat on his breastbone while he was still deciding what had happened.

"Touch," said Wray. "Candidate."

The third exchange he tried to change it, and Cael liked him for trying. He came in short, one glide only, and struck off the end of it early. It was a sensible answer and she had already read it. She read it off his back foot before he had moved, slipped it so close that his sleeve brushed her ear, and was behind his shoulder when he turned. Then the fingers were on his back, between the shoulder blades, light as a moth.

"Touch. Candidate. That's the bout."

The third-year stood for a moment with his hands at his sides, breathing, looking at the chalk at his feet as if it might have something to tell him. Then he nodded to her, once, a decent nod, and walked off the ring with the face of a boy who intends to go back to his lecture notes that evening and read them again with some suspicion.

At the table, the broad-faced woman had stopped writing. She was not writing anything at all. She was sitting with her pen lifted and her slate on her knee, simply looking at Lira, as Cael had seen people at the Ironyard look at a fighter they had come to watch somebody else beat.

"She didn't take anything," said Brom, very low. "Not one hit."

"She didn't need to," said Cael. "Not with him. Wait."

The second opponent was the Storm Path fourth-year who had stopped Cael on the stair before the exhibition to ask whether he meant to fight Edran close or at range. He had come over the threshold into Iron at the end of last term, and the board gave him Iron Rank One. That put him at the lower edge of the tier, and above Lira on every list in the building except the one this yard was writing this morning. He was quick and narrow and long in the arm, and when he took his mark on the north side the air around him already smelled faintly of rain.

He had watched the first bout. Cael could see that in how he set himself, further back than the textbook distance, his weight light and even. He was not going to give her a line to stand on.

He did not. When Wray lowered her finger he stayed out at the edge of the ring and worked from there. A Storm release was short and sharp, a slap of hard wet air off the palm that could knock a fighter a step sideways or throw grit into her eyes. He threw them small and fast and never stayed where he had thrown one from. Lira went after him, and he left. She went after him again, and he left again, out along the chalk and round, keeping the length of a long arm between them and never once committing to a strike that would have let her inside it. For the whole of the first exchange she chased him round the ring, and for the whole of it he made her pay a little for every pace. Once, she nearly had him against the north chalk, and he went out along it sideways like a cat on a fence. When Wray called it neither of them had a touch, and the yard had begun to make a low uncertain sound.

The second exchange was the same, and it was even, and it went on, and the yard began to tighten round it the way a yard did when a bout stopped being about who people had come to see and started being about which of two people would make a mistake first. Students who had drifted in late from the lecture wing stopped at the gate and did not come further. On the wall a first-year had his fist in his mouth.

Lira took the first hit crossing the middle of the ring. Cael saw her see it coming, a release thrown at her shoulder as she came in, and he saw the space where she could have slipped it, a clear half-pace to her right. She did not use the space. She took it across the top of the left shoulder, a grazing slap of storm-air that turned her a quarter round and would be a bruise for a week. She kept coming. The turn the hit had given her put her a pace closer to him than he had meant to let her be.

He was good. He left again, at once, before she could use the pace, and she chased.

Three moves later she took the second. This one she blocked, or seemed to, her forearm coming up a fraction late, so late that the release went half through her guard and rocked her back on her heels. Cael heard Brom draw in his breath beside him. But the block had been late on purpose, and he saw that too, because he had watched her do it on a circuit floor in Ardenmere with the rent due in the morning. She had let the hit move her because being moved put her exactly where she wanted to be, inside his reach on the side he had just thrown from, with his arm still out.

She had spent two hits in that exchange, and she had spent them without a flicker, the way a person counts out coins she came intending to spend and does not stop to look at them on the way across the counter. That was the whole of her argument, Cael understood, standing at the rail with his hands tight on the cold wood. She was not trying to win cleanly. She was showing three people with the Fenmark sheet at their elbows how far past a Copper ceiling she could go, and what she would pay to go there. She would pay it in front of them without looking down at the bill.

Wray called the second exchange with still no touch, and the Storm fourth-year was breathing hard.

The third exchange she finished with the barrow turn.

He had not seen her use it since Ardenmere. It was a thing she had found in the market yard behind the grain exchange, where the circuit fighters who could not afford a hall trained in the evenings between the stacked barrows. The lanes between the barrow lines were so narrow that you could not slip anything wide. You had to go under. When somebody came down the lane at you with his arm out, you ducked under the arm and turned in against him, so close that your shoulder went into his armpit, and you kept turning, the way a carter turns a laden barrow on a lane too narrow for it. His own weight, still going forward, went over his own front foot, and there was nothing he could do about it. She had used it on half the market yard in her first season. She had stopped using it when the fighters she faced got good enough to see it coming.

The Storm fourth-year did not see it coming, because nobody at Greyvane had ever seen it at all. He threw a release at her as she came in, and she went under it and turned, close, her shoulder into him. He went over his own front foot and caught himself on one hand on the chalk. Her two fingers were on the back of his neck before he had got the other hand down.

"Touch," said Wray. "Candidate. That's the bout."

For a moment the yard said nothing at all.

Then it did not cheer, because Greyvane did not cheer, but it made the low churning sound Cael had come to know, forty people turning to the person beside them with the same question in their faces. On the wall the first-year had taken his fist out of his mouth. Karis, along the rail, had her hands out of her pockets and was holding the rail with both of them, and she was smiling, openly, without correcting it at all.

Lira helped the fourth-year up. He took her hand and stood a moment with his other hand on his knee, getting his breath, and then he laughed, a short surprised breath of a laugh, and said something to her too low to carry, and she laughed back, once, and he went off the ring shaking his head.

The panel went to the far wall and talked. They talked for a shorter time than Cael had expected and a longer time than he could stand, and he stood it anyway with his hands on the rail and his eyes on the chalk. Lira stood on the south mark with her left shoulder held a little away from her side and her breathing slowing and her face as empty as a swept floor. She did not look at the panel. She did not look at the rail. She looked at the north mark, where nobody stood now, as if there might be another bout coming and she meant to be ready for it.

They came back to their chairs. Quenna opened the folder beside the ledger and took out the sheet of weak-tea-coloured paper and laid it flat, beside the ledger, where she could see both. Then she wrote, and then she lifted her pen and her voice fell into the flat slow cadence of the record, every word set down by itself.

"Re-certification review, formal. Two recorded bouts. Both won by the candidate. The panel's notation."

She read it off the ledger without hurrying.

"Advancement inconsistent with recorded tier. Recommend continued track with priority review."

Cael heard it once, and then again inside his own head, because he could not stop himself.

He knew what it was. He had spent his whole life inside records and he knew what it was, and he felt it go through him in the cold yard like a draught under a door. It did not change her tier. She was Copper on Fenmark's sheet and Copper on Greyvane's ledger and she would be Copper on the board this evening with the dot still beside her name. It did not reverse anything, or retract anything, or call anyone wrong. It only stated, in an academy's own language, initialed by three people and dated, that the recorded tier and the floor did not agree. For two years the only paper in the world about Lira had been four paragraphs written by somebody who had never watched her fight. Now there were two pieces of paper, and the second one, written by three people who had, said in plain ink that the first did not add up.

It would stay. Few people alive understood that better than he did: a line in a ledger like that one outlasts the morning it was written, and outlasts the memory of whoever wrote it. Every inch of ground he stood on in this place was made of lines like that.

"Initials," said Quenna. "And the candidate's signature that she has heard the notation."

Lira walked to the little table. She took the pen and signed, quickly, in her slanting hand. Then she stood a moment and looked down at the ledger, at the line Quenna had written, and Cael saw her read it, once, as she had read nothing else that morning. Her face did not change. Her shoulders did.

She came off the ring toward the rail with her water flask, and stopped in front of him and Brom, and did not quite meet either of their eyes.

"I'm going to put cold on this shoulder," she said, "and then I'm going to sit somewhere by myself for an hour. Don't come and find me."

"All right."

"I mean it." She drank. "The wall, at dusk. Both of you. Not before."

She went out through the gate toward the residence wing, holding the shoulder. Gerda watched her go from the end of the rail with an expression Cael could not read at all. Then she looked up at the clock above the main hall door, and went in.

He spent the fifth bell in section four with the post, as Thursday required, and Karis did not say a word about the morning. She timed him and wrote and read back. Once, near the end, when he was getting his breath by the felt, she looked up and said, "She took both of those on purpose." He said, "Yes." She nodded and wrote nothing at all, and that was the whole of it.

At the sixth bell he went to the defensive floor. Brom had said at the midday meal, with a careful face, that Wray had asked him to stay late, and Brom never said anything with a careful face unless he did not yet know what it meant.

The far section was nearly empty. Hobb stood at the edge of the chalk with his hands in his pockets, plainly told to wait and not told why. Brom stood in the middle in his low loose stance, his weight sunk into his heels, and across from him stood Wray, with her brown coat off for the first time Cael had ever seen, folded on the boards at the edge of the section.

She was going to strike him herself.

Cael understood it as he reached the rail, and understood too that he had never seen her do it. In two months he had watched her measure Brom against Hobb, against the fetch drill, against two partners at once and against a Stone fourth-year told to commit everything. He had never once seen her stand across the chalk from him. Shield Path, Bronze. He had written on her page that Shield believed nothing should be spent that didn't have to be, and he had written it from the way she stood, because he had never seen anything else.

"Redirect," said Wray. "Whatever I send, take it and turn it. No more than that."

She struck.

It was not fast, the first one. It was a flat hard shove off her forearm, and as it came a faint pale plane went along the outside of her arm from wrist to elbow, like a pane of glass seen edge-on, so that the shove arrived as a wall arrives, all at once along its whole width. Brom took it on the forearm and gave, the inch and then the second inch, and turned it. It went back round on her along a line she plainly had not braced for, and she took it on her planted feet without moving at all, as if she had expected it to the last ounce.

"Again."

She struck again, a little faster.

Cael watched her count, though she did not count aloud. He could see it in the stillness of her face between strikes, as he had seen Karis count. Every strike was a measurement, each a fraction quicker than the last, one condition changed and everything else held still. She went up the speeds the way a person goes up a stair in the dark, one step at a time, feeling for the next before putting weight on it.

On the seventh strike she stopped.

It had been fast, faster than anything Cael had seen Hobb throw or Edran either, a Bronze-tier strike from a woman who had not spent a single unnecessary motion since he had known her. Brom had taken it and given and turned, and the turn had been clean. But Cael had seen something in it that he had seen before without ever once seeing it as a thing, and when Wray lowered her hands and stood still he knew she had seen it too.

"Again," she said, quietly. "Same speed. Brom, I want you to do nothing different."

She struck. Brom took it, and gave, and waited, and turned.

The wait.

It was the thing Karis had asked him about in the first week, the second half that he held longer than anybody taught. Cael had written it on Brom's page as the best thing about him, the patience that let a strike commit itself fully before Brom took it away, because if he turned too soon the other fellow felt it and kept his weight back. It was the whole of what made his redirect work against people who meant it. And at this speed, for the first time, Cael could see the shape of it as a shape. Between the instant Brom's body had read the strike and the instant his body began to turn it, there was a gap. It was very small, small enough to live inside a breath with room to spare. At Iron speed it was invisible, and at Copper speed it was a gift.

Wray stepped back and put her hands down at her sides. She was not breathing hard; Cael had never seen her breathe hard.

"There's a gap," she said, "between the moment you've read a strike and the moment you begin to turn it. You hold it on purpose. It's the best thing you do." She looked at Brom steadily. "And it's a gap. Against anybody you've ever fought, it's worth holding, because they can't use it. I can see it. I'm Bronze, and I'm not quick enough to use it, but I've stood in front of Silver, and I can tell you what a fast Silver would do with it. He'd be through it before you'd started your turn."

Brom stood very still in his stance.

"Can you fix it?"

"I can show it to you. I've just done that." Wray bent and picked up her coat and put it on and buttoned it to the throat, one button at a time. "Closing it is another matter. You'd close it by meeting strikes fast enough to punish it, every day, for months, until your body learned to start the turn before the wait was done without losing what the wait gives you. That needs somebody faster than the gap." She buttoned the last button. "I haven't got anybody faster than the gap. Not me. Not Edran, not the Ternhall girl, not anybody on this academy's roster. Greyvane doesn't have one."

Hobb, at the edge of the chalk, took his hands out of his pockets.

"So it's a ceiling," said Brom slowly. "After all."

"No." Wray said it at once, and firmly, and Cael saw that she had been waiting for him to say it so she could say that. "You've made me careful with that word, and I'm not going to waste the care now. A ceiling is a place people stop because somebody drew a line on a board and told them to. Your column says I drew it in the wrong place, and I'm watching your column." She looked him in the face. "This is a wall. It's a real thing in the road, in your body, not in anybody's belief. You can see it now. Seeing a wall isn't the same as getting over it, and you'll not get over this one here. I'm sorry for that. I'd rather tell you today than let you find it on a floor somewhere with somebody fast on the other side."

For a long moment Brom only watched her. Then came the nod, single and slow, the nod he gave a fight that had gone the way he thought it would and he had not wanted it to.

"A wall."

"A wall," said Wray. She turned to Hobb. "Thank you. You were here in case I needed something slow and heavy to show him the difference, and I didn't. Go and eat." Hobb nodded and went, and passing Brom he stopped, and put one broad hand on Brom's shoulder, and took it away, and went on without a word.

Wray stopped at the rail where Cael stood.

"You saw it," she said. It was not a question.

"On the seventh."

"So did I." She looked at him with her level measuring eyes, and he could not tell what she was measuring. "Write it down properly. He'll want somebody to have seen it besides me."

Lira was on the wall at dusk, as she had said she would be, with a cold cloth folded under her coat over the shoulder and her knees drawn up. When they came out she moved over so that the gap beside her was exactly the width of two people.

She did not wait for them to ask.

She told them what was on the sheet. She told it flatly and in order, the four paragraphs, the one signature that belonged to nobody she had ever met, the nineteen words. She said the nineteen words aloud, all of them, and Cael counted them as she said them and hated himself a little for counting and could not stop. She told them about the threshold rule, formal hearing not required, and the room with the green cloth that had not been a hearing at all, only a reading. Then she told them about the sentence the man at the end of the table had added out loud, it means you have no control of yourself, and how she had looked for it on the sheet and it was not there.

"He made it up," she said. "Two years I've had that sentence in me like a splinter, and it isn't even written down anywhere. They didn't think it was worth writing."

Brom said nothing. He put one hand flat on the stone between them.

Cael thought before he said anything, because it mattered, and because the things that mattered most to say to Lira were the ones she would know at once if he had not thought them through.

"When Vell gave me the sheaf," he said slowly, "the last night in Ardenmere. Her copy of my whole record off the Ironyard ledger, every bout. She said, the records know you existed here. I didn't understand what she meant. I thought she meant it as comfort, because the registry had me down as a word and nothing else, and her ledger had me down as everything I'd done." He looked out at the yard going dark. "I think she meant it as a fact. Whatever anyone writes somewhere more important, the people who were there and wrote it down honestly, their page stays. It knows what happened. Nobody gets to argue it away by writing something different in a better building."

Lira was very still beside him.

She said it slowly, weighing each word before she put her own on it. "The records know what happened here. Nobody gets to say otherwise."

"That's the one I'd keep."

She sat with it a while. Then she did a thing he had not expected, which was to laugh, really laugh, a sound that came up out of her as if it had been kept waiting on a stair for two years and had just been told it could come down. She took the four paragraphs out of her coat. Quenna had given the original back to her after the panel, he learned later; the file kept a certified copy. She folded them once more along the old crease and put them back inside her coat, against her ribs, on the side away from the bruise.

"Evidence," she said. "For when it's obvious."

"When what's obvious?"

"That they were wrong." She said it with no heat in it at all. "I'm not filing a dispute. Not now. Maybe not ever. This morning's line does more for me here than any argument with Fenmark would, and I'd have to stand up in front of more people who were never in the room." She patted the coat. "But I'm keeping these. For the day the proving runs the other way, and some office owes me an admission instead of me owing it proof."

She turned to Brom. "You've been sitting there with a face on since you came out. I noticed. I've had my turn. Say it."

Brom looked at the yard.

"Wray found my wall," he said.

He told it as plainly as he told everything, the gap between the read and the turn, the wait that was the best thing he did, a fast Silver going through it before he'd started. Nobody at Greyvane quick enough to teach him to close it. Not Wray, not Edran, not Karis.

"She called it a wall," he said. "Not a ceiling. She was very particular. A ceiling is a thing somebody draws. A wall's a thing in you." He was quiet a moment. "It's an honest wall. Nobody's fault. Just the sort of thing you hit if you get good enough to hit it."

Lira leaned across to bump his shoulder with hers, winced, since it was the bruised one, and bumped him again with the good one on principle, and Brom laughed once, down in his chest.

The three of them sat on after that without saying anything, while the yard went from grey to dark and the hill town's lamps came on below them. Cael thought about the two things that had been found that day, one in a ledger and one in a friend, and how differently they sat. Lira's had been paper all along, and paper could be answered with a floor. Brom's was bone and habit and two years of being right, and there was no ledger anywhere that could be argued with about it.

That night it went into the binder.

Lira's review. Two bouts, two won. She spent two hits in the second like coins and finished with the barrow turn from the Ardenmere market yard. The notation, read aloud, in their words: Advancement inconsistent with recorded tier. Recommend continued track with priority review. First paper anywhere that says her file might be wrong. She's keeping Fenmark's four paragraphs. No dispute.

Brom's wall. Wray struck him herself and found it on the seventh strike, the gap between the read and the turn. She called it a wall and not a ceiling and meant the difference. Nobody here is fast enough to close it.

He looked at the two paragraphs side by side, and then wrote the line underneath them that he had been carrying all the way up the stairs.

Some walls come down when you finally push. Some stand because nobody ever built a door in them. I think learning to tell which is which might be most of what this place is for.

Chapter 27 — Correctly

[Patient, lucid narration; make repeated failure feel cumulative rather than repetitive]

Nobody fetched the rumor market out of bed for Gerda.

The yard at first bell on Friday was colder than it had been on Thursday, and emptier, and the frost lay on the benches unbroken because nobody had sat on them. Five people stood at the rail on the open side. Cael was one, and Lira beside him with her bruised shoulder strapped under her coat, and Brom, and Karis a little along with her hands in her pockets and no notebook again. He had watched her. He had no reason to go into it. A standings bout scored touches, and a touch had to be made by somebody, and if neither of them made one the exchange was empty and so was the next. He circled the edge of the haze, and she turned inside it to keep him in front of her. He circled the other way, and she turned again. He would step into the edge of the haze and out again before it had properly closed on him, a feint and a withdrawal, a feint and a withdrawal, his fast hands never quite committing. Gerda turned and turned. Cael watched her shoulders and her feet, and saw the moment she decided to go out after him, the weight shifting onto her front foot. The instant she was out of it she was only a tall careful girl on swept earth with nothing slowing anyone down, and the Blade boy's hand flicked out and touched her shoulder before she had finished setting her foot.

He knew what she had said. He had heard her say it twice before, at the board in the main hall, about other people's petitions.

Correctly.

It took him most of the walk back across the yard to understand what he had just watched, and when he understood it he did not like it at all.

Nothing had gone wrong. That was the whole of it. Nobody had cheated her, or lied, or made a sentence up out loud at the end of a table. The procedure had worked precisely as its writers meant it to. Three people had read her originating record and watched her fight twice on a cold morning and written down what they saw. What they saw was a careful Copper fighter who did not move out of her own haze unless she had to and never once took a risk she could avoid, which was the tier and rank the record said she was, and so the record and the floor agreed. Yesterday a floor had disagreed with a file, and the disagreement had been written down and would stand. This morning the floor had agreed with one, and the agreement had been written down too, and it would stand just as long.

No floor had come to rescue her, because she had not let it.

Lira had stopped walking. She was standing in the middle of the yard with her strapped shoulder held away from her side, looking back at the gate, where Gerda had gone out toward the training hall with her coat over her arm, not hurrying, checking the clock above the door as she passed it.

"I'm going to help her," Lira said.

Cael looked at her.

"That's Lira deciding," Cael agreed.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

Gerda came to the scarred table at the midday meal on Saturday, because Lira brought her. She sat at the end of the bench with her bowl in front of her and ate with the careful economy of somebody who had once been very hungry for a long time and had decided never to waste anything again.

She did not speak at first, and Lira did not push. Karis was at the other end of the table with her notebook shut, and Brom was opposite, and the long room was full of the noise of a Saturday, second-years arguing about tiles and somebody laughing by the hatch. Cael had begun to think that Gerda had come only to sit near people for an hour and would go away again without a word.

Then she put her spoon down.

"You'll want to know why it's Rank Nine and a termination," she said. "Anybody would."

"We don't need to know anything," said Lira.

"No. But you'll wonder." Gerda laid both hands flat on the scarred wood on either side of her bowl, as Cael had seen Karis lay hers. "I'd rather you knew than wondered. Wondering gets things wrong."

She told it in her procedure voice, flat and level and very exact.

She had been in her second year at a school in the south, Copper Rank Nine, one rank short of the threshold, and her instructor had told her in the autumn that she would cross before midwinter. In the winter her mother had fallen ill at home, three days' coach away. Gerda had gone to her instructor and asked for leave, and he had given it to her in the corridor outside the floor, nine days, go, and she had gone. In the nine days three of her recorded bouts had fallen due, and she had not been there to fight them. The leave had never been written down. Her instructor had meant to; she believed that still. Before he did, he had been offered a post at a larger academy in the north and taken it, and gone, within the week.

"The three bouts were entered as forfeits," Gerda said. "Correctly. I wasn't there. A forfeit is what you call a bout where one fighter isn't there. Three forfeits in a term means the standing requirement isn't met, and that means a review, and the review looked at the record and found three forfeits, which were there." Her hands did not move on the table. "I filed a petition. I said I'd had leave. It was posted. It was answered. There was no record of leave. The forfeits stood."

"Correctly," said Lira, very quietly.

"Correctly." Gerda looked at her bowl. "That's the thing nobody understands, when I say it. Everyone wants somebody to have been cruel. Nobody was. Everybody did their job. The instructor meant to write it and didn't, and the clerk entered what happened, and the review read what the clerk entered, and the petition was answered by people reading the same page I was reading. If any one of them had done anything wrong I could have stood up and said so. They didn't. That was the worst of it."

Nobody said anything. At the far end of the long room somebody won at tiles and the second-years groaned.

Then Gerda's voice changed. It was a small change, and Cael almost missed it, but he had been listening to her procedure voice for two months and he heard it go.

"She got better," Gerda said. "My mother. She's well now. She writes to me every month, on the day the coach goes, and she never once mentions it. She thinks I don't know she feels it's her fault." Her right hand lifted off the table and came down again. "I check the clock because a clock is a thing that's written down. Every slip I sign, I write the hour on it, and I look up to make sure the hour's the hour, and I get my initials before the sixth bell, every day, because nobody is ever again going to find a thing about me that should have been written and wasn't."

She stopped. Her hands lay on the table in front of her, and she looked at them.

"So yesterday," she said, "I fought the way you fight when the only thing you're afraid of is giving them something to write. I didn't go out of the haze. I didn't take a hit. I didn't do one thing that could go wrong." She looked up at Lira. "And they wrote down that nothing happened. Which was correct."

Lira had not moved during the whole of it. Now she leaned forward on her good elbow.

"What does the provision say about reconsideration?"

Gerda answered at once, without having to think, as Cael would have answered with the three words of his own provision.

"A candidate whose review recommends reconsideration may elect, before the term's end, to fight one supplementary recorded bout before the same panel, by written request delivered to the presiding assessor with the hour noted. The panel shall consider the supplementary bout with the review."

"Then do that."

"I don't file things." Gerda said it simply, the way a person says they don't eat fish. "I filed one thing in my life. You've heard what happened."

"It isn't a petition. It's a form." Lira did not raise her voice. "Nobody posts it. Nobody answers it on a board. You write down that you want one more bout, and the hour, and you hand it to Quenna, and Quenna writes a date on the calendar. That's all it is." She held Gerda's eyes. "I'll sit with you while you write it. I'll stand at the desk while you hand it in. And between now and the bout, I'll get you out of that haze if I have to drag you."

Gerda looked at her with her pale level eyes, and Cael could not tell what she saw.

"Why?" said Gerda.

Lira sat back.

"Because on Thursday a floor got me out of a file," she said. "And yesterday there wasn't one for you. I'd like there to be one."

The second null was that afternoon, in the quiet room, with the slate on the nail outside saying K. — declaration practice.

Brom came as witness. He sat on the floor against the wall by the door as Lira had, with his knees up and a heel of bread in his coat. For the first quarter of an hour he watched with the grave attention he gave a bout. Then, a little after Karis had begun her paired points, he took out the bread and began, very quietly, to eat it.

Karis did not stop working. She laid a point and held it and let it go on her count, and laid the next, and between the third and fourth she reached down to the ledger on the boards beside her without looking and wrote something short, and went on.

At the end, when Cael had said nothing for the third time in his life and she had written the result, she turned the ledger round so he could read it under the fourth clause, and he read it.

Session two. Source: K., Iron Rank Three, demonstration intensity, consent given aloud. Distance nine paces. Duration one quarter-hour. Declarations: single points only, eight. Subject's reach: attention alone, held throughout. Witness: B. Witness eating. Result: null.

"You wrote that I was eating," said Brom, from the floor.

"It isn't relevant."

"I don't know yet what's relevant," said Karis. "That's why I write everything down. If it turns out bread is the missing condition, you'll be very glad I noted it."

Brom considered this with great seriousness, and then took another bite.

The third was that evening, after supper, at five paces. Karis worked in pairs, two points at a time a pace apart, held to a count of twenty and let go together. Cael tried invitation, with his eyes shut between each pair and open for the bloom, the space held open in him beside the four like a hand held out across a room. Nothing came of it. Session three, the ledger said. Source: Iron Rank Three, Ember, demonstration intensity. Distance five paces. Declarations: paired ignition points, held to count twenty. Subject's reach: invitation, eyes closed between declarations. Notice: none. Result: null.

The fourth was on Sunday morning, before the first bell, with nobody else in the quiet room at all. Karis had asked whether he wanted to try it close, and he had said yes, and they had argued a little about how close. She settled it by walking up to a pace from him and saying, "Here. If it's too near, I'll know before you do." From one pace he could feel the heat of her points on his face. Each one bloomed a hand's width from his cheek, steady as a coin of lamplight, and the warmth came across his skin like standing near a hearth with his eyes shut. He wanted, plainly and with his whole chest, as hard as he had ever wanted anything. Nothing happened.

"Null," he said, when she had let the last point go.

"Null." She wrote it. She looked up at him from a pace away, close enough that he could see the tiredness at the edges of her eyes that he had not known was there. "Was it too near?"

"Good." She wrote that too. "Then we know distance alone, at the nearest I'm willing to go, isn't sufficient either."

He told Lira at the midday meal, in the general shape the third clause allowed. When he got to the part about one pace and the heat on his face, Lira stopped with her bread halfway to her mouth. She put it down. "One pace," she said. "With the thing in you reaching as hard as it can, and her hand's width from your face." She picked the bread up again. "If anything had gone wrong, at one pace, how fast would the clause have stopped it?" He did not have an answer, and she saw that he did not, and she let it go because the second-years were at the next table, but she did not eat the bread, and she did not look at him again until the meal was over.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

At the sixth bell on Sunday Lira took Gerda onto the open floor, and she brought Hobb.

Cael never learned how. He suspected Brom had been asked to ask, and that Brom had gone to the defensive hall and stood beside Hobb until Hobb looked at him, and said one sentence, and that Hobb had said nothing back and simply come. However it had happened, Hobb was there, at the near section of the open floor, standing on the chalk with his feet a shoulder-width apart and his hands loose, as patient as a gatepost.

"He's going to stand there," Lira told Gerda. "That's all. He's Stone. He doesn't move unless he's made to. You're going to make him."

Gerda looked at Hobb, who looked back at her with his broad calm face and said nothing at all.

"With what?"

"With your whole weight. Out of the haze. You can lay it if you like, but you can't stand in it. You have to come out and put yourself into him, and he'll hit you back exactly as hard as Wray would tell him to, and you'll take it." Lira folded her arms on the good side. "Then you do it again."

Gerda laid her haze. It went out from her across the boards, grey and slow, and reached Hobb's feet and climbed his shins. Hobb did not move. A Stone fighter standing still in slowness was only a Stone fighter standing still, and the haze had nothing to do to him.

Gerda stood at the edge of her own grey and looked at him.

Cael watched her shoulders from the rail. He had watched them yesterday in the formal yard, the weight going forward and coming back, and he watched it happen again now, forward, back, forward, back, three times, four. On the fifth she came out of the haze, two quick steps, and put her shoulder into Hobb's chest. It was a good honest shove with real weight in it. Hobb took it the way a wall takes rain. He put one broad hand flat on her collarbone and pushed, not hard, exactly hard enough, and she went back two paces into her own haze and stood there with her breath gone and her face white.

"Again," said Lira.

Gerda did it again. Hobb did it again. She went back two paces.

She did it eleven times in the hour, and eleven times Hobb sent her back, and not once did she move him a finger's width. She did not take a single hit she had not been made to take. Every time she came out of the haze Cael could see her decide it, as if she had to make the choice from the beginning each time. And every time she went back into it, he could see her relief.

At the end of the hour she stood at the edge of the chalk with her hands on her knees, breathing.

"That's nothing," she said, to the boards. "Eleven times and nothing."

Hobb, who had not spoken once in the hour, took his hands out of his pockets.

"Eleven," he said. "Yesterday, none."

He nodded to Lira, and to Gerda, and went off across the floor toward the defensive hall without another word. Gerda straightened and looked after him until the hall door had shut behind him.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

On Monday morning of the tenth week, in the archive, Gerda read the reconsideration clause aloud to Prynn.

Cael was there because he was always there at that hour now, at the far end of the long table with the statute book and a cup of tea he had not yet found the courage to drink. Lira had brought Gerda in at the second bell. Prynn looked up from her high stool, took off her spectacles, and looked at the two of them for exactly as long as it took Gerda to wonder whether she ought to leave. Prynn came down off her stool, took a thin bound volume from the end of the nearest aisle, laid it on the long table, and opened it without looking to the right page. Then she set a sheet of heavy paper square to the table's edge and uncapped her pen.

"May elect, before the term's end."

Prynn considered her over the top of the spectacles.

"It does." Prynn dipped her pen. "Most people who have been bitten by a procedure read may as may not. They hear it as a door somebody might shut. It isn't. It's a door you hold." She wrote. "Go on."

The candidate elected to fight one supplementary recorded bout before the term's end, as the provision allowed. At the bottom she wrote the hour.

Then she looked up at the clock above the door.

Quenna took the sheet, read it, initialed it in the margin, and wrote something in the calendar book on her desk.

Lira, beside her, did not say anything at all. She only put her good hand on Gerda's elbow, for a moment, and took it away again.

Chapter 28 — Boundary Conditions

[Patient, lucid narration; make repeated failure feel cumulative rather than repetitive]

Lira took his pen out of his hand just before Karis laid the first point of the ninth session, and would not give it back.

It was the Thursday evening of the tenth week, the second week of the nulls, in the quiet room with the slate on the nail outside it saying K. — declaration practice. Lira had come as witness under the third clause and had proposed, with suspicious enthusiasm, a variable nobody had tried: whether the thing in him would reach any differently if he were annoyed. So she held the pen behind her back where he could not get at it, for the whole quarter-hour. Between declarations she told him, in a pleasant low voice, about every time in Ardenmere he had been wrong about the weather.

He was very annoyed, and under it he wanted as hard as he could. Karis laid her points and held them and let them go on her count.

Null.

"That isn't a variable," Cael said, at the end.

"Irritation is a state," said Karis, writing. "States are variables. She's quite right." She looked up. "Was he irritated?"

"Very," said Lira, and gave him back his pen.

Session nine, the ledger said. Source: K., Ember, Iron Rank Three, demonstration intensity, consent given. Subject's reach: want, under irritation supplied by witness L. (pen withheld). Notice: none. Result: null.

They ran a session every day of the tenth week, and on three of the days they ran two. The slate on the nail said K. — declaration practice so often that a Current Path first-year, who wanted the room for a declaration of his own, began to take it personally, and Karis gave him the evening hour without a word and moved them to the morning. She did not think it a sacrifice. She thought it a variable, by the rule she had set herself on the first night: no two sessions the same. A failure repeated under the same conditions only told you that you had repeated it.

Cael kept the week in the binder's margin, in the short hand he used for things that were not fragments.

Five and six: seven paces, the second with her back to me, only her shoulders and the blooms rising past them. Seven: every point laid on the floor between us, a path of coins of light stopping a pace short of my feet. Eight: announced. Nine: unannounced, and L. took my pen. Ten: run tired, straight after her own standings bout (won, three exchanges). She said "Consent given" before she had shut the door. All null.

Brom, when he came, asked every time whether there was a clause about barley yet, and every time Karis wrote Witness requests barley clause. Declined. By the end of the week the line stood four times in the ledger, word for word, and Brom read it over her shoulder with deep satisfaction.

And out of all of it, out of ten nulls and hours of a girl laying small fires in the air, the binder filled up with Karis.

He could not help it. He had never been able to help it. He had watched eleven Paths from the edges of floors in his first fortnight because watching was what he had, and now he was standing a few paces from one person for an hour a day, with nothing to do but look, and the looking went down into her like water into dry ground. He charted her tells to a quarter of a second, and then, because a quarter of a second turned out to be too rough, to less. Her off hand went still before every ignition; he had known that since the first week. Now he knew how long it stayed still: a quarter of a second at her freshest, a little more by the end of an hour, never less. Before every sustain, every point she meant to hold beyond its first count, she took a half-breath, short and shallow, through the nose, so small he doubted she knew she did it. And her release, the third of a breath of shimmer that lingered after a point went out, was not a fixed thing at all. It grew. Under fatigue it stretched, a few hundredths of a second in the second half of a long session, then more, so that by the end of the tenth session, after her standings bout, he could have told the hour of the afternoon by how long her points took to die.

He told her about the release, because she had a right to know what he was writing about her, and because it was the kind of thing she would want.

"The lag grows when you're tired. After the first half-hour. You can't feel it, I think."

She stopped with her pen above the ledger.

"No," she said slowly. "I can't." She looked at the place in the air where her last point had been. "Ternhall timed it at the start of sessions. Never at the end." She wrote something, and turned the ledger round for him to read. Extinguish-lag lengthens under fatigue. Observed by subject. Not felt by source. Ternhall never measured late.

"You could have kept that," she said. "None of the clauses covers what you write about me."

"You'd have wanted it."

"I would." She closed the ledger. "That's the second time you've counted the way I count. I'm starting to think it isn't an accident."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On the fourth night of the tenth week he tried the whole push, in Brom's room after the eighth bell, by a shaded lamp. A month ago, on Brom's floor, he had caught half of one of Brom's slow pushes and sent it back, once, at double the cost. That half had sat in the Compression section of the binder ever since like a door left open.

"You're sure," said Brom.

"No. But I'll never be sure. I'm ready."

"That isn't the same as sure."

"No," Cael agreed, and set his left forearm across his chest and braced it.

He had been thinking about the full push since the day the half came. The half had come not from reaching harder but from choosing a wider road before the force arrived, a channel cut for twice the water. A whole slow push would need the whole road, as broad as Brom's arm, laid out back along the line the push would come in and held there, steady, the whole time the force was arriving. If he reached for more than he had chosen, or chose the whole and then flinched from the size of it, it would go into a joint. The size had to be decided first and then not changed, and that was the entire difficulty, because nothing in him wanted to stand still while a thing that large came in.

Brom knelt and laid his palm on the forearm and let the Iron Skin come up under it, and leaned.

The first three tries did nothing; he had chosen the whole road and then, in the instant before reaching, narrowed it without meaning to, the way a hand closes a little on a rope when the weight comes on. The fourth caught a quarter, out of old habit, and cost what a quarter cost. The fifth he narrowed again. On the sixth he caught himself narrowing and opened the road again in the same breath, and the force slid sideways off it and went into his left elbow with a deep sick throb, and he sat back on his heels with the arm folded against him.

"Elbow," said Brom.

"Elbow." He flexed it. It moved, unhappily. "I changed my mind in the middle. It went where I hadn't decided."

"Then don't change it."

"That's the whole problem."

"That's the whole answer," said Brom, as he had said it in the pine needles two months ago, and settled his hand again. "Choose it and leave it chosen. Like Glass. Again."

The seventh did nothing. On the eighth, he did not narrow.

He laid the road out before Brom leaned, the whole width of Brom's forearm, out and back along the line. He held it, and did not look at it. The force arrived. It came in slow and heavy and settled into the bone, the whole of a push Brom could have held all night, and the fragment woke low in his chest and gathered, and went on gathering long past where it had ever gathered before. It ran up out of his forearm into his shoulder and across his chest and down into the floor of him, and for a moment he held the entire push inside himself like a lungful of air taken much too deep, and could not believe there was room. Then he sent it home.

It went back into Brom's arm with a sound like a door slammed in the next room. Brom's whole body rocked back off his knees onto his heels, and his hand came off the forearm, and he sat down hard on the boards and stayed there, staring.

Then the bill came, and it was not a bar this time, and not a beam. It was a weight laid on the whole of his chest at once, as if somebody had set a sack of grain on him where he knelt. He could not breathe. He counted, because counting was the only thing he could do: one breath gone, two, three, four, five. On the sixth he got air into himself in a long tearing gasp, and it came back out as a cough that bent him over his knees, and he coughed until his eyes ran. His right shoulder had locked solid. His hands, when he looked at them, were shaking, both of them, the fingers jumping against each other like a man's in a hard frost.

"Whole," said Brom, from the floor. He was holding his own wrist. "That was the whole of it. It came back whole."

"Whole," Cael managed, when he could.

He wrote it down in the morning at his desk by the window, with his right arm resting on the table because he could not lift it past his ribs, and every deep breath finding the ache under his breastbone and leaning on it.

Compression-adjacent. Brom's room. Full slow push, caught and returned whole, on the eighth try. Done by choosing the whole road first and not changing it. Benefit: none in a real fight yet, but now I know the size of what it can hold. Cost: six breaths gone and a cough, both hands shaking for an hour, right shoulder locked until morning, breastbone too sore to lie on. The sixth try misrouted into the left elbow when I changed the size mid-reach. The price doesn't double with the catch. It more than doubles. Integration: partial. Whole, once.

Underneath, smaller:

Lira has read what half cost. She is going to read this, and she is going to say something.

She did, at breakfast, when he came down holding his right arm against his side. It was short and sharp. Then she spent the rest of the meal cutting his porridge into neat squares with her spoon so that he could eat it with his left hand, without once remarking on what she was doing.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Oona had found him earlier that Thursday, at the board in the main hall, in front of the calendar, which by now he thought of as her office more than his.

She was not looking at his line. She was looking at a line far down the column, weeks off, in the clerk's small even hand. He knew what it was before he read it. He had been counting the weeks too, without ever deciding to.

Kindling assessment, observer track. Oona. Registered Arbiter Station, town. Second bell.

"You've been counting."

"Everybody counts. My mother counts in letters. She writes every week now instead of every month. She's never written every week in her life." She looked up at him then. "Can I ask you something rude?"

"You can ask."

"What was yours like? Not short and then very long. That's what you said before. I want to know what it was like."

He looked at her in the busy hall, with students going past behind them toward the second bell. He had been waiting since the first week for her to ask it properly. He had promised himself, and her, that he would not lie to her.

"There's a room," he said. "Yours is the grey building on the corner, at the bottom of the hill. Mine was in Denvash, and it had a floor somebody had scrubbed so hard you could smell the soap from the door, and a bench outside it to wait on. I waited a long time. I was more frightened than I'd ever been, and I'd been frightened plenty before that." He thought about it. "There was a man with me. Hesk. He had a workshop and I lived in it. He didn't say anything while we waited, and when they called my name he put his hand on my shoulder, here, and left it there until I stood up. That was the best part. I still remember exactly how heavy it was."

Oona was listening with all of her.

"Then you go in. It doesn't hurt. Your mother's right about that, and your uncle's wrong; it isn't like being hit by a door." He chose the next words carefully, because they mattered more than the others. "Everything goes very quiet inside you, like a breath held, and then your Arbiter comes, and you'll know it's come. You won't have to be told. And for nearly everybody it gives you your Path, and your first ability, and the words that say what it is, and they're yours and nobody else's. Brom says it's like a receipt."

"And yours?"

"Mine stayed quiet longer than it should have," said Cael. "And at the end of it they had a word for me that wasn't a Path. That's the strange kind. It's very rare. I've never met anybody else who had it." He held her eyes. "Yours won't be the strange kind, Oona. You decided in the first week it was going to be ordinary, and I believe you. Ordinary is what nearly everybody gets."

She thought about that as she thought about every sum, all the way to the bottom.

"Who'll put a hand on my shoulder?"

"Whoever goes down with you. Your mother, if she comes. Ask her to. Tell her it's the best part. She'll want something to do with her hands."

"And if she doesn't come?"

"Then ask me," said Cael. "I'll be at the top of the hill anyway."

Oona looked at him with an expression he had not seen on her before, and then nodded once, briskly, and wrote something on her slate and underlined it twice, and went off toward the lecture wing holding the slate very tight against her chest.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The twelfth session was the long one.

Karis had proposed it on the Friday night, at the end of the eleventh session, a short one after supper, in the voice she used for proposing a variable. Every session so far had run an hour or less. None had run past the point where her sustain began to cost her. If duration was a condition, it was one they had not yet tested at its edge.

"How long?" said Cael.

"Until I can't lay a clean point. Then a little longer, so that we know what not clean looks like." She closed the ledger. "Saturday. After the midday meal. Bring something to eat; you'll be standing a long time."

It ran most of the afternoon. Brom came for the first hour and Lira for the second, and for the third there was nobody but the two of them in the whitewashed room with the high window going from white to gold to grey. Karis laid single points and paired points and channels. The thin singing lines of her Drawn Channel ran between pairs of coins of light laid on the floor and the whitewashed walls, at every length the room allowed. She held points to counts of twenty and forty and sixty, and once, near the end of the second hour, to a count of a hundred. It was a steady small sun the size of a coin, hanging in the air at the height of his heart, while she stood perfectly still behind it with her off hand motionless and her face going slowly pale.

He watched, and reached, every way he knew, in turn, and again, and nothing happened at all.

But something else did, in the third hour, and he almost missed it.

He was at three paces. They had come in closer in the last hour, because closer was the only variable left that day that they had not run long. He had opened the read, the Iron-adjacent pressure-sense along his skin, not because it had any business with Ember but because he had begun to open everything he had, every channel of attention at once, on the theory that if something was going to come in, it might come in by a door he was not watching. The read had nothing to do. There was no weight in the air between them to tell him anything. Karis stood still and her points bloomed and died, and the read lay open on the surface of his skin like a hand on a still pond.

Then, a breath before one of her points bloomed, the air at the place where it would bloom was heavier.

It was so faint he did not believe it. A density, a thickening, in that one small place, as the felt on the training post had thickened before Brom shifted. A breath later the point bloomed there, exactly there, a dim coin of light where the heaviness had been.

He said nothing and waited for the next.

It came again. Not every time; twice in the next ten, and then once more. Each time the place where her point was about to bloom grew faintly heavier, a breath before any light appeared.

"Karis."

She held the point she was holding and did not look round.

"Before your points light. At three paces. I think the read picks up the place they're going to be. A thickening, where it'll bloom, before it blooms." He made himself say it exactly. "Three times in about a dozen. Not every time."

She let the point go on its count, and the shimmer of it hung a long time in the air, because she was very tired now. Then she bent and wrote, slowly, and her hand was not quite steady. She wrote it in his words, and read it back to him, and he listened and changed nothing.

At three paces, with the surface read open, subject reports a thickening at the coordinate of the next point before ignition. Three in about twelve.

"That's yours," she said. "Not mine. I can't see it, and I can't feel it, and I've never heard of anything that could." She looked at the place in the air where the last point had died. "It isn't an acquisition. Nothing happened to you. It's the read you already have, doing something to my Path I didn't know it could." She capped her pen. "Write it down. "Prynn says that."

"Prynn is right about most things," said Karis, and sat down on the scrubbed floor all at once, with her back against the wall and her hands in her lap.

He went and crouched in front of her. She was white to the lips, and her hands, when he looked at them, were cold and very slightly grey at the fingertips, which he had not known Ember could do.

"Sustain cost," she said, before he could ask. "It comes due all at once at the end. It's all right. It's like running too far. I'll be cold for an hour and then hungry for two." She tipped her head back against the whitewash and shut her eyes. "Was it null?"

"It was null."

"Good," said Karis. "I'd have been very annoyed if it had worked on the day I was too tired to write it down properly."

He had nine pages from that afternoon in the binder by the time he went to bed: eight of Karis's Path and how it changed as she tired, and one of the thickening at three paces, with no theory under it at all. Not one line was about a fragment, because there was nothing to write.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

They ran the thirteenth and fourteenth on the last day of the tenth week, two short ones, a quarter-hour each, one at dawn and one before supper, at five paces, because Karis was still cold at the fingertips from the long afternoon. Both were null.

That evening Karis read the ledger back to him in the archive, at Prynn's long table. She read all fourteen sessions in order, as the fourth clause said she must before any of it existed anywhere else.

She read it in her flat even voice, the voice she used for timings, and he listened to fourteen sessions of his own failure set down in another person's handwriting. Distance nine paces. Distance one. Source's back turned. Declarations unannounced. Source tired. Witness eating. Witness withholding pen. Duration three hours and some minutes. And after every one of them, the same word, written the same size, with the same care.

Null.

He waited to feel what he had always felt, all his life, when somebody read him back a list of the things he could not do. It did not come. He had been studied his whole life by people for whom his failures proved something they had already decided about him, assessors and clerks and a patient official in a district office somewhere. When those people wrote down what he could not do, they were adding a stone to a wall that had been going up since before he was born. Karis wrote down what he could not do as if each failure were a stake driven into a field she was surveying, a small exact mark that said the edge is not here, look further on. Even his nothing, in her hand, deserved to be got exactly right. Nobody had ever told him, in all the years of being written down, that a person could be measured and feel kept company by it.

"Fourteen," she said, when she had finished. "Fourteen boundaries." She did not sound tired, though she had been grey at the fingertips the day before. She sounded like somebody a long way into difficult country with a map that, so far, was right. "Every one of them is a finding. A boundary condition you know is worth more than a hope you don't."

"It's still fourteen times nothing."

"It's fourteen times this isn't it." She laid her hand flat on the closed ledger. "That's not the same as nothing. That's a shape. I can see the outside of it now, the way I could see the outside of you from Ternhall." She looked at him across the table. "Something closes it. Whatever it is, I haven't found it yet."

He did not say anything. He sat with the binder shut in front of him, and under his breastbone, where the bruise from the whole push still ached, he felt a certainty growing that he did not want and could not argue with. The thing he had promised himself on a frozen wall to find out was not going to come to him in a whitewashed room on a schedule. He did not want to stop. Karis had eight more sessions written into the plan in the back of her ledger, and he meant to stand in every one of them and reach every way he knew. Only he had begun to suspect, at Prynn's table with the lamp between them, that the room was missing something, and that whatever it was, nobody could carry it in through the door.

Chapter 29 — What Gets Used

[Patient, lucid narration; make repeated failure feel cumulative rather than repetitive]

He worked it out that night, alone, at the desk by the narrow window, with the lamp turned up past the oil allowance and the binder open at the front, where the four sections began.

He did it as he did everything that mattered, on paper, slowly, and without letting himself skip to the end. He had read the binder backward once already, on the night after Karis said aimable at the stable table. He had found on every page what she had found from outside: every fragment had come after long close watching. That had been true, and he did not doubt it now. But fourteen nulls had just told him, in Karis's careful hand, that it was not the whole truth, because he had watched Karis longer and closer and more deliberately than he had ever watched anyone in his life, and no fragment had come, and no notice.

So he asked the binder a different question. Not what had he been doing when each one came, but what had been happening to him.

Wind-adjacent was first, and Lira's. He made himself go back past the notice to the mornings themselves, not the summary of them but the things themselves. A cold yard in Ardenmere before either of them had money for a hall. Lira across a chalk circle scratched in the dirt with a stick, teaching him to survive the circuit because if he did not learn he would not last a month on it, and both of them knew it. He had not been watching her from a safe distance. He had been losing to her, every morning, badly, with his ribs and his pride and the rent riding on whether he learned fast enough. Every slip she taught him had been taught by her coming at him with her whole weight and his failing to get out of the way.

Pressure-adjacent was Feryn's. He had watched Feryn, a Bronze-tier fighter, for six days before the bout, and he had lost the bout anyway, fairly, in the fourth exchange, with a shoulder against his that had real weight behind it, and a crowd at the rail, and a rating that would go into Vell's ledger whichever way it went. It had not been a lesson. It had been a fight, and he had lost it, and the redirect had come to him in the losing.

Iron-adjacent was Brom's. Weeks of sessions in Brom's sparring circle, and for most of them the read had not come at all. It had come after he asked Brom to stop being careful with him. He had wanted to learn faster, and Brom had obliged, and for a fortnight every wrong read had meant a hit that rang in his bones until the next morning. He had been reading a body that was trying, honestly and on purpose, to hurt him.

Compression-adjacent was Reydan's, and he did not need to make himself remember that one, because he remembered it every time he breathed deep. Six hundred people. An Iron Rank Eight across the chalk. Everything he had built in Ardenmere riding on the third exchange, and the third exchange going wrong, and the notice arriving so late that a moment more would have made it useless to him.

He laid the four of them side by side on the page, and then he laid Karis beside them: fourteen sessions in a whitewashed room, nine paces and five and one, a quarter-hour and three hours, every one at demonstration intensity, with consent given aloud, and a rule at the bottom of the page that ended everything the moment anything happened she had not chosen. Nothing in that room had ever been used against him. Nothing in it had been trying. Nothing in it had cost anything if he failed except a line in a ledger that said null, which Karis was glad to write.

Four moments with something real riding on them, and fourteen with nothing riding on anything, and the four were the ones that had paid.

It held him. Then he wrote it out underneath in full, slowly, in his square hand.

Watching is necessary. It isn't enough. Every fragment came when the person I was watching was using what they had against me, for real, with something on it — my ribs, my rating, the rent, the fight. Nothing has come from watching Karis show me what she has with nothing on it, however long and however close. Whatever is in me doesn't take what it's shown. It takes what's used on me. If that's right, then the stakes aren't the weather round it. They're part of how it works.

Read back, it sounded like something true. It closed on the shape of the last three months like a lid on a box. He distrusted it exactly as much as he liked it. He liked it a great deal, and he had learned long ago that a thing he wanted to be true was a thing he had to check twice. It might be the missing condition. It might be a story he was telling himself because fourteen nulls had made him want one. No amount of thinking at a desk would tell the difference.

He wrote underneath it, smaller.

Don't know if this is true. It can only be tested by something with real stakes in it, and nobody can arrange that honestly. Not Karis. Not me.

Then he sat with the pen in his hand and made himself look at the last thing. He had promised himself on the wall that he would stop not-knowing what he was doing, and this was a thing he was doing.

Some part of him was waiting for the test. He could feel it, now that he had written the sentence down, as he could feel the bruise under his breastbone when he breathed. It was not dread. That was the trouble. Dread he would have understood. It was something nearer to the feeling before a circuit bout he expected to win, a leaning forward, an appetite with its eyes open. Somewhere ahead there would be a floor, and somebody across it using everything they had, and the part of him that was waiting was not afraid of that floor at all. It wanted to know what would happen there.

He did not like it. He made himself write that down too, because the binder was the one place he never lied.

Part of me is waiting for it. Not afraid. Interested. I don't like that part, and I'm not going to pretend it isn't there.

On the Monday of the eleventh week, on the open floor at the sixth bell, Gerda took a hit on purpose.

The third week of the nulls had begun on the Monday, with the fifteenth session before the first bell. Standing at the end of the whitewashed room at seven paces while Karis laid her first point, Cael had gone quiet inside, in a way he had not been in the first two weeks.

Chapter 30 — Real, Unexplained, Keep

[Patient, lucid narration; make repeated failure feel cumulative rather than repetitive]

Lira came to Brom's room for the fast catch on the Wednesday night of the eleventh week. She had read the page about the whole push. She had told him at breakfast, cutting his porridge into squares, that the next time he did something new to his chest she was going to be in the room for it with a cold cloth and a very bad temper.

She sat on Brom's bed with her back against the wall and her boots on Brom's blanket, which Brom permitted from nobody else, and a folded cloth from the kitchen pump in her lap, dripping slightly. She did not speak. She had said she would not, and Lira kept her word about speaking less often than she kept it about anything else, so that when she did keep it, it meant something.

"It's different," Cael said, kneeling on the boards with his left forearm braced across his chest. "Everything so far has been a push. A push arrives slow. It comes into the bone and sits there and I've got time to choose the road while it's sitting. A strike doesn't sit. It arrives and it's gone."

"So you can't wait for it," said Brom.

"So I can't wait for it. I have to choose the road before it lands. Before I know the size, or the line, or anything." He flexed the left hand. The elbow the whole push had found was nearly quiet. "Not much. A quarter. If I can catch a quarter of a strike and send it home, that's a thing I've never done."

"How fast?"

"Fast. Not your fastest. Fast enough that it's a strike and not a lean."

Brom considered him with his chalked hands on his knees. Then he looked across at Lira on the bed, and Lira looked back at him and said nothing, with great force, and Brom looked back at Cael.

"Quarter," he said. "Fast. I'll call it."

He brought up the Iron Skin along his right palm, the faint dull sheen coming over the skin, and drew the hand back a little, and struck.

It was not his fastest. It was a short flat palm strike at the braced forearm, with weight behind it and speed in it, the kind of strike Brom used on the floor when he meant a thing to land. Cael had chosen the road before Brom's hand moved, a quarter's width out and back along the line it would come in, and he held it, and the strike arrived. It was in the bone and gone again before the fragment had finished waking, and the fragment reached for the place where it had been and found the bruise and nothing else.

"Nothing," said Cael.

"Nothing. Again."

Seven times it was nothing. The fragment was too slow for a strike; it woke for force that was already his, and a strike was never his for long enough. On the eighth he did something he had not known he could do. He did not wait for the fragment to wake when the force arrived. He woke it first, before Brom moved, the gathering low in his chest begun and held half-ready like a breath drawn and not let out, with the road laid open in front of it, so that when the strike landed the thing in him was already reaching. It closed on the strike in the instant it was in the bone, a quarter of it, and sent it home.

The quarter went back into Brom's palm with a crack like a dropped plate.

And the bill did not wait for anything.

With a push it had always come a moment afterward, rising through the shoulder and across the breastbone in its band of heat. This came all at once, at the same instant as the catch, as if it had been waiting behind the strike. A white flash went across the inside of his eyes. His knees were not under him; he did not remember them going. He was on his side on Brom's boards with his cheek against the wood, and he could not breathe, and he could not feel his left hand at all, and somewhere a long way off Lira was saying his name in a voice he had not heard her use since a night on the Ardenmere road.

He came back slowly. The cloth was on his breastbone, cold and wet through his shirt. Lira was kneeling over him with one hand flat on top of it, pressing, not hard, and her face was very close and very white. Brom was on his other side holding his left wrist in both hands, chafing it.

"Breathe," said Lira. "Breathe, you idiot. I don't care if it hurts. Breathe."

He breathed. It hurt a great deal. He breathed again.

"How long?" he managed.

"Not long. Long enough." She did not take her hand off the cloth. "Long enough that I've got something to say to you, and I'm going to say it tomorrow."

"Say it now."

"Not while my hands are doing this." She held up the one that was not on the cloth, and it was shaking.

Brom was still chafing the wrist. "Can you feel that?"

Cael tried. The hand was a long way off, numb and heavy, like a hand that had been slept on. Then, slowly, the pins came into it, hot and prickling, from the wrist toward the fingertips.

"Coming back."

"Good." Brom let go of the wrist and sat back on his heels and looked at his own right palm. There was a red mark across it where the quarter had come home, and he looked at it with a kind of grim respect. "That was a quarter of a strike. That was only a quarter."

"Only a quarter," said Cael, from the floor.

Lira took her hand off the cloth at last and sat back against the bed, and put both hands over her face, and stayed like that for a moment. Then she took them away.

"Write it down," she said. "Now, before you sleep. All of it. The part where you were on the floor too, not just the catch. I want it in your hand, so you can't make it smaller tomorrow."

He wrote it lying on Brom's bed with the binder held above his face, because sitting up was not yet a thing he could do.

Compression-adjacent. Brom's room, L. present. First fast catch: a quarter of a quick palm strike, caught and returned, on the eighth try. Done by waking the fragment before the strike, held half-ready with the road laid open. Waiting for the force, the way I do with a push, doesn't work on a strike; it's gone before the fragment wakes. Cost: all of it at once, no delay. A white flash, legs gone, on the floor. Couldn't breathe for long enough that Lira used my name the way she did on the road. Left hand numb, then pins, for most of an hour. Integration: partial. A quarter of a strike, once.

He read it back, and then he added the line Lira had asked for.

It is not cheaper because it's smaller. A quarter fast cost more than the whole slow. Speed is its own price.

Lira read it over his shoulder, upside down, from where she sat on the floor against the bed. She did not say anything. She took the binder out of his hands, closed it, and put it on Brom's shelf in the neat row beside Brom's crest-up tag. Then she put her hand on his forehead for a moment, and took it away.

"Tomorrow," she said. "I'll say it tomorrow."

She said it the next morning on the stair, low and fast and sharp, with one hand flat on the rail.

"I counted. On Brom's floor, with my hand on a wet cloth. I counted six breaths, and you weren't taking any of them." She did not look at him. "I sat there and thought, so this is how I find out. Not in a ring, with a crowd and a reason. On a bedroom floor, because you wanted to know if a thing could be done faster." Her hand tightened on the rail. "I walked over that hill with you and Brom. I'm not doing the rest of it with one of you short because you were curious on a Wednesday. You write choose the size first in that binder every week. Choose the size of what you're willing to lose, too. And tell me before, not after."

"Before," he said. "Not after."

At the end of it she put her forehead against his shoulder for the length of one breath. Then she went down to breakfast ahead of him and stole his bread.
