The Thursday session in section four was a bad one, and Quenna saw it.

He had known she would. His recovery between passes at the working speed had gone from three counts to five. The framework, which had not minded the ribs, minded this. The quarter of a breath of lead that Karis had measured since the first week held, but only just, and twice in the hour he felt it thin. Karis timed it and wrote it down without comment and read it back: Recovery slower by two counts. Lead held, narrowly. Cause not stated by subject. He said nothing to that. The cause was a strike in Brom's room, and it belonged to neither of the two arrangements and to nobody's ledger.

Quenna did not write anything at all for most of the hour. She stood at the chalk with her slate against her hip and watched him. Twice, when he came back to his mark breathing harder than the work had any right to make him, he felt her eyes on him with the weight he had felt on his first afternoon in the intake room, when she had been looking for words for him and not finding them.

At the end she signed the strip and tore it off and held it out, and did not let go of it at once when he took it.

"The fourth sitting is next week," she said. "The calendar has it at the first bell, the eighth day."

"I've seen it."

"Whatever it is you're doing that isn't my session," said Quenna, "is making you tired." She said it flatly. "I'm not asking what it is. I said I'd rather not know, and I meant it. I'm telling you what it looks like from the chalk. Come to the fourth sitting rested."

"I will."

She let go of the strip.

"And Cael." She had turned to go and turned back. "I'll want to see you after it. Both of you." She glanced at Karis, folding her stool, and back. "Not about anything you're doing. About something I'd like to do."

She went out. Karis stood with the stool under her arm and looked at the door after Quenna had gone.

"Something with structure," said Karis quietly.

"You think so?"

"I asked her a question once," said Karis, "and asked her to keep it. I think she's kept it."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The nineteenth session, on the Friday evening, ended early. Karis had fought a standings bout that morning, an Iron Rank Four from the Edge floor who had heard what she had done to Edran and wanted to find out whether it could be done to him, and it could. It had cost her three exchanges and most of her reserves. She ran the session at seven paces anyway, because she had said she would and she did not move a session for her own tiredness. A third of the way through, her off hand went still for longer than a quarter of a second, and her next point came up dim and late and went out on its own, without her count. She let the rest go and sat down on the scrubbed floor.

"I'm calling it," she said. "Not because anything happened to me. Because I can't lay a clean point, and a session with dirty points is a session with a second variable in it." She was already writing. "Null, as far as it went."

They did not leave. They sat on the floor of the quiet room with their backs against opposite walls and the two notebooks open on their knees, her ledger of the nulls and his own pages of session notes, all of her Path and none of his. She would read a line from the ledger and he would find the same session in his pages, to see whether what she had seen from outside matched what he had felt from in. It had become a ritual since the third week without either of them deciding it would: two notebooks open and two pens moving, in a whitewashed room with the high window going grey.

She got through the fourteenth session and the fifteenth, shut the ledger, capped her pen, and raised her eyes to him across the room.

"May I ask you something about the shape of the whole?"

He knew by how she asked it that she had been holding it for some days.

"You can ask."

"I won't ask what you have. That's the first clause, and it stays." She set the closed ledger flat on her knees and laid both hands on it. "You told me before the first session that there are more than the two I've seen. I've never asked how many, and I won't. I want to ask one thing about all of them together, from outside." She paused. "Is there anything that has happened to you only once? Something you've never been able to make happen again, that doesn't fit with the rest? I'd like to know whether the shape I've been drawing from outside is the whole shape, or whether there's a piece of it I've never been near."

He could have answered narrowly. It was a question that stood with its toes on the very line of the terms. She was not asking for the binder or for a source or a mechanism, only whether the outline she had been allowed to see was the whole outline. He could have said no and been truthful about every fragment in the front of the binder. He would have said nothing at all about the page behind them, the one set apart, the one he turned past every time without adding anything.

He did not. He had decided in an archive on the first day that she was a person who could hold an honest I don't know, and nineteen sessions of her writing null in the same careful hand had done nothing but prove it.

"Yes," he said. "Once."

Karis went very still, the way she went still before an ignition, all of her listening at once.

"Months ago. Before Greyvane, before the road. A session with Brom, in his sparring circle in Ardenmere. The read was open; we were working on it the way we always worked on it. Nothing about that afternoon was different from a hundred others." He could still see the circle, the scuffed chalk, Brom's forearm under his hand. He did not reach for anything else. "And for less than a second, through the read, there was something like water. Water moving, somewhere there wasn't any water. Then it was gone, before I could even turn toward it. Nothing came after it. No notice. I've never had it again."

"Tide," said Karis.

"If it was anything. That's the only word I've got that's anywhere near it."

"Did you try to make it happen again?"

"A dozen times. More. The same circle, the same time of day, the same work, as near as my notes could make it. Nothing."

"Give me the conditions. Every one you can remember."

He told her. It did not take long, which was the worst of it. There had never been much to tell, and he had told it to himself so often that the telling had worn smooth. She listened without moving. When he had finished she took him through it again, from the other end, starting from the moment itself and working backward to the morning, and then a third time from the morning forward. She asked about the weather, and what he had eaten, and whether Brom had been tired, and what Brom had been drilling that week, and whether anyone else had been in the circle or near it or had just left it, and whether anything at all, anything, had been different. He answered all of it. Every answer built the same picture his notes had always built, a working afternoon like a hundred others with one second in the middle of it that did not belong.

Karis was quiet a long time.

"There's no Tide practitioner in that," she said at last. "Nobody near you with a Tide Path. Nobody you'd watched. Nothing for you to have watched." She frowned at her own hands on the ledger, and it was not a frown at him. It was the frown of somebody whose model has just been handed a stone it has no pocket for. "Everything I've drawn from outside says you watch first, and then something follows. This has no watching in it at all. It breaks the one thing I was surest of." She looked up. "It shouldn't exist."

"It exists."

"I know it exists. That's the trouble with it." She said it without heat. "Either the shape I've drawn isn't the whole shape, or there's a second thing in you working beside the first that I've never been near, or it happened once and a thing that's happened once can't carry a theory on its back. I can't tell which from here. I don't think anybody could."

He said nothing. He thought, privately, of the page in the binder with his own hypothesis on it, it takes what's used on me, and of the afternoon in Brom's circle where nobody had been using anything on anybody. It broke his rule too, and he did not say so. It was not for saying yet, and it changed nothing about the second in Brom's circle, which was what it had always been.

"So what do we do with it?" he said.

"We keep it."

She opened the ledger again, but she did not turn to the nulls. She turned past them, past the plan she had drawn for the last sessions, to a page near the very back that he had never seen. There was a single short line on it in her small upright hand. She must have written it in the few minutes he had been talking. He could read it from across the room only because she turned the ledger toward him. Session nine, Ardenmere, with B. One reading, Tide-like, under a second. Never repeated. Beside it she made a small mark with her pen. It was not a letter or a number, nor any symbol he knew, only a short precise shape, made slowly and deliberately, as a person signs a thing they mean to stand behind.

"That mark goes on exactly one thing in this whole notebook," she said. "Real, unexplained, keep. It isn't a failure, and it isn't a hypothesis waiting to be proved. It's something true that I don't understand, and I've written it down as exactly that. I haven't bent it to fit an explanation, the kind that comforts you and teaches you nothing." She looked at the mark. "Most people can't bear to leave a thing like that alone. They explain it, because an explanation is more comfortable to carry than a question. Then they've got an explanation, and it's wrong, and they build on it."

Across the scrubbed floor his eyes stayed on the mark.

Session nine had ridden with him since the road, small and shapeless, the kind of load you cannot show anyone because there is nothing to hold up. He had never once been able to set it down in front of anyone who would neither explain it away nor shrug at it. Lira had believed him and been frightened; Brom had believed him and been puzzled. Neither of them had known where to put it. Karis had just set it down in front of him in her ledger, under the one mark that ledger kept for nothing else, and left it there as it was. It was not answered. Nothing about it had been answered. But it had been witnessed, properly, by somebody who knew what witnessing was, and he had not known until this moment how much of the weight of it had been the being alone with it.

"How many other entries have that mark?" he asked.

"None," said Karis. "Until tonight." She closed the ledger. "I can't tell yet whether that's a compliment to you or a warning. I'll let you know when I've worked it out."

He wrote it that night in the binder, on the page set apart from the rest, behind the four sections. For the first time since the road he added something to that page, and he was careful that it was only one thing, and true.

Told Karis, in the third week of the nulls, because she asked properly whether the shape she could see was the whole shape. She took me through it three ways. No Tide anywhere near. Nobody watched. Nothing on it. It shouldn't exist. It exists. Her mark on it is real, unexplained, keep. Nothing else in her notebook carries that.

He looked at the line above it, the one he had written on the road and never once touched since, and left it as it was.

Her mark is worth more to me than any answer would be. Any answer this soon would only be a guess in a good coat. The mark says plainly that nobody knows.

He told Brom at breakfast, because Brom had been in the circle that afternoon and had a right to know the stone had been shown to somebody.

Brom listened, chewing slowly, and when Cael had finished he set his spoon down.

"I remember the afternoon," he said. "I've thought about it more than you'd guess. You went white for a moment and then you said did you feel that, and I hadn't felt anything." He looked at his porridge. "I could tell her what day it was and what we'd eaten and which of my hands was sore that week. I've gone over it that often, every time I saw you turn past that page." He picked up his spoon again. "I'm glad she's got a mark for it. I never had anywhere to put it either."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On the evening before Gerda's supplementary bout, Cael found Lira and Gerda on the open floor after the last bell. Everybody else had long gone. One lamp was lit at the far end, and the high windows were black.

They were not sparring, and Hobb had gone. They were sitting side by side on the edge of the chalk with their backs against the rail, a water flask between them, not talking. Gerda had her slip for the morning in her lap, already filled out, the hour already written on it in her careful square figures, and every so often she looked down at it.

Cael stopped at the rail above them. Lira tipped her head back against the wood and looked up at him upside down.

"She won't sleep," said Lira. "So we're not sleeping here, instead of not sleeping in our rooms. It's better. There's a floor."

"I'll sleep," said Gerda. "Later."

"She says that."

Gerda looked down at the slip again. Then she did a thing Cael had never once seen her do, in two months of watching her at desks and rails and the floor. She folded the slip in half, so that the hour was on the inside where she could not see it, and put it in her coat.

"Tomorrow," she said, "I'm going to come out of the haze. I'm going to take whatever they put on me, on purpose, where the chairs can see it. And then I'm going to put my whole weight into somebody." She said it in her procedure voice, every word set down separately, as if she were reading a clause aloud to Prynn. "Whatever the panel writes after that, it'll be about what happened. Not about what I was afraid of."

Lira did not say anything. She put her hand on the flask between them and pushed it a little toward Gerda.

"Drink," she said. "And then we're going to bed. Both of us. I'm not getting you up in the morning if you've sat on this floor all night."

Gerda drank.

Cael went up to the residence wing and left them there. Halfway up the stair it came to him that the part of him he had written down a week ago had been listening too. Part of me is waiting for it. None of the nulls since had moved it. It had heard Gerda say she would come out of the haze and take what was put on her where the chairs could see, and it had leaned toward the words, because somewhere ahead there was still a floor that was his. He did not like it any better than he had at the desk. He went on up. At the turn of the stair he looked back through the doorway once and saw them still sitting side by side in the one circle of lamplight at the far end of the empty hall, two girls with dots on their tags and their backs to a rail. Neither of them was looking at the clock.

Chapter 31 — Twenty-Two

[Patient, lucid narration; make repeated failure feel cumulative rather than repetitive]

There were eleven people at the rail for Gerda's supplementary bout, six more than had come to her review, and Cael counted them as he came through the gate, because he could not help it, and because he thought that Gerda, who counted hours, would want somebody to have counted this.

Lira was at the front, with her shoulder unstrapped at last and a purple-yellow bruise showing at the edge of her collar. Brom was beside her, and Karis, with her hands in her pockets and no notebook. Hobb was at the far corner, as always, with his hands in his pockets too. The other seven Cael had not expected. Two of them were Current Path second-years from the movement floor. One was the girl whose footwork never stopped, who had lost to Gerda at the review and seemed to have come to see what she had lost to. Three were from the heat-Paths floor, Ash and Ember first-years standing together. They had the shy bright look of children who have heard that somebody from their own floor is going to do something, and do not want to miss it. One was the second-year tout, who had no wager on it, because nobody was taking wagers on a re-certification candidate's supplementary bout at first bell, and who had come, he told Cael, out of professional interest.

The last was Edran. He stood by the standings board with his arms folded, as he had stood for Lira's review. He did not look at the board.

The panel sat at the north end: Quenna in the middle with the review ledger open and Gerda's request beside it, Wray on her left in the brown coat, the heat-Paths instructor with scorched cuffs on her right. The same panel, as the provision required.

Gerda came through the gate as the first bell finished. She did not stop to look at the clock above the main hall door. Cael watched her walk past it with her chin level and her stride unbroken and her eyes on the ring, and he saw her not look, and he knew that it had cost her something and that she had decided to pay it.

"For the record," said Quenna. "Supplementary recorded bout, elected by the candidate under the reconsideration clause of the re-certification provision. The candidate: Gerda, Ash Path. Recorded tier, Copper. The bout will be considered together with the candidate's formal review, and advancement assessed against the originating record. The candidate takes the south mark."

The opponent was the Blade fourth-year with the very fast hands. Cael did not know whether the panel had chosen him on purpose, and suspected Wray had, and suspected that Gerda had been told and had said nothing but Good. He took the north mark and stood light on his feet with his fast hands loose and his face listening to whatever it always listened to.

Wray lowered her finger.

Gerda laid her haze. It went out from her across the swept earth, low and grey, two paces in every direction, as it always had. The Blade fourth-year stopped at its edge and waited, as he had waited before, light and patient, outside the slowness, with nothing to make him go into it.

Gerda came out.

She came out at once, before he had settled, two long strides out of her own grey onto clean ground. She went straight at him with nothing slowing anybody down at all, and his fast hand flicked out and caught her on the shoulder, exactly where it had caught her at the review, and she took it. Cael saw her take it. He saw her see the hand coming, and see the space where she could have turned from it, and not turn. She let it land on the point of her shoulder, where everyone at the rail and all three chairs could see it land.

"Touch," said Wray. "Opponent."

Gerda went back to the south mark with her shoulder held a little away from her side and her face white and absolutely calm. She did not look at the rail. She did not look at the clock. She looked at the Blade fourth-year, and Cael, who had watched her for two months, saw something in her face he had never seen there before. It was the look Lira wore on a circuit floor after a hit she had chosen. That one cost me. Now you owe me.

"She took it," said the tout behind Cael, in a reverent whisper.

"She bought it," said Lira, without turning round.

The second exchange she won with Hobb's lesson.

She laid the haze again and came out of it again. This time when the fast hand came she took it on the forearm and turned from it, and the turn put her in under his arm, close, closer than a Blade fighter ever let anybody get. She put her shoulder into his side with the whole of her weight and the whole of her height, the way she had put it into Hobb on the fourth evening. A Blade fourth-year was not a Stone fourth-year. He went three steps sideways and nearly off his feet, and her two fingers were on his breastbone before he had them back under him.

"Touch. Candidate."

At the far corner of the rail Hobb took his hands out of his pockets.

The third exchange went by slower. He had learned; she had shown him twice now that she would come out, and he met her at the edge of the haze instead of waiting outside it. For a long moment the two of them circled on the border of the grey, his fast hands against her height, neither committing. Cael held his breath. He could see the old weight on Gerda's back foot, the pull toward the haze, the relief that waited for her two paces behind her. He saw her feel it, and he saw her leave it there. She stepped forward onto clean ground, took his next strike on the outside of the forearm without slipping it, and turned under it. Her fingers were on his breastbone. Wray called it, and called the bout.

Two touches to one.

The yard did not cheer, because it never did. But the three heat-Paths first-years at the rail made a sound of pure delight they could not keep in. The Current Path girl who had lost to Gerda at the review clapped twice before she remembered where she was and stopped. Lira, at the front of the rail, put both hands flat on the cold wood and leaned on them and let her head drop between her shoulders, and Cael heard her breathe out for what he thought must have been the first time since the first bell.

The panel did not go to the far wall. They talked at the table, low, for no longer than it took the Blade fourth-year to walk across the ring and shake Gerda's hand, which he did, formally and in silence, as he did everything. Then Quenna wrote, and lifted her pen.

"Supplementary recorded bout. Won by the candidate, two touches to one. The panel considers it together with the formal review." She read off the ledger in the slow flat cadence of the record. "The candidate came out of her own declaration under live opposition and committed fully, at cost, twice. The recommendation of reconsideration is withdrawn. Continued track."

She looked up from the ledger at Gerda, across the frosted earth.

"Initials," she said. "And the candidate's signature."

Gerda walked to the table and signed, carefully, every letter separate. Then she stood and read the line Quenna had written, as Lira had stood and read hers, and Cael saw her lips move once.

She came off the ring toward the rail. She stopped in front of Lira, who had straightened up and folded her arms and arranged her face into something she clearly hoped looked unconcerned, and did not.

"Answered," said Gerda.

"Correctly?" said Lira.

Gerda considered the word, as she considered every word.

"Correctly," she said. "And the right way round, this time."

Then she did look at the clock above the main hall door. Her eyes stayed on it. And she laughed, a short, surprised, rusty sound, as if it had not been used in a long time and had had to be found at the bottom of a box. Lira, who had kept her face still through two bouts of her own and one of Gerda's, did not manage it through that, and put her good arm round Gerda's shoulders, bruise and all, and held on.

Hobb passed them on his way to the gate. He did not stop. He slowed, as he had slowed at the rail after the exhibition, and looked at Gerda once.

"Didn't go back," he said, in his deep slow voice, and went on out of the yard.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The twenty-second session was that evening, and all four of them came, because it was the last one written into the plan in the back of Karis's ledger and none of them meant to hear about it afterward. Lira had said at the midday meal that she was not going to let a thing end without being in the room for it, especially a thing that had produced nothing.

Lira sat on the floor by the door with her knees up and Gerda's laugh still visible somewhere at the corners of her mouth. Brom sat beside her with a heel of bread he did not take out of his coat. Karis stood at the far end of the whitewashed room with the ledger closed on the boards at her feet. Cael stood three paces from her, as close as the room had ever brought them except for the one morning at a single pace.

"I consent," said Karis, "to this session," and wrote the hour.

She had told him at breakfast what the last session would be. It would not be a variable; it would be all of them, everything the twenty-one before it had tried, put into one hour at the nearest distance and the longest duration she could sustain without her points going dirty, and she would run it fresh. He would reach every way he had ever reached, in turn and then all at once, with the read open on his skin and every channel of attention he owned turned toward her like lamps.

"If it doesn't close in that," she had said, "it doesn't close in this room. And then we'll know that, which is the finding."

So she began, and he reached.

He knew her now. That was what he understood, standing three paces from her in the last hour of the series while the first point bloomed at the height of her shoulder and held. He knew her better than he had known anybody he had ever watched, better than he had known Reydan at the top of the bout and better, in this one narrow way, than he knew Lira. He knew where she would lay the next point before she laid it. Twice in the hour, with the read open, he felt the air at that place grow faintly heavier before the light came, as it had on the long afternoon. He could have shut his eyes and rebuilt any one of twenty-two sessions from the sounds alone, the small hiss of a point, the kettle-song of a channel, the click of her pen. He had learned her past memory, down into the place below memory where Lira's footwork lived in his feet.

And every way he reached, and all of them at once, nothing came.

There was no settling, and no space being filled. Nothing arrived anywhere in him, and no line appeared in anybody's handwriting. There was a boy standing three paces from a girl in a whitewashed room, wanting, and the girl's small exact fires blooming and going out, and the light in the high window going from grey to dark. Lira and Brom by the door did not move once in the whole hour.

At the end Karis let her last point go and watched its shimmer hang and fade, and then she bent and picked up the ledger.

"Null," said Cael.

"Null." She wrote it, in the same careful hand, at the same size, as she had written the first. Session twenty-two. All conditions of sessions one to twenty-one, combined. Result: null. Then she did not close the ledger. She looked at the page, and drew a line across it under the last session, straight from one side to the other, as a person rules off a column of figures before writing the total.

Under the line she wrote one more sentence. She did not read it aloud. She turned the ledger round and held it out across the three paces so that he could read it under the fourth clause.

Twenty-two controlled sessions. Twenty-two nulls. We are missing a condition.

"I don't know what it is," said Karis. Her voice was perfectly level. "The pattern's real. I'd stake both notebooks on it. You watch, and then something comes. But watching isn't closing it, not at demonstration intensity, not at any distance or for any length of time I can sustain, not however hard you reach. Whatever closes it is something else, and it isn't here with us." She lowered the ledger. "I can't think of anything I could bring into this room that would be it, without breaking the line at the bottom of our page."

Cael said nothing. He stood with his hands at his sides and the binder under his arm, and he felt Lira's eyes on him from the door, steady, and did not look round. It was the hardest thing he had done in twenty-two sessions, harder than any of the reaching.

Karis looked at him. Perhaps she knew there was something behind his silence. She had a page, after all, called Not asked. She did not ask.

"So that's the end of the plan," she said. "But I want to say one more thing, with all three of you here, so that it's witnessed."

Brom took his hand out of his coat.

Quenna has put a match on the calendar for the fifth sitting, week sixteen, against Karis. Both versions true. Karis wrote her own consent and underlined one line of it. Quenna read the word source and didn't ask. I have the fair copy in the back pocket.

Edran says nobody has crossed her grid at Ternhall in two years.

Lira's rule: go in to fight her. Not to find out. The first day after, whatever happens, Karis gets the whole page.

He looked at that, and then wrote one more line under it, because the binder was the one place he never lied.

I don't know if I can walk into a ring with that sentence in me and not be waiting for it. I'm going to have to learn how in four weeks.

Chapter 33 — Sixteen Promises

[Taut, spatially clear narration; build the directed match without sacrificing comprehension]

Karis trained at the fifth bell in section two, on the heat-Paths floor, and on the first afternoon of the study she stopped at the floor desk before her block and said something to the lean old instructor with scorched cuffs that made him look across the hall at the rail.

Cael was at the rail with the binder open on his arm. The instructor looked at him as a farmer looks at a stray dog that has wandered into his yard and sat down as if it lived there. Then he said something short back to Karis, who nodded, and picked up his slate and went to his chalk.

"What did he say?" Cael asked her afterward.

"I told him the observer would be watching my blocks until the fifth sitting, with my leave. He said, 'Then he'll see how it's done properly.'" She did not smile. "He meant it as a compliment to Ternhall. I've decided to take it as one to me."

He watched four blocks that first week, and by the end of the second he understood why he had learned more about Ember in an afternoon than a whole season on the circuit had ever taught him about one Path.

On the circuit, people learned to fight from whoever was nearest. A Storm fighter in Ardenmere had been taught by a cousin who had been taught by a man in a tavern. Each of them had added something of his own and left something out, so that by the time the Path reached the ring it came wrapped in a whole family's habits. Cael had spent his whole time on the circuit reading those habits: a dropped elbow here, a breath held too long there, a shoulder that always came up before the hard ones because somebody's uncle had taught it to come up. They were tells, and they were gifts, and every one of them was an accident.

Karis had no accidents.

That was the first thing he wrote down, and it took him most of a page to say it properly. Ternhall did not train its students out of their tells; it put the tells in, on purpose, and called them correct form. The off hand went still before an ignition because a still off hand steadied the one doing the work, and Ternhall had decided it should and drilled it into a thousand students until it happened by itself. The half-breath before a sustain was there because a sustain held cleaner on a settled chest, and every commitment showed exactly as much as correct form required it to show, no more and no less. He had thought, on the first afternoon, that all this would make her easy to read.

It made her the hardest person he had ever read.

There's nothing extra, he wrote that night. Every tell is in the right place and is the right size. On the circuit the tell was the mistake. Here the tell is the form, and the form has no mistakes in it. I know when her points are coming to a quarter of a second. Knowing doesn't help. She's built so that knowing doesn't help.

He read it back and added a line under it.

A good school is a kind of honesty. It shows you everything and hides it all by being exact.

Edran was at the same rail on the third afternoon, at the far end, with his arms folded. He had been there every afternoon since the notice went up, coming in at the fifth bell to take the same place and stand without moving through the whole of Karis's block, and going out again at the sixth without speaking to anybody. That day, when the block was over and the section was emptying, he did not go out. He came down the rail instead, stopped a pace from Cael, and looked at the binder open on Cael's arm.

"You watch her early," said Edran.

"Early?"

"The start of her block. The first points." Edran nodded at the empty section, where a faint warmth still hung over the boards. "I watch her late. The end of the block, when she's tired. I've been trying to see whether it changes." He was quiet a moment. "It doesn't, much. She's the same at the end as at the start. I've never seen anybody like that."

"It changes a little. The release gets longer."

Edran turned his head and looked at him properly.

"How much longer?"

"A few hundredths of a breath, after the first half-hour. More after an hour." Cael closed the binder on his finger. "She can't feel it. She didn't know until I told her."

"You told her."

"She'd have wanted to know."

Edran looked at him a while with his flat honest face, and Cael could not tell whether he thought that admirable or mad, or both.

"When she beat me," Edran said at last, "I didn't see the first six points until the end of the second exchange. Six coins on the floor round my feet, and I'd walked over all of them." He unfolded his arms and looked at his own right forearm. "I've thought about that every day since. I was watching her. I thought I was. I was watching her hands."

"Everybody watches her hands."

"You don't." Edran held out the right forearm, palm down, the free arm, the one he had been teaching all term to build a third structure while the second still stood. "Since you watch everyone. Is it thicker?"

Cael had watched him in the corner by the high windows every morning he could, as he had promised to, and did not need to look now. He looked anyway, because Edran had asked him to.

"Thicker," he said. "Not thick. It came up whole three times in four this morning. A week ago it was two."

"Three in four." Edran turned the arm over and back. "Wray said a term."

"It's been five weeks."

"Five weeks. Three in four." Edran let the arm fall. "I'll take it." He looked back at the empty section. "The match won't move the board. I read the notice. It's a sitting, not a standings bout."

"No. It won't move anything."

"Good," said Edran, with more feeling than Cael had ever heard from him. "I'd like the board to stay about the board. Whatever you two are doing out there, I'd like it not to be about where anybody's name is written." He nodded once, to Cael or to the section, and went out through the north door without looking back.

The second thing Cael learned that week was how she talked.

Circuit Ember fighters, the few he had seen, talked about heat: how much, how hot, how wide a sheet they could throw across a ring. Karis never once said heat in a block. She said lay and hold and join and let go, answering every count her instructor called with one of those four words and an action to match, and after a week Cael understood that they were the whole of her vocabulary, and that the vocabulary was the Path.

Hers ran on control, not output, and he underlined that when he wrote it down, which he almost never did. If a small release would do a job, she never spent a large one on it. She set a point, a dim warm coin of light the size of a thumbnail, exactly where she meant it, and it stayed there exactly as long as she meant it to. When she joined two of them the line of heat between them along the boards was thin and faint and singing, never a wall, never a sheet. Everything she did was small, and nothing she did was weak.

"Why small?" he asked her at the rail at the end of the fourth block, when she came to drink.

She considered the question as if it deserved more than the answer she already had, which was how she considered all his questions.

"Because a big fire tells everyone where it is," she said. "A small one only tells the person it's for." She drank. "And because I can hold sixteen small ones longer than I could hold two big ones. That isn't a philosophy. It's arithmetic."

"Sixteen."

"Sixteen is as many as I've ever held at once." She looked at him over the flask. "You've seen nine. Against Edran. I'll show you sixteen before the sitting. That was the agreement."

The heat-Paths instructor came to the rail on the fifth afternoon, while Karis was drinking at the far end of the section, and stood beside Cael without looking at him. He was a lean old man with a long, weathered face, his cuffs scorched brown in a ring round each wrist from a lifetime of standing too near other people's fire. He had sat the exhibition and Gerda's review, and he would sit the fifth sitting by rota, and Cael had wondered more than once whether the rota knew what it was doing.

"You're the observer," said the instructor.

"Yes."

"I've read your record. All four sittings. It's very short." He watched Karis cap her flask. "You've been at my rail every block for a week. I don't usually allow it. She asked."

"I know. Thank you."

"Don't thank me. Thank Ternhall. I wanted to see how long a Ternhall girl would let somebody watch her before she found it uncomfortable." He was quiet a moment. "She hasn't. I find that interesting."

Cael waited. He had learned with Wray that people who taught Paths for a living often said the important thing second.

"You'll have noticed she talks in four words," said the instructor. "Lay, hold, join, let go."

"Yes."

"That's Ternhall. Every Ember school in the country teaches the same declarations; the Arbiter gives what it gives. What a school teaches is the order you use them in." He nodded at the section. "Ternhall teaches orders the way a grammar teaches sentences. Points first, always. Joins last, always. Never join what you can still move. A Ternhall Ember child can lay you a dozen different drawings by the time she's fifteen, all from the same two declarations, like a clever child saying a dozen different things with the same forty words." He sniffed. "Ternhall calls it a lattice. Most schools haven't got a word for it at all, because most schools can't do it. It isn't a declaration. It's a habit of putting them in the right order."

"Can it be broken?"

The instructor looked at him for the first time.

"Anything can be broken," he said. "I've never seen a Ternhall one broken from inside. Only from outside, by somebody stronger crossing it, and nobody here is strong enough to cross hers twice." He looked back at Karis, who was coming back to her chalk. "If you want my advice, and I don't give it to observers, you'll stop her before she's composed anything. After that, it's grammar, and she's better at grammar than you are."

He went back to his slate. Cael wrote Never join what you can still move in the binder and Stop her before she composes under it, and looked at the second line without knowing yet how a person would do it.

On the sixth block she showed him a thing that went into the binder on a page of its own. She laid a point at the centre of her section on her instructor's count, held it, and let it go. Its third of a breath of shimmer hung in the air after it, the release Cael had timed in every session since the quiet room, and on the next count, while the shimmer was still dying, she tried to lay another in the same place. Her off hand went still and her breath went in, and the air in that one small spot did nothing at all. She waited until the shimmer had gone, laid it again, and it bloomed at once.

"You did that on purpose," Cael said, when she came to the rail.

"I did it for you." She wiped her hands on a cloth. "A point won't take where there's still heat standing. It needs cold air to stand in. Even my own heat. My last point has to finish dying before I can lay another in its place, and you've seen how long mine take to finish dying when I'm tired." She shrugged. "Nothing can set fire where a fire already is. It's the first rule they teach an Ember child, and most of us forget it's a rule because we never think about it after we're eleven."

"Why show me?"

"Because it's true about me, and you didn't know it." She folded the cloth. "Symmetry. If you're going to study me, you should study the real thing, the edges as well."

He wrote it in the binder that evening as plainly as she had said it, under the heading he had begun to keep for her: A point won't take where heat already stands. She has to wait out her own lag to lay twice in one place. Then he sat and looked at it without knowing why, as he had once looked at the line about Brom's wait before anybody knew it was a wall.

On the last afternoon of the second week she built the whole thing.

She had asked Wray for a partner, for somebody, she told Cael, who would not be told how hard to hit and would not be told to lose, who knew he was outmatched and meant to be expensive about it. Wray had looked at her and then sent Hobb.

The heat-Paths floor had never had so many people at its rail. Word had got round, as word always got round at Greyvane, that the Ternhall girl was going to fight a full bout in the open with the observer watching. Edran was there with his arms folded at the end of the rail, and Lira and Brom and Gerda, and the second-year tout with a stub of pencil behind his ear, and Oona standing on the bottom rung to see over a third-year's shoulder.

Hobb stood at the north mark of section two with his hands loose and his feet a shoulder-width apart, and he did not look like furniture today. What was different, Cael could not have said. Perhaps it was the set of his jaw, or perhaps only that nobody had bent to his ear before the bout to tell him what to do.

The heat-Paths instructor called it, four exchanges, no touches counted, the bout to end on a yield or on his word.

Hobb came out hard.

It was a good opening and Cael admired it. A Stone fighter could not be moved and could not be hurried, and Hobb knew exactly what Karis's points preferred, which was room, so he took the room away. He pressed her early, with short honest steps and his heavy forearms up, refusing her the distance her point-work liked; he did not chase her, he walked her down, as a wall walks somebody down by standing where they wanted to stand.

Karis gave ground.

To the untrained half of the rail it looked even, and then it looked as if Hobb was winning. He came forward and she went back, a step at a time, and twice he got close enough to put a forearm into her guard and rock her. Cael heard the tout behind him say, "Oh, now, that's interesting," in the voice of a man reconsidering his book.

Cael was not watching the fight. He was watching the floor behind her.

On every step she gave, she left a point. He saw the first one go down on her second step, a dim coin of light on the boards where her heel had just been, her off hand going still a quarter of a breath before it as it always did, and the coin stayed there glowing faintly, like a coal through paper. Then another, and another a little to the left. None of them flared or did anything at all. They sat on the boards behind her as she retreated, patient and small, each one beneath anyone's notice, and Hobb walked her back across them without once looking down.

Four in the first exchange. Five in the second. Cael counted aloud under his breath, and Lira, beside him, stopped watching Hobb.

In the third exchange Hobb looked down.

Cael watched him see them: nine coins of light on the floor round him in a loose curve, and the Stone fourth-year standing among them with his broad calm face, understanding all at once that he had been walking into something for two exchanges. He did not panic; Hobb did not have panic in him. He stopped pressing and set his feet, and Karis, a pace beyond him, joined two of her points.

A single line of heat ran along the boards between them, thin and faintly singing. It lay across Hobb's path to her like a rope laid on a floor.

Hobb looked at it. Then he did the thing nobody had told him to do, and stepped across it.

The channel answered. Cael had not known it would, and he would not forget what it looked like. The moment Hobb's shin broke the line, the heat in it did not simply burn. It came up out of the floor at him in a single hard push, like the breath out of a stove when the door is opened, and the push took Hobb in the shins and knees and threw him back a full step, Stone or no Stone. He came down on his heels, braced, smoking faintly at the boots. The channel had gone out. It had spent itself on him, all at once, as a trap spends itself on the foot that springs it.

Hobb stood where the push had put him and looked down at his own shins, and then at the dark line on the boards where the channel had been.

"Huh," said Hobb.

The rail made a sound. Karis did not. She laid two more points while Hobb was looking at his boots, and one more as he looked up, and the exchange ended with twelve on the floor.

The fourth exchange lasted perhaps three breaths.

The instructor dropped his hand, and Hobb set himself, and Karis, standing quite still with her off hand motionless at her side, laid four more points in the space of a breath. Then she joined everything she had, so that the channels lit across section two together, with a sound like somebody drawing breath, faint lines of heat running from point to point to point along the boards in every direction a body might want to go, too many and too fast for Cael to count before he saw what they had made. He counted sixteen points. The section had been an open floor, and now it was a drawing of a floor, and between all the lines there were exactly two places a person could stand without crossing one. She was already walking toward the nearer.

The other was three paces from Hobb, across two channels.

Hobb's eyes went down to the floor and stayed there. Cael watched him look at the two lines he would have to cross and remember the stove door, and weigh his boots, and his shins, and how far a body travels when it is thrown back twice.

He put his hands down.

"Yield," said Hobb.

That night Cael drew it.

It took him an hour and most of a lamp's oil. He sat on the floor of his room with the binder open on the boards and Brom on his bed reading over his shoulder, because Brom had seen the bout from the rail and held views on heat that no notebook was going to give him. Cael drew section two from above, as a bird would see it, putting in every point where it had gone down and numbering them in the order she had laid them, and he drew the channels last, in a different ink, so that he could see what they had been for.

When he had finished he sat back and looked at it.

"She never fought him," he said.

"No," said Brom.

"Not once. Four exchanges, and she never tried to hit him. She spent three of them walking backward and dropping coins, and he thought he was winning, and he was standing in her sentence the whole time." Cael touched the page. "The bout was four exchanges. The fight was one. It was the first, when she chose where his feet would be three exchanges later, and he walked there for her."

He wrote it at the bottom of the diagram, because it needed writing.

She doesn't beat people. What she wins is an argument, and she builds it out of the floor. Most of them never notice it's about the floor until it's over.

Brom took the binder off his knees and looked at the drawing without a word, and then put one blunt finger on a channel line.

"I'll tell you what it's like to stand near," he said. "I was on the rail at the north end, two paces from the chalk, with the read open. I couldn't help it." He frowned at the page. "It's like standing near somebody who's already made up their mind. You can feel the air's decided before she has. It leans."

"That's what I felt in the quiet room. At three paces. Before her points."

"I know. I've read your page." Brom tapped the channel. "So listen to me. The joins are where you'll be tempted to get clever. Don't. She's proudest of the joins, so the joins are where she's drilled the most answers. Anybody who's ever beaten a—"

"A lattice. The instructor says that's Ternhall's word."

"Edran uses it too. I asked her, after, whether it was a declaration, and it isn't." Brom shrugged. "It's her points and her channel, the two things on her card, laid in an order. Like a sentence is just words in an order." He went back to the drawing. "Anybody who's beaten one has beaten it before it was one. While she's still laying. While it's just points."

"Points," said Cael.

"Sixteen small promises she hasn't kept yet." Brom handed the binder back. "That's all a lattice is while she's building it. Promises. And I've never met anybody who reads a promise before it's kept the way you do." He lay back on Cael's bed with his hands behind his head. "You won't out-draw her. Nobody's out-drawn her in two years, according to Edran. You'll have to out-early her."

At the head of a clean page, in the square hand, Cael wrote out-early her, and under it, smaller, the entry for the night, which was shorter than most.

Sixteen promises she hasn't kept yet. That's Brom's. Once it's lit there's no answering it, so whatever answer there is has to come while she's still laying. All four exchanges are really the first one, drawn out long. The early part costs her nothing and makes no noise and looks like retreat, and it's the only part that matters. Watch her when she's quiet. By the time it's loud she's only collecting.

He found Hobb the next morning on the defensive floor before the second bell, standing at the edge of the chalk with his hands in his pockets, waiting for Wray. Hobb's shins were wrapped under his training trousers, a lump of linen showing above the boot, though he did not seem to be favouring them, and he turned his head when Cael came along the rail and looked at him with the same patient, unhurried attention he gave everything.

"Can I ask you about yesterday?"

Hobb thought about it.

"You can ask."

"The channel. In the third. Nobody told you to cross it."

"No."

"Why did you?"

Hobb was quiet for long enough that Cael began to think he had asked the wrong thing. Then he looked down at his own boots.

"Wanted to know," he said. "Four years, people tell me where to stand. Stand there, hit this hard, don't win." He considered the boots. "Nobody told me yesterday. So I wanted to know what it did."

"What did it do?"

"Shoved." Hobb took one hand out of his pocket and made a flat short push in the air, low, at shin height. "First thing. Hard. Like a door. The shove's what stops you. Stone or not." He put the hand back. "Then hot. The heat's what you remember after. But the shove's what puts you back where you started."

Cael stood very still at the rail.

"The shove first," he said. "And then the heat."

"Both. Same moment, near enough. But the shove's what stops you." Hobb looked at him with something faintly curious in his broad face. "You're going to cross one."

"I don't know."

"You're going to think about it." Hobb nodded at the far door, where Wray had just come in with her slate. "Don't, if you can help it. My shins say so." He took his hands out of his pockets and went to meet her, and halfway across the chalk he stopped and turned back. "She lays early," he said. "Before you think it's started. Watch for it."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He went over it all that evening on the wall, alone, with the binder shut on his knees because it was too dark to read and he did not need to read it.

The trouble was not the lattice. He had expected the lattice, in some shape, since the afternoon she had walked Edran into a drawing of a ring. The trouble was where the lattice sat.

His framework had a seam, and he had known it since Ardenmere. When the Wind-adjacent read put a strike into his head a half-beat before it arrived, it gave him the strike and nothing else, not which way to go, so that he had to choose a direction before he could move in it. In the tiny space between choosing and moving he was nobody, neither here nor there, committed to a turn he had not finished. Against most fighters it did not matter, because most fighters gave him one strike at a time and one choice to make. Against Reydan it had mattered: Reydan had found the seam in the third exchange and leaned on it, and it had nearly been the end of everything, but the seam had been a door Reydan had to find.

Karis did not need to find it. Her lattice sat on top of it the whole time. Every point she laid was a small promise of a line that might run from it, every line was a direction he could not go, and every step he took inside a lattice was a choice about which way to turn with a dozen small threats standing in every direction at once. Reydan had made him choose once, hard. Karis would make him choose all the time, a little, until the choosing itself was what wore him down.

The seam was a door, and against her it would be standing open on every side.

He stayed out in the cold with that, and then he went in and found Lira in the corridor outside her room, with her coat off and a towel round her neck from the pump.

"I need you," he said. "Every night until the sitting. I need you to be a lattice."

Lira held the towel in both hands and looked at him, and her face did the slow thing it did when she had been waiting to be asked for something and was too proud to be glad about it in front of him, and was glad anyway.

"Chalk," she said. "And a sack of something to throw. I'll find the sack. You find the chalk." She went into her room and turned in the doorway. "And Cael. You'll hate it."

"I know."

"No," said Lira. "You don't. But you will."

Chapter 34 — Pick Faster

[Taut, spatially clear narration; build the directed match without sacrificing comprehension]

The sack turned out to be Brom's.

Lira had gone to the kitchen and come back with a flour sack and a bag of dried peas the cook had given her for reasons nobody ever learned. Brom took one look at them on the stable table, sighed, and went to his room for his leather needle and the waxed thread he kept for boots. By the sixth bell on the first night there were a dozen small heavy bags on the table, each the size of a fist, each sewn shut along two sides with stitches so small and even that Lira picked one up and turned it over and looked at Brom with real suspicion.

"Where did you learn that?"

"Velmere," said Brom. "Boots are expensive. Feet aren't."

They took them out at dusk to the training yard, the open square of packed earth below the wall where nobody went after the sixth bell in winter because there was nothing out there but frost and a pump. Lira drew a ring on the earth with a stick of chalk the size of her thumb, eight paces across, the size of a formal ring. Then she stood in the middle of it with the chalk in one hand and a bag in the other and explained the rules as if she were reading them off a board.

"I'm her," she said. "I'm also her floor. When I say point, I draw a circle." She drew one by her foot. "That's a point. It's lit. You don't stand in it. Every time I say point, there's one more, and the ring gets smaller."

"And the bags?"

"The bags are channels." She tossed one to Brom, who caught it without looking. "Brom throws them. Flat, along the ground, from one circle toward another, whenever he likes and without telling anybody. If a bag touches you, you've crossed a channel, and I count it out loud, and I don't feel sorry." She looked at him. "And I'm also me. I'll be pressing you the whole time. Making you turn. Because she won't just stand there laying coins and waiting for you to trip. She'll be making you choose."

"She never touched Hobb."

"She didn't need to touch Hobb. Hobb was walking forward. You won't be." Lira set her feet. "Framework. Panel speed is for panels. Go."

It was the worst hour of practice he had ever had, and it was not close.

She came at him from the first breath. She did not strike, not really, but she moved as if she would, short sharp feints off the front foot that made the framework wake and read and want to slip. Every time it slipped him she said point and bent and drew a circle on the earth where he had been about to go. Within a few minutes there were six, and the ring that had been eight paces across was full of small chalk mouths. Every step he took had to find the space between them, and every slip the framework offered him had to be checked against the floor before he could take it.

Then the first bag came, low and flat along the frozen earth from Brom's hand at the edge of the ring, skidding from one circle toward another, and Cael never saw it because he was looking at Lira. It caught him on the ankle with a soft heavy thump and fell over.

"One," said Lira.

The second caught him on the shin while he was choosing between two gaps. The third he saw, and jumped, and landed in a circle.

"Three. And that was a point, so four. You stood in her fire."

He did not argue; he set his feet again.

By the end of the hour she had drawn sixteen circles and Brom had thrown more bags than Cael could count, and eleven of them had touched him. He stood in the middle of a ring that had become a forest of chalk, breathing in hard white clouds, his ankles sore and his legs gone heavy in a way the framework never made them, and understood what Lira had meant.

"Eleven," said Lira, who was breathing hard too, and bent with her hands on her knees. "That's your number. Tomorrow we beat it."

"Was that what it'll be like?"

"No," said Lira, straightening. "She's better than me at this, and she won't be throwing peas."
