"The third exchange," she said. "I won't ask. I have my ideas. They can stay in my head. I'll not write them down, and I'll not ask you to put anything into words, because once a thing is written or spoken I can't shelter it any longer. Then it's evidence." She left that there a moment. "What I need to know — not for the file, for me — is whether you can not do it. In front of people who wish you harm."

The question dropped through him and went on dropping, like a stone down a well that turned out far deeper than he had thought.

He made himself stand and look at it instead of reaching past it for something easier, because it deserved that much. In the third exchange, had there been an instant when not doing it was there for the taking? He went back over that half-second as honestly as he could: the fourth channel forming, his angles gone, time spreading wide. He had stopped running. He had been awake for it. He had chosen it, and he was almost certain of that.

But almost was bearing more weight than it was built for. There was a choice, and there was the kind of reflex that looks like a choice when you remember it afterward, and the whole of Quenna's question lived in the gap between those two, and he could not tell her which side he had been on. He had one reach to go by, under conditions that had arranged themselves round him as neatly as if someone had drawn them up, and no sane person would make a promise on a sample of one.

He wanted to tell her yes, because yes would let her sleep, and yes would keep the record clean. But she had earned the truth, and lying to Quenna would be a worse sort of mistake than lying to nearly anyone else, so he gave her the truth.

"I don't know yet."

She kept her eyes on him while the answer went in. It was not approval that came into her face. It was something harder and plainer than that: the respect of someone who would always choose an honest problem over a comfortable lie put on file.

"Find out before the Compact does," said Quenna.

That was the end of it. She turned the record back toward herself, laid it in a folder, and tied the tape. He took the sentence down the narrow stair with him, and he was still carrying it at supper.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

All that day, under everything else, the new one was there.

He left it alone, as he had promised Lira and written down that he would. But leaving it alone did nothing to stop him knowing where it was.

It was not like the others, and he kept coming back to that without ever finding the bottom of it. The four he had carried longest lay in him like a craftsman's tools rolled in their cloth, each one separate and silent until wanted, and each so much his own by now that he could no longer feel the seam where it had been joined to him. The fifth was nothing but seam. It sat warm, not hot, doing nothing that any instrument on any panel's table would ever have registered: only a faint, even warmth, like a stone in a sunny wall still giving back the afternoon after the sun has gone.

And in the warmth there was something he knew, from six weeks spent learning it: exactness, patience, small promises kept to the letter. It had come to him partial and rough, its edges torn by the clumsiness of his taking, and still there was no mistaking whose it had been. A page of someone's writing holds their whole hand. This held her. It felt like her.

Late in the afternoon he sat at the desk by the window with the bad arm in his lap, and for the first time he let himself look at that.

He had carried the oldest of the four since Ardenmere and never once noticed a person in any of them. Or he had never let himself notice. He did now. He turned toward the Wind-adjacent with great care, not reaching for it, only paying attention. It was there, and it had been there all along: a quickness that had never been his, a habit of leaving early off the back foot, a stubbornness in the turn. Lira. Lira in a freezing yard in Ardenmere, teaching a boy to stay alive because a boy who did not learn would not see the month out. Under the read lay Brom's patience. Under the redirect lay a weight he had met once across a chalk line, from a Bronze fighter who had beaten him fair. And low in his chest, under the Compression, was a ferocity that had once faced him in front of six hundred people and very nearly finished him.

All this time he had been carrying his people with him. Not as the saying meant it. As the words meant it, taken at their word.

He had no idea what to do with that, and he did not write it down; he sat with it until the window went dark. Then he went down to supper, where Karis's place at the far end of the scarred table stood empty, and Lira had put a heel of bread on it anyway.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Lira was on the wall after supper, and he went out to her, because it was the first night she had not been in a room with other people since the yard.

She did not say anything when he sat down. She had her knees drawn up and her coat round her, as always, and she was looking out at the black training yard where the chalk ring from the drills still showed faintly pale under the frost. He waited. He had learned long ago that the things Lira most needed to say came last, after a long silence, and that the silence was part of the saying.

"When you crossed," she said at last, "I counted."

He did not answer.

"I watched you go through her fire with your arm down, and I counted, and you were through before I got to two and reaching for her. Then on the walk back I counted three, the way I counted six on Brom's floor, and you weren't taking any of them, and I couldn't breathe till you did." She did not look at him. "I knew what you were going to do before you did it. I saw you look at the short one. I knew you'd chosen it. I'd read it upside down off Brom's floor, the thing about choosing a burn. I stood at that rail and watched you choose it and couldn't do anything at all."

"I'm sorry."

"Don't be. You told me before. That's the rule, and you kept it." She was quiet a moment. "I'm only telling you what it was like on my side of the rail. You never get to see that part. You're always in the ring."

The cold came up through the stone into them both.

"And when you went down on one knee in the third," said Lira, "I thought you'd fallen. I thought she'd finished it and your legs had gone. I had both hands on the rail and I'd decided I was going over it, Quenna or no Quenna." Her voice changed, very slightly. "And then there was a light under your hand. And she stopped. And she laughed."

"You saw the light."

"I was looking at your hand. I'm always looking at your hand." She turned her head then and looked at him in the dark. "I told you on this wall, twice, not to make her the stakes. I've been sitting here working out whether you did."

He waited.

"You didn't." Lira looked back at the yard. "Nobody made her anything. She walked out there and made herself into it, in writing, with a line under it. And you went in to fight her. I watched you. You weren't looking for anything in the first two exchanges. You were losing, and you were fighting, and you crossed fire to stand closer to her because it was the only way left to try to beat her." She drew a long breath and let it out white. "Whatever happened in the third, it happened to somebody who was busy. That's the only version of it I could ever have lived with. It's the one I got."

"Karis told me the same thing. In the archive. Fight me."

"Did she." Lira almost smiled. "Then we worked it out separately, the two of us. Without clauses. I think that's the first time she's ever arrived anywhere without writing it down first."

They sat on after that, until the cold had come right through his coat and into the burn, and the burn had begun to ache in the slow dull way that he knew meant it was starting to mend.

"The first day after," said Lira. "You told her. All of it."

"All of it."

"Good." She stood up off the wall and shook out her coat. "Then I'm not holding anything with you any more that she doesn't know. That's a weight off." She looked down at him. "It's lighter than I thought it'd be. Isn't that strange. I thought I'd miss it."

She went in. He stayed on the wall a while longer with his arm against his chest, and he was not afraid of anything that night; he was only tired, all the way through, as a field is tired after harvest.

Chapter 38 — Inside

[Taut, spatially clear narration; build the directed match without sacrificing comprehension]

Karis woke on the Friday with warm hands, and the first thing she did, before she had sat up or looked at the window, was check whether she was still all there.

She held her left hand out over the blanket, palm up, close above her face, and her off hand, the right, went still at her side. She counted it without meaning to, the way she had counted it since she was fourteen: a quarter of a second, near enough, a hair less than at the end of yesterday. Then a point bloomed over her palm, small and dim and steady, a coin of light the size of a thumbnail, and its warmth reached her skin.

It was exactly as it had always been.

She held it to a count of twenty and let it go, and watched its third of a breath of shimmer hang over the blanket and fade. Then she laid another, and joined the two along the bedpost with a thin singing line, and let that go too, and lay back on the pillow and looked at the ceiling.

Nothing was missing. Nothing in her had been taken away.

She had known that, really, since the yard. She had felt nothing leave her in the third exchange; she had felt something answer her, which was not the same. But she had wanted to check it in the morning, cold, with her own hands, before she let herself believe it. Whatever he had done, it was not theft; her Path was exactly the size it had been on Wednesday, and it had not been divided. It had been, she thought, carefully, trying the word in her head and not yet trusting it, copied. No. That was not right either. She did not have the word yet.

She got up and washed and dressed and sat down at the little table by her window with both notebooks, because that was what she did with mornings.

The first notebook was easy.

She wrote the match into it as she would have written any bout: the conditions, the panel, the three exchanges, her point counts in each, the time she held them through the resets, the sustain cost that had come due afterward in her fingertips and gone by morning. She wrote that the candidate had read her near points before they lit, and that she had moved her floor outward in the second exchange to answer it. She wrote that he had crossed a channel, the shortest one, and that she had not believed he would. She wrote that her fourth channel's last point had failed to take, because the place she had laid it was already burning, and that the assembly had lost its sequence. She wrote, because it was true and hers to record, that she had been holding every lit channel on that count, and that when the count broke she had lost her hold on all of them at once, and they had gone out.

Then she stopped, with her pen over the page, at the next line.

She did not write by what. Clause five of the first terms forbade it, and clause two of the second, in Brom's square capitals, forbade it twice over; she had agreed to both and written one of them herself, and she would not have written it anyway. There were things she did not put on paper because a rule said she must not, and there were things she did not put on paper because she would not, and since yesterday this was both.

She closed the first notebook.

The ledger was harder. It was the ledger of the nulls, twenty-two sessions in her small upright hand with the ruled line under them and the sentence about the missing condition. It recorded conditions and results and nothing else, and a match was not a session; it had not been run in the quiet room, or under her consent spoken aloud, or by any rule she had written. But it had been the twenty-third time she had stood in front of him while he watched, and she could not leave the ledger without it.

So she wrote it under the barley clause, under everything.

Supplementary. Not a session. Formal yard, fifth sitting, full intensity, under the presiding assessor's conditions. Source: K., Ember Path, Iron Rank Three. Consent: written, filed. Distance: from eight paces to one. Duration: three exchanges. Result, as reported by the subject: a fragment notice. Ember-adjacent. The field reads: acquisition, directed.

She looked at it for a long time, the first entry in the ledger that did not end in null. Her hand did not want to write anything under it, and she let her hand have its way, and closed the ledger.

Then she opened the second notebook, the one that held everything the standard model got wrong. She turned to a clean page, and wrote the date at the top, and did not write anything else for an hour.

She stood at the end of the whitewashed room where she had stood twenty-two times, and laid points.

Single points, pairs, a channel along the end wall, a sustain to a count of sixty: she did not do it to learn anything, but as some people walk, to keep their bodies busy while their minds got on with something else. And somewhere in the second quarter-hour, with nobody at the far end of the room, she laid a point a fraction early.

She knew why. She had always known why.

For three years at Ternhall there had been a second set of points across the paired floor from hers, always a breath behind or a breath ahead, so that every ignition she laid was half of a conversation and the other half was always coming. She had learned to lay early into that. She had come to Greyvane and laid her points on a lean old man's count into nothing at all, and she was still doing it. She corrected it every time and never wrote the correction down. She had decided long ago there was a small amount of data she would rather carry than file.

She stood in the quiet room with her off hand very still and let herself think about the third exchange.

She had been trying. That was the thing he had read aloud from the back of his binder by a shaded lamp, and it was true, and she had known it was true before he had finished the first sentence. She had been trying with everything she had, for the first time since the paired floor. She had come out of her mark mid-argument and laid sixteen and held them through two resets and never let one go. She had spent more of herself in three exchanges than in any bout of her life, because she had wanted very badly to win, and she had wanted to win against him.

And in the third exchange, at the very end, when she had been certain, when the fourth point was going down and the whole drawing was about to light, something had answered her.

It had answered in her own language: not a channel of somebody else's fire, not a counter, not anything she had a column for, but a point. One small, rough, crooked point, laid exactly where hers was going, a breath before hers, so that hers could not take. It was the oldest rule there was, the first rule they taught an Ember child, nothing can set fire where a fire already is. She had shown him that rule herself, on the sixth block, for symmetry. He had said it back to her in the middle of her own sentence, in her own words, with a hand on the frozen ground.

She had not been hurt. She had not been diminished. She had been answered.

She stood very still in the whitewashed room. Through the whole of the long cold night she had expected to feel something she would have to put a name to; she had expected to feel taken from. Robbed, or violated, or at the least strange, with some part of the thing she had drilled since she was eleven now lying inside somebody else, for good, because she had signed a sheet and the sheet had worked.

She did not feel any of that. She had gone looking for it, the way she went looking for a fault in a timing table, carefully and on purpose, and it was not there.

What she felt instead was the thing she had not felt since she had walked out of Ternhall's gate nine days before its term. Across a floor, for the length of one breath, she had not been alone in it.

She let the last point go and sat down on the scrubbed floor with her back against the whitewash and her hands in her lap, as she had sat after the long session in the tenth week, and cried. It did not go on for long, and she had not done it in front of anybody since she was eleven, and she was not in front of anybody now. When it was over she wiped her face on her cuff, and noted, because she noted everything about herself, that she felt considerably better, and that she did not know whether that was a finding.

There was half a dark loaf outside her door when she came back up the stairs at the seventh bell. It had been set on the floor squarely in the middle of the doorway, so that nobody could open the door without seeing it. Beside it was a small stone pot with a lid, still faintly warm to the touch, with a spoon laid across the top. She lifted the lid. Barley.

She stood in the corridor and looked at them.

She knew whose they were. Lira stole bread from everyone in the building and gave most of it away again, and she had never once in Karis's sight given anything to anybody in a way that could be thanked for. Brom did not give barley to people. Brom defended barley to people, at length, with real feeling, and ate it in front of them. A pot of it outside somebody's door was not a gift so much as a statement of position.

Neither of them had knocked or left a note.

Karis carried both inside and sat down at the table by the window and ate all of the bread and most of the barley. Then, because she was who she was, she opened the first notebook at the back and wrote, very small, under the last page of timings: Friday. Bread at the door (L.). Barley at the door (B.). No knock. Her window looked down across the corner of the training yard to the low wall at the end of the residence wing. Late in the evening, when she got up to draw the curtain, there were two shapes sitting on it in the dark, close together, with their knees drawn up. One of them had a coat pulled round her in a way Karis would have known at any distance. The other sat with one arm held against his chest.

She stood at the window with the curtain in her hand and watched them.

They were not doing anything or, as far as she could see, talking, and neither of them moved. She had watched the three of them on that wall from this window on other nights, and she had always noted it, as a fact about the academy. Tonight she did not want to note it. She wanted, quite simply and without any method at all, to be down there on the cold stone with them, not saying anything.

That was new, and she examined it, standing at the window, as carefully as she had examined her own hands that morning.

At Ternhall she had never once wanted to be anywhere she had not already earned. She had been first, and first had a place, and she had sat in it. She had not known until this moment, at a window in a minor academy in the cold, that a person could want a place she had not earned and could not rank for. Nor had she known that the wanting could feel so plain, like being hungry.

One of the shapes on the wall stood up, shook out her coat and went in, and the other stayed. Karis watched him sit there alone with his arm against his chest until the cold must have come right through him. Then she drew the curtain. Watching him any longer without his knowing was a thing she had promised herself on a coach in the autumn that she would never do, and she meant to keep every one of those promises, including the ones nobody else knew she had made.

She did not sleep much. She did not mind.

On the Saturday she wrote the paragraph.

She wrote it the first time at dawn, at the table by the window. It came out as a report, which was the only shape she knew how to make a thing come out. Session subject reports no distress. The finding is anomalous and the source is unable to account for it. It went on like that for half a page. She wrote it the second time at the third bell and it was the other way, all feeling and no shape, so that she could not bear to read it back past the second sentence, and she tore that out too.

The third time she tried to say only what was true and nothing more, and she went slowly. Twice she stopped and went to the window and looked at the yard and came back. Once she wrote a sentence and then scraped it off the paper with her penknife, very carefully, because she did not want a crossing-out on this page, and the ghost of it stayed in the grain of the paper anyway. The source is not distressed by the result. I have no framework that explains that, and I am writing it down as unexplained rather than dressing it in language that would make it look solved. This much I can say plainly. At no point did I feel examined. Since the third exchange I have not once felt like the thing being tested. "I told her she could stop asking properly." Lira went past him to her own door. "She's in. She can be as rude as the rest of us now. I said she'd need practice." At the door she turned. "And I told her about the binder."

He looked at her.

She went in. He stood in the corridor with the soft-cornered page in his hand, and then he went and put it in the back pocket of the binder, with the papers that proved things. It did not prove anything that would ever stand up in front of a panel. He put it there anyway, behind Karis's consent, because the two of them belonged together, and because the back pocket was where he kept the things he meant to have read again when it mattered.

In the morning there were four bowls at the end of the scarred table, and Karis was sitting at the fourth, and nobody said anything about it at all.

Chapter 39 — Three Clean Days

[Taut, spatially clear narration; build the directed match without sacrificing comprehension]

Lira's door had shut and the corridor had gone quiet, and it was late on the Saturday, and the binder lay open on the desk by the narrow window under a lamp he had turned down almost to nothing.

For two days the match had been sending him its bill, and the bill had come in three different hands.

Quenna had written hers in the record's language. Her page would stand only until someone unfriendly watched him do it a second time, and under it sat a question he had no answer to. Whether you can not do it. Karis's had been the stranger and the kinder, for she had spent two days searching herself for a cost, as patiently as she would search a table for a bad figure, and where the cost should have been she had found something she wanted more of. That was dizzying in its own way, because it meant that whatever lived in him did not only take; it joined, the join ran both ways, and none of them had a word for it yet. The third hand was his own and the oldest, the binder's: two misfires, with the date and the hour, a price charged in half-seconds of nothing for a thing he had done without ever being told what it cost.

So he put it in columns, because a frightened mind will lean on a sentence and cannot lean on a column, and he needed something that would not let him lean.

Known. A directed acquisition is possible. Once. Under six weeks of close watching, and then a match where she was trying with everything she had, against me, and I had nothing left.

Known. It costs the others. About a day. Two misfires in the Wind, this time, and then clean.

Known. The panel saw an effect and not how. The record is drafted. It will hold unless I give somebody a reason to open it again.

Unknown. Whether I can not do it, if the same things ever line up again without my wanting them to. In a real fight. Against somebody who means it. In front of exactly the people Quenna is afraid of.

Unknown. Whether the cost grows, and with what. Whether some later one asks for something the older four can't pay.

The last column stayed empty a long while, and when he did write in it, he wrote slowly.

Unknown. What it is for. Whether it's for anything.

Round that line he drew a small box, his own mark for not yet, which he had used before: round the session-nine page at the back, round the line he had copied out of Vell's archive in somebody else's hand, round every door he had found before he had the key to it. He sat back and considered it; for what it held, the box looked very small.

The sentence had been gathering in him since he knelt on the frozen ground of the formal yard. He picked up the pen again and wrote it down plainly, because he knew no other way to hold a thing this big.

I need to understand what I'm actually doing before it gets someone killed.

He read it back, and it was the truest line he had put in the binder since the week of Karis's hypothesis, and it was only half finished; he could feel the rest of it waiting. So he sat with the pen lifted until he could make himself say the rest exactly instead of bravely.

It isn't me I'm afraid for. I can carry my own bill; I've decided that. It's the three people who keep standing close enough to be in the room when I find out what the next one costs.

Some while after the corridor had gone silent, Brom let himself in without knocking and lowered himself onto the floor across from the desk, put his back to the wall, and stretched his legs out in front of him.

He said nothing at first, sitting as he had sat in the Ardenmere market square, the judge of interesting problems settled at his post, with nowhere else to be and nothing that needed saying yet. The lamp sank a knuckle's width while somewhere beneath them the old building ticked and settled.

What he finally talked about was not the misfires, and not Quenna's question, and not the soft-cornered page in the binder's back pocket.

"I said a thing to you once in Ardenmere," said Brom. "That the word for you would end up yours. Not something handed down to you by somebody else." His chin went toward the wet ink on the open page. "You just started choosing."

Cael looked down at the page.

Nothing about it felt like winning, but he had never before put a true number to something heavy, and the honest weight sat easier on him than a vague and comfortable one would have. Thursday had taught him that the reach was there. The two days since had taught him its price, and whose shoulders the price might fall on, and that there was only one way of carrying it he could bear to live inside: the slow way, counting and dating, with no glory in any of it. Taking was something anybody could do. The choosing happened in the ledger.

"It's a heavier word than I expected," Cael told him.

"Most of the good ones are," said Brom. He stayed where he was, on the floor against the wall, until the lamp had burned so low that nothing was left that either of them needed to say.

Nothing glowed.

He had expected a coin of light under his palm, a warmth climbing into his skin as Karis's points warmed the air above her hand, something he could feel gathering and hold for a count before he let it go. There was none of that. There was no gathering at all, and no holding, and no light that he could see through the cracks between his fingers. He took his hand away.

Under it, in the middle of the grey oak, there was a ring of char about the size of a copper coin, black at the centre and brown at its edges. From the centre of the ring a thread of smoke was going up, thin and pale, straight as a plumb line in the still air of the room. As he watched, the black centre showed a bead of yellow, then a small true flame no bigger than a barleycorn. The flame was not dim, not faint, nothing like Karis's patient coins; it was an ordinary small fire, the colour of any candle, and it was eating along the grain of the wood toward the split edge as if it had somewhere to be.

"That's bigger than a thumbnail," said Lira.

Brom put it out. He did it with one scoop of sand, without hurry, as he did everything. Then he pressed the sand down with the flat of the scoop and held it there for a count of five, and when he lifted the scoop there was a grey crust over the char and no smoke at all.

Then the cost came, and it came in a way he had not prepared for, because none of the others had ever sent their bill like this.

It began under his breastbone, a sudden cold drop, the feeling of putting a foot down in the dark for a stair that is not there. He caught his breath on it before he could stop himself. Then the cold ran out from his chest and down his right arm, into the hand that had been on the post, so that by the time he looked at the hand the fingertips had gone pale and faintly grey and the palm was cold through. It was not pain. It was more like being emptied of something he had not known he was full of, all at once and without any warning. And the warmth that had sat in him since Thursday, so faintly and steadily that he had stopped noticing it, was gone. Where it had been there was the old space, the shape he had learned in the quiet room by failing to fill it, and it was cold.

"Cael," said Karis.

He looked up. She had not moved from the end wall, but she was watching his face with all of her attention, as she watched a point in its last third of a breath.

Lira had come round the bucket and taken his right hand between both of hers without asking, and was chafing it hard. She was looking at him and not at the post.

"I know."

"I'd never have known." She kept chafing. "Somebody on a bench would never know. Somebody at a panel would never know. That's the thing I don't like."

Karis came forward then, slowly. She stopped at the post and looked at it, and then at Brom.

Brom lifted the scoop. Karis brushed the grey crust of sand away with two fingers and bent over the ring of char, close, with the absolute attention she gave a timing that did not agree with anything she had written before. She did not touch the black. She held her hand flat above it, a finger's width off, and then laid one fingertip on the oak beside the ring, and then on the ring's brown edge, and took it away.

"That isn't my point," she said.

Nobody answered her. She was not talking to any of them.

"My point is a held heat. I lay it and it's mine, and it stays as long as I hold it, and it dies when I let go. That's the lag you timed, the dying." She straightened. "There's no point here. There was never a point here. You didn't lay anything. There's a fire in the wood, and the wood was keeping it, and it would have gone on keeping it until it ran out of wood." She looked at him, and her face was doing the thing it had done in the formal yard, the researcher arriving first and something else coming up behind her. "It doesn't behave like fire at all. Not like mine. Mine never catches anything unless I make it."

"I don't know yet," said Karis. "Ask me again when I've seen it twice."

He could not do it twice, not at once.

The space was there, but it was empty and cold, and asking it for anything was like asking an empty cup to pour.

She counted aloud, slowly, in her even voice, the numbers going up through the quiet room like a clock with nothing else to do. Before he turned inward at all he fixed it, a thumbnail and not a hair more, as you might decide how much of a loaf to cut before you lift the knife, and he held the size in his mind. On the Wednesday and the Thursday they went back to the quiet room at the sixth bell, and on both days he did nothing but choose sizes.

He came to understand, over those two afternoons, that this was going to be the whole of the work for a long while. It was the same work he had done with every fragment he had ever been handed. Finding out what it could do was the easy part, and could be done in an hour. The work was finding out what he could make it do on purpose, every time, with nobody holding his hand. The Wind framework had taken him the better part of a year in Ardenmere before it would stay at the speed he asked for. He had been at the Thursday session in section four an hour before, as on every Thursday, with Quenna at the chalk and Brom leaning on the post, and the warmth had sat in him through all of it like a coin in a pocket, and he had not spent it. Chapter 41 — The Bench

Lira walked with him as far as the top of the hill and then stopped.

It was a hard bright morning, the frost still white in the shadow of the gate and the town below them sharp in the cold air, every roof and chimney drawn clean against the slope as if somebody had inked it. The road went down from Greyvane's gate in long turns between stone walls, past the draper's and the bakehouse and the street worth walking, to the corner at the bottom where the grey building stood with its board over the door. From up here it looked very small. He had been looking at it from the wall every evening since the autumn and had never once let himself look at it for long.

The town was waking round him, shutters coming open, a cart backing into the bakehouse yard, the draper's boy sweeping the step under the post-counter sign. Somebody was frying onions. It was an ordinary Saturday in an ordinary town, and the closer he came to the corner the more ordinary it was, and none of it helped at all.

The grey building was two storeys of plain dressed stone with a slate roof and a single door, painted dark green and recently. The board over it said Registered Arbiter Station. Certification and Evaluation. in square black letters that somebody had also recently painted. The door stood open. Inside was a short flagged passage with a door at the far end, shut, and along the left-hand wall of the passage, under a window of thick old glass, a wooden bench.

He smelled it from the doorway. Soap, and the wet stone of a floor scrubbed that morning, and under it a smell of lamp oil and paper.

He stood on the step with his good hand on the door frame, and the bench in Denvash came up out of him all at once and stood in the passage in front of the real one, the way a reflection stands in a dark window with the room behind it.

He had sat on the end nearest the far door. He stood on the step of the grey building in a strange town with the soap in his nose and his heart going hard, and he could feel the exact weight of that hand.

Then the far door of the passage opened and a clerk looked out, and the morning was this morning again, and Oona and her mother were sitting on the bench.

"But mostly I'm glad. It was built for you. It was never built for me. You used it the way it's meant to be used, and now you've walked out of it the way it's meant to be walked out of. That's what it's for."

Oona thought about that for several steps.

"You said I could study you," she said. "After. In the second month. You said after my Kindling, if I still wanted to."

"I did."

"I still want to. I'll have to sit on a different bench in the taxonomy lecture now. With the hardening first-years. But I'll still study you." She glanced at her mother. "With permission."

"With permission," said Oona's mother gravely, and did not explain what she meant by it.

Lira was where she had said she would be, sitting on the low wall by the gate with her knees drawn up, and she did not get down when they reached the top of the hill. She looked at Oona, and at her face, and at the card in her fingers that Oona had not put away.

"Well?" said Lira.

"Anchor," said Oona. "Copper. It's ordinary."

Lira looked at her from the wall, with an expression Cael had seen on her face once before, on the morning she had read four paragraphs from Fenmark and decided they did not get to say who she was.

"Ordinary's the best kind," said Lira. "Nobody can take it off you. It's on every chart there is." She slid down off the wall. "Congratulations. You'll want breakfast. Everybody wants breakfast afterward. I'm going to steal you some bread and give you most of it back."

Oona looked at her with something close to alarm.

"She does that," said Cael. "It's the rule."

"I know," said Oona. "I've seen it. I didn't know it was going to be me."

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

On the Tuesday of the eighteenth week Karis asked if she might try two things, and asked it at breakfast, formally, before the porridge, so that everybody at the scarred table could refuse it in front of witnesses if they wanted to.

"Both inside the terms," she said. "Contact only. Brom's post. Lira's buckets. I write nothing." She turned her cup a quarter turn on the table. "I'd only like to know what single channel means. It's in the notice. I'd like to know whether it's true."

Nobody refused, and at the sixth bell they were in the quiet room again with the post in its sand.

The first thing she asked was whether he could light two at once. She did not mean two in a row with the count between; she meant two together, his palm and his fingertips, one ring under the heel of his hand and another under the pads of his fingers, at the same instant. He chose both sizes, and held both in his mind, and turned inward, and asked.

One ring came, under the heel of his hand. Under his fingertips the oak was clean.

He tried it the other way round, fingertips first in his mind, and one ring came under the fingertips and nothing under the heel. He tried it a third time, wanting both equally, holding the two sizes side by side like two coins in one palm. This time he felt the thing in him hesitate for the smallest part of an instant. Then one ring came, under the heel, and the cold came after it as it always did, and not one hair more.

"One," said Karis softly. "Whatever you ask for, it's one." She had knelt by the post to look at the clean wood under where his fingertips had been. "It doesn't divide. It isn't weaker when you ask for two. It simply picks."

"Single channel," said Cael.

"Single channel. The notice was right again. I can lay sixteen. You can lay one. And yet." She did not finish the sentence, and he did not ask her to.

The second thing she asked for was paper. She had brought a sheet from the back of one of her old notebooks, blank, torn along the fold, and she laid it flat over the top of the post and held it there by its corners with her fingertips well clear of the middle.

"Through it," she said. "If you can. Your palm on the paper, the paper on the wood. I'd like to know which one it belongs to."

He laid his palm on the paper and chose the size and asked.

The paper caught. Not the wood under it; the paper. A ring of brown went through the sheet under his palm, and in the middle of it a bead of flame came up and began at once to eat outward across the page, fast, as paper burns. Karis let go of the corners, and Brom put it out with a scoop of sand before it had reached the edge. When they brushed the sand away the oak beneath was barely marked, a faint brown shadow where the heat of the burning paper had warmed it and nothing more.

Karis bent close and looked at the shadow on the oak.

"It belongs to whatever you're touching," she said. "Not to whatever's under that. Not to what you meant." She picked up the scrap of charred paper and turned it over. "That's the spark again. You strike it on the first thing your hand is on, and after that it's the paper's business, or the wood's, or whatever's there."

"Is that a second word?"

"No." Karis folded the burnt scrap in half, and then in half again, and did not throw it away. "It's the same word with more evidence under it. I'll have a better one some day. I can feel it sitting somewhere just past where I can reach it, like a name you've forgotten." She looked up at him. "I'm not going to force it. A wrong word's worse than none. You'd carry it about for years thinking it was true."

Lira, at the bucket of water, had said nothing through all of it. Now she looked at the scrap in Karis's fingers.

"You're keeping that," she said.

"I'm not writing anything," said Karis. "That's the term. It doesn't say I can't keep a piece of paper." She tucked it into her coat. "It's the first thing he's ever lit that I gave him. I'd like to have it."

He wrote the session in the binder that evening, reading it aloud to her as he wrote, as he had promised.

Tuesday, week eighteen. Asked for two at once, three ways. Always one. It doesn't split and it doesn't weaken; it picks. Single channel. Then through a sheet of K.'s paper laid on the post: the paper burned, not the wood. It belongs to whatever my hand is on. Count between, ninety-four. K. kept the paper.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

At the regional registry office, on the Wednesday after the girl came back up the hill, a clerk with a cold that had not gone away since the autumn entered one line in a book under the heading for Greyvane Academy. The notation sheet had come down from the town station by the station's own courier on the Monday.

Kindling assessment entered. Candidate formerly enrolled under demonstration provision. Classification: Anchor Path, Copper. Category of enrollment vacated; standard enrollment to follow.

That night the line went into the long index with all the others and was run against every standing file, as every line always was, and it matched nothing. But it was copied, the next morning, onto the short daily sheet that went to the officer who had asked to see anything the registry received about that academy, because he had asked, a fortnight before, for exactly that. It reached Coss at his borrowed desk on the second floor at a little after the third bell, between a bound volume of enforcement digests and a sheaf of drafting records tied with faded tape, and he read it.

He had been working on the packet at the regional office since the autumn, longer than he had ever spent on any challenge.

The briefing had taken one afternoon. Everything after it had taken the season, and he had known that it would, and had not minded. A challenge to a chartered academy's enrollment was not a request for papers. It went before a magistrate in public and into the permanent registry, and every line of it would be read aloud by people who wanted it to be wrong. So every line had to stand on something that could be produced in a room and handed across a table. He had spent the season finding those somethings, one at a time, from offices that kept their papers in the order that suited them and not in the order that suited him.

The plain-face argument had been sound from the first night, at the waystation table, with its two true lines. A category whose gloss kept it, word for word, for a candidate who has not yet undergone formal Kindling assessment. A respondent who had undergone it, at the station in Denvash, on a date the registry held. That much he could have filed from his district office. But a tribunal did not like to be told that a provision meant what its plainest sentence said, if another sentence of the same provision said something wider; it liked to be shown. So he had gone looking for what the provision had been written to do.

The drafting records had been in three places, none of them where the index said. He had found them at last in a basement room under the regional chamber, in a box marked for a different provision entirely, and he had read them in an afternoon by a window that let in more cold than light. The demonstration provision had been written long ago, and it had been written as a kindness. The guilds in those days had sent their families travelling, carters and drovers and pedlars with a guild licence, and their children came to fourteen on the road, a month from any station, and arrived at the gates of the academies untested and unplaced. A chartered academy could not take an untested child. The provision let it, under watching, until the child could be brought to a station and found out. That was all it was for. It had been amended three times since, and every amendment had widened who it covered by a little and narrowed what it was for by not at all.

He had sat with that in the cold basement room. He had thought it was a decent law. He thought so still.

Then he had found the precedents, which had been easier, because the enforcement digests were indexed by people who expected to be asked. Three times in other districts, across the long life of the provision, somebody had tried to stretch it over a person it had not been written for. Once it had been a youth past the age of Kindling who had refused to be tested. Once it had been a disputed assessment the family would not accept. Once it had been a clerk's honest mistake, never caught until it was challenged. Three academies, three enrollments, three challenges. Each enrollment had been voided. None had survived the hearing, and one had not survived to a hearing at all. He had read each digest twice and copied the citations onto a clean sheet in his small plain hand.

And now this line, on the short daily sheet, from the academy at the top of the hill.

Candidate formerly enrolled under demonstration provision. A child, then, a real one, of the kind the drafters had meant. A child who had come to Greyvane untested and sat under watching and gone down to the station at fourteen and been found to be something ordinary on every chart there was, and moved out of the category by the plainest procedure there was, as the provision had been built to do. Coss read the line a second time and thought that if he had been asked to invent an exhibit to show a tribunal what the provision was for, he could not have invented a better one. The academy had sent it to him itself, on the third-day post, because the procedure said it must.

He did not take any satisfaction in it. He noted it. That was different.

The roll of the observer track at Greyvane, after this line, held one name.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

"You're sure you want to go up yourself?"

The senior officer who had briefed him in the autumn asked it from the doorway of the borrowed room at the end of the afternoon, with his coat already on. He was a heavy, courteous man near the end of a long career, who signed whatever was put in front of him after reading every word of it, and Coss had come over the season to like him a good deal.

"I'm sure," said Coss.

"The standard procedure is service by the regional channel. A sealed packet to the provost by courier, a copy to the magistrate's office, the date set from there." The senior officer looked at the packet on the desk, which was now as thick as a hand and tied in two directions. "It's a good packet. I've read it. It will stand up by itself. You don't need to walk it up a hill."

"No," said Coss. "I don't need to."

He did not try to explain the rest, because the rest did not fit on a form, and the senior officer had been in the service long enough to know that a man who said I don't need to in that voice was not finished. A packet sent by courier was read first by a provost alone at his desk, and then explained to its subject secondhand, by people who loved him and were frightened for him and would explain it in their own words. Secondhand bred errors. Errors bred appeals. And under that, where he did not need to look at it for long, there was a borrowed office in Ardenmere and a boy with his hands pressed white on his knees saying Thank you. Coss had stamped a summons closed-pending that afternoon with more force than a stamp required. He did not intend to do this one at the end of a courier's arm.

"The subject attends a proceeding on his own status by right," he said instead, which was true and fitted on a form. "I'd prefer he hear it from the officer who drafted it, in the room, with the provost present. It saves a step later."

The senior officer looked at him a while.

"I'll sign it," he said. "Put the request in tonight."

He put it in that night, in the flat language the form demanded, and it came back approved by the middle of the next morning. That was faster than the senior officer could have signed it and sent it up and had it back, and so it had not gone through the senior officer at all. It had gone to the same desk as before, somewhere above, where somebody had been waiting. The registry returned the challenge packet to him stamped for service. On its cover sheet the last field before the seal was the one he had stopped expecting to read: the short ruled bar, as neat as a line drawn under a sum, and the small type beneath it. Field restricted. Recipient clearance insufficient. He tied the packet up again in both directions and left it tied.

The credential came the same day, from a different window. It was a small card, stamped, plainly printed, his name and his grade and the seal of the Compact's field service, the sort of card that did not need to be large because the people it was shown to had been taught to recognize it. He had carried one for many years and almost never shown it. A Warden was a word a district would accept at its gate without thinking twice. A field agent of the Compact was a word that made a gate think. He had found, over a long career, that the first word got more honest work done than the second, and he had let it.

He would show the card at Greyvane, at the gate and again in the provost's room, because the procedure required that the respondent know what kind of officer was standing in front of him. That, too, he did not mind. He had been honest with the boy every time they had sat across a desk, as honest as the job allowed, and the job now allowed a little more.

An aide was assigned him the same afternoon, a young man two years out of the regional school who could carry cases and copy fair and did not yet know when to stop talking. Coss liked him well enough. He told him they would leave before dawn on the Saturday and reach the academy on the Monday, two days by the coach to the hill town and half a morning on the road up from there. The aide was to bring the bound digests and the drafting records and a great deal of clean paper. He would not need anything to read on the coach, Coss told him, because there would be the file.

That evening he wrote to his daughter, as he did every week, a short letter about nothing: the regional town's bad bread, a chamber bell that rang the hours wrong, the senior officer's coat. He did not mention the case, and never had. At the bottom, after he had signed it, he sat for a moment with the pen over the page.

I'm going up into the hills for a few weeks, he added. It's a long road. I'll write from the other end.

He sealed it and put it in the evening bag. Then he went back to the borrowed desk and untied the challenge packet after all, and read it again from the first page, slowly, as if he had never seen the subject's name before.

The seal was new to the gate clerk, and her face could not settle on what to do about it.

It was the middle of the morning on the Monday of the nineteenth week, between the second bell and the third, and the yard was full of the ordinary traffic of a school between lectures. Students crossed with books under their arms and kit over their shoulders, a cart of flour sacks was being checked in at the kitchen gate, and a second-year was being shouted at by somebody for leaving a door open. Cael was sitting on the low step of the lecture wing with the observation notebook on his knee, halfway down a page about Edran's off arm. He had watched the third structure come up whole four times in five that morning at the high windows, and he was trying to write down why, when something at the gate pulled his eyes off the page as a wrong note pulls a listener's head round.

There were two travellers at the clerk's booth. One was young, with a satchel on each shoulder and a case in each hand, standing the half-step back that an aide stands from the person he carries for. The other was older, in plain travelling clothes the colour of the road, and he was holding out a small stamped seal on a card, and waiting.

The clerk had it in her inky fingers and was turning it over. She looked at it much longer than she looked at anything that came through her booth, and Cael watched her look and knew what the look was. It was the look of somebody checking a thing against her memory and finding nowhere in her memory to put it. She said something. The older man answered, patiently, and took a second paper from a document case under his arm, folded once: a careful traveller's spare proof. The clerk read it, and put her finger on her list, and found something on the list, and the gate opened as it opened for anybody the list expected.

The second paper he never needed to see.

He had sat across a borrowed desk from that patience once, in Ardenmere, with his hands pressed together on his knees and a paper of his own that he had found in a district archive in two days. He had learned its shape that afternoon without meaning to: a man who wrote everything down and never seemed to hurry, and never once, in the whole afternoon, wrote anything that was not so. The shape was older now, and more travelled, and there was more grey in it. It was built the same way underneath.

He watched Coss cross the yard.

That was the part he would turn over afterward and never get to the bottom of. He did not stand, or call out, or move at all. He sat on the step with the open notebook on his knee and the pen loose in his fingers, and watched the man who had carried his file since Denvash cross the middle of everything Cael had made for himself at Greyvane. Coss walked it at the unhurried pace of somebody whose authority was so complete that it never needed showing. He did not look round the yard. He did not have to. Somewhere in that document case, Cael knew with a certainty that went cold all the way to the bottom, the next thing was already written down with his name at the top of it, and had been written long before the clerk turned her key.

Coss and the aide went in at the door of the old building, the one that led to the worn stair.

Cael looked down at the notebook. He had written third structure, four in five, whole and then nothing. He did not write anything else. Whatever had just happened was real already; the notebook could add nothing to it.

Naveth's runner found him in the archive twenty minutes later.

He had gone there because he could not think of anywhere else to go, and because Prynn had been in the middle of explaining to him, the evening before, the way she numbered the slips she left in place of a pulled volume, and he had asked her to finish. He had asked only so that his hands would have something to do. She had seen that at once, and finished anyway, in more detail than the subject strictly needed, and he had been grateful.

The runner was a first-year with a cold nose who put his head round the iron-banded door and said, all in one breath, "Provost wants you in his office. Now, he says, not after," and was gone again before Cael was fully on his feet.

Prynn looked at him over her spectacles from the high stool.

"Whatever it is," she said, "the shelves will still be here."

No other comfort was to be had in that archive. She had meant it that way, and he knew it going out. It did more work in him on the way up the stair than it had any right to.

The walk took four minutes, and he spent every one of them counting, because counting was easier than looking at the one thing he was not ready to look at. Fourteen students crossing the yard. Three crows along the kitchen ridge. His boots loud on the flags and then quiet on the trodden earth, and the wind cold on one cheek. He had rehearsed this day since Denvash in more versions than he could number, and in every one of them it had come as a knock: a courier on Hesk's front step on the second morning, one knock, a polite wait, a satchel. In none of them had it come as a patient man in road-coloured clothes holding up a seal at a gate, and the gate swinging open for him because nothing about him was wrong.

That was the lesson about the machine he seemed to need teaching over and over. It did not kick doors in. It never had to. Whoever had hung every door he had ever sheltered behind had hung it with the machine's leave.

The provost's door was open.

He saw it from the bottom of the last flight, the worn stair dipping at the centre of every step under his boots, and he slowed on the landing. Naveth shut his door on the conversations he meant to keep and left it wide on the ones he did not mind anybody hearing, and Cael had learned in the fourth week what a wide door meant in this building. A shut door meant something private. A wide one meant a procedure, with nothing in it the room was ashamed of. And Quenna had taught him, across a dozen sittings and without once putting it into words, that you fought a procedure differently from a secret.

He stopped on the threshold for the length of a breath. Over the visitor's shoulder Quenna looked straight at him, and there was no comfort in her face at all, only an order as plain as chalk: say little, hear everything. He had been taking that look across a panel table since the first sitting.

He went in.

"...which is why I'd rather the provost heard it from me than from the regional channel." Then he stood, as a courtesy, and looked at Cael, and sat down again.

The category's own gloss reserves it for a candidate who has not yet undergone formal Kindling assessment. You were assessed, at the station in Denvash. Naveth did not move his hands, and Cael, watching him, saw nothing at all on the long face, and understood that this was the most he had ever seen it hide.

He had watched Naveth slow a records request to the last legal hour, one requisition slip at a time. He paused, and chose the next word. "Nobody had been inventive enough. This won't be a hearing about forty years. It'll be a hearing about a single student."

The room went still round the packet on the blotter, and when Cael looked at Quenna he saw only the blank, careful face of somebody deciding which of several things to do would actually help.

She went back up the stair, and he went on down it alone, one hand on the cold wall.

Coss had meant every word, and that was what Cael kept turning over on the way down, because it was the hardest part to hold. He knew how to be angry at cruelty, since cruelty told you where to aim, but nobody in that office had been cruel. A decent man had climbed a hill so that a boy would hear it from the hand that wrote it. The whole long road from Denvash had needed no cruelty at all; it had only needed people like Coss to be good at their work.

He could not hate that cleanly, and he did not yet know how to fight it either. He stood at the bottom of the stair with both of those, and then he went to find the others, because the rule was the day you knew a thing, and he had known since the gate.

The aide was in the yard when he crossed it, standing at the clerk's booth with a satchel on each shoulder, asking the way down to the draper's in a voice that carried. He saw Cael and stopped in the middle of a word.

He was perhaps nineteen, with a new coat and ink on his cuff, and he plainly had not been told whether he was allowed to speak to the subject. He decided, visibly, that nobody had told him he wasn't.

"He read your file on the coach," he said. "Both days. Every page, and then from the front again. He does that with all of them, they told me at the office, but I thought you'd —" He stopped, and went red to the ears. "I don't know what I thought. He's fair. That's all. Everybody at the office says he's the fairest man on the floor."

"I know," said Cael.

The aide opened his mouth and shut it again, and then the clerk said something sharp from the booth about the draper's, and he turned back to her with both satchels swinging.

Brom was stacking cups, one on top of the next, slowly, and Cael knew from it before he sat down that some of the news had already climbed the stair ahead of him, and that Brom was waiting to have the rest of it given to him properly.

Lira had her boots up on the bench. "All of it," she said. "From the beginning. Not the quick version."

So at the end of the scarred table, under the bricked-up hay door, he gave them the slow version, as plainly as he had ever given them a fragment: the seal at the gate and Naveth's open door; the card, and the word Warden, and what lay under the word; a file kept on him since the day he Kindled; the gloss, and Denvash, and the charter; a magistrate, the assembly room, three weeks. I have never seen it survive.

At field agent Lira lifted both boots off the bench and set them down on the floor together, without hurrying.

She said nothing, but he watched her face go back two years, to a girl being handed nineteen words from Fenmark that had already been used against her before anyone let her read them. It was the face of someone who had learned early how far the machine reached above any office with a door you could knock on.

Karis had left her notebook shut, and both her hands lay flat on the wood.

Brom set another cup on the stack. "Three weeks," he said. "In public. On paper." The next cup went on with great care. "And who speaks for Greyvane?"

"The academy's counsel, I think." Cael rubbed his face with his good hand. "That can wait for tomorrow. Tonight I just wanted you to hear it from me."

"Coss," said Lira.

She said it quietly, in the voice she kept for things she meant to get exactly right on the first try.

"You were fourteen, and he sat down across a table from you. Then he wrote you down in a file, and followed you round the country with it, and waited for you to put a foot wrong." Her eyes came up to his. "And that's his job."

"He meant it."

"Of course he meant it. I can hear that in the way you tell it." She leaned in. "So be angry. Only point it somewhere." One finger came down on the scarred wood between them. Karis lifted her hands off the table at last. She opened the notebook to a clean page and uncapped her pen, slowly, the way a fighter takes a blade down off a rack.

"What do you need?" she said.

"I don't know yet."

"Then I'll begin without you." She was ruling columns already. "A war fought on paper goes to the side with the better index. I've kept indexes since I was eleven."

Brom put the last cup on, seven high, and it did not lean.

And today one man with one card climbs the hill to tell us the paperwork can't hold you." He lifted the whole stack in both hands, as though weighing the argument itself. Lira nearly laughed, and Karis wrote something down, but Cael gave none of them an answer yet, because the real one was still taking shape somewhere under his breastbone, and he was not going to hand them a piece of it until he could see what it would be whole.

Lira was on the wall afterward, and he went out and sat beside her, because there was nowhere else in the building he wanted to be.

The night was clear and very cold. Below them the hill town's lamps were scattered down the slope as they always were, along the street worth walking and the street worth avoiding, and going out one by one as the town went to bed. One of them did not go out. It burned in an upper window above the draper's shop, at the back, a steady small square of yellow, long after the windows round it had gone dark.

"That's him," said Lira.

"The draper told me on Saturday. She's a room over the shop she lets to people's mothers. Oona's mother had it." Lira drew her knees up. "She told me this morning she'd let it again. To a gentleman from the Compact and his clerk, for three weeks, paid in advance." She looked at the lit window. "He's in the mothers' room."

Cael laughed before he could help it, and it came out of him in a way that hurt his chest, and Lira did not laugh, but her shoulder knocked against his, once, the old knock.

She went in. He stayed on the wall until the lamp above the draper's went out, which was a long time, and then he went in too, and lay awake thinking about a case at the back of the archive, floor to ceiling, as deep as an old woman's arm.

Chapter 43 — The Case at the Back

[Dry, controlled narration; let legal pressure tighten through exact language]

The clerk pinned the notice up before the seventh bell, a brass tack in each corner, pressing each one home with her thumb. She did not look round while she did it. She knew he was standing behind her, because everybody in the main hall knew where he was standing, and she pressed the last tack in very hard and went back to her desk without meeting his eyes.

Public adjudication. In the matter of the enrollment of the candidate on the unclassified observer track, on challenge filed by the Compact's field service. A magistrate of the Compact presiding. Assembly room, lecture wing. The first day of the twenty-second week, first bell. The record will be public.

He read it through, while a second-year with an armful of practice staves went past behind him and slowed and went on.

On his first morning here his name had gone up on this board as well, on the assessment calendar, and that had been a door somebody built for him to walk through. This was the same board and the same small even hand, but it was not a door. It was a date.

He read the last line again. The record will be public.

Somewhere in that line the fear in him changed into the other thing, which he knew well. It had come in Ardenmere the week Reydan's name went up beside his on the circuit board, and on the morning of the first sitting with Hobb waiting at the chalk. It was what fear turned into when it had been given time and something to lean against. A hearing had rules, and the rules had been written down by somebody, once; and whatever somebody had written down, somebody else could sit and read, slowly, until it showed him how it moved.

He went to the archive, walking faster than he meant to, with the notice still in front of his eyes.

Prynn was not at her high desk; her stool stood empty, her ledger shut, and he stood inside the iron-banded door not knowing what to do with that. Then he saw the lamp at the far end of the long room, moving among the shelves, and went toward it.

She was putting a box back on a high shelf, standing on the little step she kept for it, and she did not turn round.

"The runner talks," she said. "So does the kitchen. Three weeks."

"Three weeks."

She settled the box, came down off the step, and looked at him over her spectacles with the lamp between them. It was the look she gave a request before she decided whether it was worth what it would disturb.

"Where do you keep the Compact's code?" said Cael. "The registry code."

She did not answer at once.

"Not a digest," he said. "Not what the digests say it says. The code itself, the way it was written down."

Something came into Prynn's face that was not surprise. It looked more like somebody hearing a knock she had been expecting for a very long time, at a door she had stopped quite believing anybody would use.

"This way," she said.

She took him past the end of the academy's own records and past the founding stock, to the very back, where the old waystation wall came up out of the floor in blocks of grey stone the size of a man's chest, where a pillar stood out from the wall, and behind the pillar, in a corner the lamp had to be carried into, was a case.

It reached from the flagstones to the ceiling and was as deep as Prynn's arm. Bound volumes stood in it, dark-spined and all alike, row above row, and beside them the amendments were filed in thin paper fascicles tied with faded tape, so many that the ends of the tapes hung down like roots. The spines had their names in worn gilt. Charter. Schedule of Recognized Paths and Standings. Obligations of Practitioners. Enforcement.

He knew those words, because he had lived inside them since Denvash as a fish lives inside a river, and he had never seen them in ink.

The old stir came up in him under the fear, the one he was half ashamed of, the one he had felt at the rail of the training hall in the second week looking down at eleven Paths he did not know. Appetite. Everything Coss had brought up the hill in his document case grew out of the books on these shelves, and they were within reach of his hand.

"I'll tell you three things about it," said Prynn, "and then you can do as you like." She held the lamp higher. "It's long, and it's drier than anything else I keep. I've caught it disagreeing with itself four times, and there's never been a soul down here to tell." She paused. "And I don't believe one person who enforces it has read it from end to end in my lifetime. They read the part that lets them do what they came to do. Then they stop."

Cael looked at the case.

"The last one," he said. "That's the best thing anybody's said to me today."

"It usually is." Prynn's hand went into the case without her eyes following it, and came out with the first volume, which she laid in his arms. It was heavy and cold, and it smelled of old glue. "The table's where it's always been. I lock up at the eighth bell. You know what that's worth."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The whole academy was a degree too warm for two days after that, the way a house is warm with somebody ill upstairs.

He felt it everywhere he went. In the stable at meals the talk came in two volumes now, the ordinary one and a lower one that followed him from the hatch to the scarred table and stopped when he sat down. In the lecture wing an instructor lost the end of his own sentence when Cael came in late, and the whole room performed not turning round. In the main hall the notice had been read so many times by the second afternoon that its corners had gone soft as cloth. There were something over two hundred students at Greyvane, and by his own careful count every one of them knew that in three weeks a magistrate of the Compact would sit in their assembly room and rule on whether the observer could stay. A few were sorry for him, and showed it; others stared with the interest people give to a house that has had its roof blown off in the night. And some, more of them than he would have expected, and he counted them honestly, had started giving him a small firm nod as they passed, the nod people give to somebody whose side they have privately chosen.

He spent both nights in the archive.

Prynn did not lock the door either night; he did not mention it, and neither did she. On the first night she came down off her stool at the eighth bell and put a cup of tea at his elbow and went back up, and on the second she did not come down at all, and the cup was there anyway when he looked up from the page, though he had not heard her bring it.

He read the enforcement provisions first, because that was where the teeth were, and the teeth were what Coss would use. He read them as he had learned to read a fighter's declaration timing, not for what any single clause did but for how all of them moved, and he copied their shapes into the observation notebook as he went, one structure under another. They were dense and old and cross-referenced to death, and they were full of words like voidance and sanction and removal that he had never seen written down before, though he had lived inside every one of them. By the middle of the first night his eyes ached and he had nine pages of nothing.

Past midnight on the second night, the code showed him its joint.

It did not arrive as an idea, and it never had, for him, with a fighter or with anything else. It came by piling up: hour after hour of reading with the lamp hissing low and the cold rising out of the flagstones under the table, until the same small thing had happened in front of him so many times that he could no longer pretend it was not there. He checked it until the letters swam, chapter by chapter, and it held: there was not one power in the whole of enforcement that came in any shape but this. Authority over classified practitioners. Sanctions proportionate to classification and standing. Procedures that came into force upon classification. Powers exercised according to classification. He had read the word four hundred times in two nights. It carried weight in every sentence it was in. The whole of the Compact's reach rested on it like a roof on a single beam.

And nowhere in the enforcement chapters did the code say what the word meant.

He sat back in the cold and looked at that for a long time.

It was not proof of anything. It might be nothing at all; it might only be that the word was defined somewhere else, in some chapter he had not reached, in a clause so plain and so obvious that no drafter of enforcement had ever needed to look at it again. Codes did that, he supposed, and so did fighters. A fighter who had built a whole style on one strong leg never thought about the leg. But a fighter who had built a whole style on one strong leg had built it on one leg, and if somebody ever looked at the leg properly, the whole style was standing on whatever they found.

He told nobody that night. He wanted to have tried hard to prove himself wrong before he allowed himself to be right. He spent what was left of the second night at it, going back through the enforcement chapters looking for a single power granted in any other shape, one sanction that did not lean on the word, one procedure that came into force on anything else. He did not find one.

At the bottom of the ninth page he wrote: Every power they have attaches to the classified. Every one. The word carries all of it. Where does the code say what the word is?

He drew the small box round the last line.

Oona was waiting for him outside the stable on the Tuesday evening, between the two nights, with a new tag on the string round her neck.

He saw it before he saw her face. The hollow circle was gone, and in its place hung the academy's ordinary crest, a tower above a road, the same tag Brom wore, cut from the same tin by the same clerk. She had polished it. It caught the light from the stable door.

Wray stopped him at the rail of the defensive floor early the next morning, on his way to the provost's stair, with her slate on her hip and her brown coat buttoned to the throat. She did not waste anything on a greeting.

"They'll read my lines aloud," she said. "At the hearing. Every sitting I've sat in. The Warden's had the first of them since the autumn, and he'll stand up and read them into the record in front of a magistrate and two hundred people."

He did not know what to say. Wray did not seem to need him to say anything.

"That's all," she said. "It isn't advice. I've given you my advice. It's a fact about my lines." She turned back toward her chalk, and then stopped, and turned half round, and considered him as she considered a strike before she decided whether it had held.

"Whatever you do in that room," she said, "do it the way you fought Edran. Find what it's proudest of, and go there." She went back to her chalk, and called Again to somebody, and did not look back.

There were six of them and five chairs, and Brom stood.

Nobody disagreed, and the clock over the door ticked twice into the quiet before anybody moved.

Quietly, before the hearing. We go to the Compact on our own account and admit the mistake. Cael's standing falls back to what the provision really covers, and it covers nothing. He leaves. Greyvane keeps its charter, and two hundred other students keep their places, most of them clerical errors of one sort or another, which is the only reason any of them are here."

Naveth looked at her, and then down at the blotter, where his long hand lay flat on the challenge.

We made the category fit him because the alternative was a boy with nowhere to go, and I'm not sorry. But the gloss keeps the category for a candidate who has not yet undergone formal Kindling assessment. He has, and the Warden can prove the day. A magistrate doesn't rule on whether I'm sorry. This is the best-drafted paper anybody has ever sent up my stair."

Cael saw what it cost him to say it, because Naveth's whole life was built on one belief, that careful paperwork could shelter the people the registry had priced wrong. Now the registry's own words lay on his blotter, giving the limit of that shelter, and he had known the limit and kept building.

"So did I," said Cael. "In the archive. The first night."

If that costs Greyvane, I'd rather have made my peace with it now than later." He turned to Cael, over his spectacles. "This is your enrollment, not mine to trade. So tell me what you want."

Cael had known since the notice that this question was coming, and he had walked all round it since.

"I thought about running," he said. "It's always there; I could go down the hill tonight and be somewhere smaller by spring, and the file would find me by summer." He looked at Naveth. Brom's eyebrows went up in their slow way, a step at a time, and Karis's pen was in her hand before she seemed to know she had picked it up. Naveth's eyes went narrow, and Cael could almost see counsel's objections being drafted behind them.

He watched Quenna, because Quenna had put her name to him in front of a panel. Nothing moved in her face, but something moved in her shoulders instead: a tightening, the thing a fighter's shoulders do when the bout in front of them turns out not to be the bout they trained for.

"I'll study it the way I study anybody I have to fight. Systems have architecture. Architecture has seams." He shrugged a little.
